2.       At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members to the meeting of the 
Committee and stated that the Committee has already heard the views of the related 
Ministries and some Organisations on the subject 'Cyber Crime – Ramifications, 
Protection and Prevention’. He apprised them that as per the agenda, in the present 
meeting, the Committee will hear the views of two domain experts on the subject, 
namely Dr. Pavan Duggal, Founder & Chairman, Internat ional Commission on 
Cyber Security Law and Shri Trishneet Arora, CEO of TAC Security who have been 
invited to share their views on the subject.  
 (On arrival of witnesses) 
3.       The Chairman welcomed Dr. Pavan Duggal, Founder & Chairman, 
International Commission on Cyber Security Law and Shri Trishneet Arora, CEO of 
TAC Security to the meeting of the Committee and requested them to present their 
views on the subject 'Cyber Crime – Ramifications, Protection and Prevention’.  The 
proceedings of the meeting commenced with the presentation by Dr. Pavan Duggal. 
4.       Dr. Pavan Duggal informed the Committee that cyber crimes has become an 
epidemic and it is thriving due to fear and panic among general public and these 
factors are being misused by cyber crim inals to commit frauds. He made a detailed 
presentation before the Committee and informed the Committee about the best 
practices adopted by major countries in preventing cyber crime which includes 
robust laws & public -private collaboration; harmonized regu lations & focus on 
privacy; comprehensive strategy & cyber hygiene culture; intelligence -driven 
defence & innovation. The Committee was also provided information on cyber 
crime caseloads and convictions; international nature of cybercrime & preventive 
steps; global Treaties and Conventions; international agencies in cybercrime 
prevention; global cybercrime bodies & coalitions; best practices by Indian States 
and Police agencies like cybercrime portals & helplines, cybercrime training & 
capacity building, sp ecialized units & policies, use of advanced 
technology;  limitation of IT Act, 2000 to deal with cyber crime; challenges in 
enforcement & obtaining evidence; role of Government Ministries in preventing 
cyber crimes; etc. 
  

159 
 
5.       To strengthen cybercrime  legislation, he suggested that a dedicated 
comprehensive cybercrime Law is to be formulated to consolidate offences and 
expand definitions for modern crimes like ransomware, DoS (denial of Service), and 
phishing, explicitly criminalize modern cybercrimes and provide graded 
punishments for organized or repeat offenders and mandate cybersecurity audits and 
breach disclosure for companies, with penalties for negligence. He also suggested 
for aligning with global cybercrime frameworks, incorporating provisions  like 
expedited data preservation and cross-border data sharing into Indian laws, ensuring 
crime definitions match global standards for easier cooperation.   Other suggestions 
inter alia  included specialized cybercrime courts; strengthening of data protecti on 
and privacy; need for legislation on misuse of Artificial Intelligence; strengthen 
provisions for courts to award restitution or compensation to cybercrime victims as 
part of sentencing; strengthening of legal & regulatory framework; capacity building 
for law enforcement agencies; public awareness and digital literacy; improving 
cyber hygiene across organizations; etc.  
6.       The next presentation was made by Shri Trishneet Arora, while making his 
presentation he highlighted the financial frauds, Stat e-sponsored cyber threats by 
hostile neighbouring countries; threats to critical infrastructures; technology gaps; 
involvement of multiple ministries and organisations to deal with cyber frauds, cyber 
threats and cyber security; need for comprehensive sing le nodal agency to deal with 
matters related to cyber security; best practices adopted by major countries, like 
creation of cyber security ministry. He suggested there is a need to assess the current 
state of cyber security of nationwide critical infrastru ctures, like, energy, power 
grids, ports, airports, defence system, etc.   He also suggested that only Indian origin 
cyber auditing companies be considered for auditing of national critical 
infrastructures, creation of an organisation to help victims especi ally women who 
become victims of cyber crime, online harassment; nation -wide cyber awareness 
campaign; provision for enforcement of cyber insurance for common citizens in case 
one falls victim to cyber frauds; provision for cyber ambulance facility, etc.  
7.       The Chairman and Members raised some queries and sought clarification 
pertaining to best global practices for victim compensation, responsibility of banks 
in case of financial frauds, need for improvement and changes in existing laws; 
strengthening of infrastructure, sufficient funds; very low conviction rate; children 
becoming victims of cyber crimes, best mechanism to tackle this menace and 
increase conviction, cyber attacks from hostile countries, capacity building of 
personnel of law enforcemen t agencies, cyber army and commandos for cyber 
security, time taken by Indian law enforcement agencies and US agencies to 
investigate cyber crimes, provision of cyber insurance and cyber ambulance, cyber 
threats to power grids, etc.

1.1 Overall Assessment of Demand for Grants (2025-2 6) of the MHA 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1.1 The Committee observes, based on the above-me ntioned information, that the actual 
Budget Estimate (BE) for 2025-26 is lower than the projected BE for 2025-26 across several key 
areas, reflecting a more conservative allocation th an initially anticipated. The total budget has 
been reduced from ₹184,236.94 crores (projected BE 2025-26) to ₹160391.06 crores (actual BE 
2025-26), marking a 12.94% decrease. Within the Cen tral Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), actual 
allocations fall short of projections, with reducti ons observed across the CRPF, NSG, BSF, 
ITBP, CISF, Assam Rifles, and SSB. This indicates a  recalibration of expenditure priorities. 
Similarly, significant downward revisions have been  made to allocations for the Intelligence 
Bureau (IB), NATGRID, Central Police Organizations (CPOs) and Delhi Police. Police 
infrastructure projects, particularly CAPF building  projects, have experienced a substantial 
reduction from ₹6,403.02 crores to ₹4,038.70 crores , which may potentially impact construction 
of new buildings. The Committee notes that such red uctions may adversely affect critical 
schemes under these heads and may slow down moderni zation programs as well as hinder the 
execution of developmental projects, particularly i n border areas. Hence, the Committee 
recommends that the MHA may take up the matter with  the Ministry of Finance to seek 
increased allocations under these heads in alignmen t with their original projections. This will 
ensure that the essential developmental schemes are  not affected due to insufficient funding. The 
Committee hopes that funds may be demanded for various developmental and expansion projects 
at the RE stage depending on the utilization pattern.

nd   Report)

2.1 NATIONAL DISASTER RESPONSE FORCE (NDRF)  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) informed t he Committee that for FY 2025-26, the 
NDRF has been allocated ₹1,922.59 crores against a projected requirement of ₹2,098.63 crores, 
resulting in a shortfall of ₹176.04 crores. The Com mittee notes this gap and hopes it will not 
adversely impact the functioning of the NDRF. It ap preciates the critical role of the NDRF in 
disaster response and emphasizes the need for adequ ate funding to address increasing demands, 
particularly for additional personnel. The Committee recommends that the MHA may take up the 
matter with the Ministry of Finance at the Revised Estimates (RE) stage to secure the remaining 
funds, ensuring that operational efficiency and pre paredness are not compromised during 
emergencies. 
(Para 3.3.10 ibid) 
Action Taken  
2.1.2 NDRF has been allocated an amount of ₹ 1922.5 9 crores against the projected 
requirement of ₹ 2098.63 crores. This has been allo cated based on requirement of NDRF and 
other considerations. In case, additional funds are required by NDRF, the same will be projected 
at RE stage. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1.3 The Committee notes the commendable efforts i n launching the Yuva Aapda Mitra 
Scheme to train young volunteers for disaster respo nse and recognizes its potential to strengthen 
community resilience nationwide. The Committee reco mmends developing standardized training 
modules that comprehensively cover essential disast er response skills, ensuring uniformity and 
effectiveness in community disaster preparedness in cluding local committees, youths and youth 
organisation. Additionally, the Committee emphasize s the need for regular monitoring and 
evaluation of program effectiveness to identify are as for improvement and ensure that the 
approved financial outlay is efficiently allocated to support training and resource procurement. 
Further, the Committee recommends promoting the cre ation of Community Emergency 
Stockpiles to enhance disaster preparedness. 
(Para 3.3.11 ibid) 
Action Taken  
2.1.4 Under the Yuva Aapda Mitra Scheme (YAMS), you ng volunteers from youth organisations- 
NCC (National Cadet Corps), NSS (National Service S cheme), NYKS (Nehru Yuva Kendra 
Sangathan) and BSG (Bharat Scouts & Guides) will un dergo the training based on a 
standardized module (Training Handbook) developed b y the NDRF, covering essential disaster 

36 
 
response skills and techniques. To ensure uniformit y, this training is being implemented 
nationwide using a standardized curriculum based on  geographical region i.e (i) 
Hilly/Mountainous, Semi-Hilly, (ii)Plain, and (iii)Coastal areas. 
2.1.5 For effective implementation of the scheme, t he NDMA has established a Project 
Monitoring Unit (PMU) at the national level. This apart, NDMA officials are conducting regular 
reviews and field visits to ensure the effective implementation and efficient allocation of financial 
resources for training and procurement.  
2.1.6 Yuva Aapda Mitra Scheme is being implemented in the same districts as in the Up-
scaling of Aapda Mitra Scheme (UAMS), where Emergen cy Essential Resource 
Reserves worth ₹20,00,000/- have been provided to all Districts under UAMS. 
2.1.7 Additionally, like UAMS, in YAMS also, each A apda Mitra volunteer is provided with: 
 Insurance coverage for 3 years, and 
 An Emergency Responder Kit worth ₹10,000, containin g essential items to 
support their safety and effectiveness during disaster or crisis situations.  
Recommendation/Observation  
2.1.8 The Committee emphasizes the need for the Min istry to conduct comprehensive research 
to develop a long-term roadmap for disaster resilie nce and adaptation, focusing on future 
requirements for mitigation and preparedness in lig ht of climate change and increasing disaster 
frequency. The Committee urges the Ministry to incr ease investment in disaster-resilient 
infrastructure, including critical facilities such as hospitals, schools and transport networks, to 
minimize the impact of disasters and improve recove ry efforts. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry may include new and emerging disasters  in its disaster management plans, such as 
those caused by heat waves etc. It further recommen ds establishing a formal mechanism for the 
periodic review and update of the Notified Disaster s list to ensure the Act remains relevant and 
responsive to emerging disaster risks through consu ltation with experts, stakeholders and 
affected communities.  
(Para 3.3.12 ibid) 
Action Taken  
2.1.9 Building of Disaster resilient infrastructure  is the responsibility of the respective 
Ministries/ State Governments. NDMA from time-to-ti me issues various guidelines for building 
of infrastructure which can mitigate the effect of disasters and also be resilient. NDMA has 
developed several guidelines and projects which tal ks about strengthening of codes, by-laws and 
infrastructures in vulnerable areas. The major guidelines issued by NDMA are as follows:

 Management of Earthquake (2007)

 Hospital safety (2016) 
 Guidelines on School Safety Policy (2016) 
 Guidelines on Boat Safety (2017) 
 Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019) 
 Home Owner’s guide for Earthquake & Cyclone Safety (2019) 
 A Primer on Rapid Visual Screening (RVS) Consolidat ing Earthquake Safety 
Assessment Efforts in India (2020) 
 Management of Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) (2020)

 National Guidelines on Community-Based Disaster Ris k Reduction (CBDRR)

 National Guidelines on International Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief

2.1.10 Moreover, for promotion of resilient infrast ructure across the world, Coalition for

through the strengthening of DNA and cyber forensic  facilities under the Nirbhaya Fund. It 
recommends the Ministry to continue to invest in mo dernizing forensic infrastructure, focusing 
on advanced technologies to improve analysis effici ency. The Committee suggests the Ministry 
to ensure that all forensic laboratories, both cent ral and State, are equipped with the latest 
equipment and trained personnel to handle complex c ases effectively. It emphasizes the 
importance of maintaining a centralized database of  forensic data to aid in investigations and 
policy-making. Additionally, it suggests that the M inistry to consider establishing more regional 
forensic laboratories to increase accessibility and  reduce the burden on existing facilities. The 
Committee notes that new Criminal Laws mandates for ensic investigation for offences involving 
punishment of 7 years or more. The Committee also n otes that there are very few forensic 
science laboratories. The Committee, therefore, rec ommends that every district of the country 
must have a forensic laboratory to deal with the cr iminal investigation. The Committee is aware 
that criminal investigation is a State subject but given the financial health of the States, the 
Union Government should financially support the est ablishment of forensic laboratories in each 
district of the country. 
(Para  4.14.6  ibid) 

50 
 
Action Taken

infrastructure and equip States/UTs with the latest equipment and trained personnel.

3.1   NATIONAL DISASTER RESPONSE FORCE (NDRF)  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.1.1   Acknowledging that the NDRF is entirely dep endent on deputation from CAPFs and 
currently faces a 21% vacancy rate, while CAPFs themselves are experiencing staffing shortages, 
the Committee recommends the Ministry to conduct a thorough review of the deputation 
policies. The Committee is of the view that the rev iew should assess the impact of the current 
seven-year deputation tenure and explore incentives , such as flexible terms or enhanced 
allowances, to encourage more CAPF personnel to vol unteer for NDRF assignments. 
Streamlining the nomination process and improving c ommunication between NDRF and CAPFs 
are also crucial steps for expediting the filling o f vacancies and ensuring the NDRF's operational 
readiness.    
(Para 3.3.13  ibid)  
Action Taken  
3.1.2   NDRF is a 100% deputationist force. The posts on deputation in NDRF are filled up on 7-
year rotational basis from CAPF’s. It is a dynamic and continuous process. Each NDRF 
Battalions has fully functional team strength at al l points of time. Besides, concerned CAPFs 
HQrs are being requested to fill up the vacancies of NDRF BNs time to time. 
3.1.3  So far as incentives are concerned, it is apprised that recently Govt. of India has approved 
Risk and Hardship allowance @ 40% of R2H2 Cell of R HA matrix to eligible NDRF personnel 
vide MHA DM Division letter dated 18 July 2024. 
Further Recommendation 
3.1.4 The Committee notes the submission that NDRF battalions maintain fully 
functional strength at all times and that CAPFs are  being requested periodically to fill 
vacancies. The Committee also takes cognizance of t he approval of Risk and Hardship 
allowance to NDRF personnel. However, the Committee is of the considered view that these 
measures, though positive, may not sufficiently add ress the structural challenge of 
persistent vacancies arising out of the exclusive r eliance on deputation from CAPFs, which 
themselves face acute shortages. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that a comprehensive 
review of deputation policies is imperative. In add ition to allowances, the Ministry may 
consider measures such as flexible deputation tenur es, streamlined nomination procedures, 
career progression incentives, and exploring a limi ted cadre of permanent staff in critical 
operational and technical roles. This would ensure both the long-term stability of 
manpower and enhanced operational readiness of NDRF. 
  

70 
 
3.2   Cadre Review of CAPFs 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.1  The Committee appreciates the efforts made b y the Ministry in conducting Cadre 
Reviews across various CAPFs to enhance promotional  avenues and improve operational 
efficiency. It notes that while some forces, such a s SSB, CISF, CRPF and ITBP, have benefited 
from recent Cadre Reviews, others, particularly BSF’s Group-B & C (General Duty) Cadre, have 
not been reviewed since its inception in 1965. The Committee emphasizes that Cadre Reviews 
should be undertaken at regular five-year intervals  as their effect diminishes over time. It 
observes that timely Cadre Reviews, as seen in rece nt cases, have significantly contributed to 
better workforce planning, increased job satisfaction and improved operational effectiveness.  
(Para 4.4.7   ibid ) 
Action Taken  
3.2.2  (i) Cadre Review is an important process thr ough which a cadre is upgraded and aligned 
with the changing work environment and requirements  for the next five years. This involves a 
better restructuring of posts, which leads to incre ased promotion opportunities and enhanced 
operational efficiency. 
3.2.3  (ii) Recent Cadre Reviews of some BSF cadres viz. N ursing & Paramedical Cadre, 
Tradesman Cadre, Stenography cadre etc. have clearl y shown positive outcomes providing 
personnel with greater career advancement opportuni ties, improved promotional flow, and 
strengthened capacity of the cadre to perform its duties more effectively. 
3.2.4  (iii)  As needs evolve over time, it becomes  essential to periodically update the structure of 
a cadre. Conducting a Cadre Review every five years  is a progressive step that helps maintain 
the cadre’s vitality and functional strength. 
3.2.5  (iv) The review process for many BSF cadres viz. Gr oup-‘B’ and ‘C’ (General Duty) 
Cadre, Veterinary Cadre, Ministerial Cadre, Water W ing Cadre and Engineering Cadre is 
currently underway with the Ministry of Finance and  all efforts are being made to strengthen 
these cadres further. 
3.2.6 (v) Steps are being taken for fast-tracking t he approval of the Cadre Review of BSF’s 
Group-‘B’ and ‘C’ (General Duty) Cadre, as well as other cadres, which will strengthen their 
overall functionality, resulting in greater benefits for the Force and the Nation. 
Further Recommendation 
3.2.7 The Committee notes the Ministry’s acknowledg ement of the importance of Cadre 
Reviews and the positive outcomes already visible i n certain BSF cadres, as well as the 
assurance that the review process for BSF’s Group-‘ B’ & ‘C’ (General Duty) Cadre and 
other cadres is underway. While appreciating these efforts, the Committee is concerned 
that the delay in completing the Cadre Review of BS F’s Group-‘B’ & ‘C’ (General Duty) 
Cadre, pending since 1965, has deprived a large seg ment of personnel of timely 
promotional avenues, retirement benefits and affect ed morale of the force. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates that Cadre Reviews must be co mpleted in a time-bound manner with 
strict monitoring and accountability mechanisms. Th e Ministry may also consider 

71 
 
institutionalizing an automatic review cycle with c learly defined timelines to ensure 
sustained workforce planning, job satisfaction, and operational effectiveness. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.8   The Committee feels that the MHA along with the Mi nistry of Finance (MoF) may 
expedite the approval of pending Cadre Reviews, par ticularly for BSF, Assam Rifles and any

3.6.2  Sufficient funds are released to executing a gencies for timely completion of all ongoing

3.6.3  Foreign Nationals staying in India without v alid travel documents are treated as illegal 
migrants. Since illegal migrants (including Rohingy a and Bangladeshi illegal migrants) enter 
into the country without valid travel documents in a clandestine and surreptitious manner, data 
of such migrants is not centrally available. Detect ion and deportation of illegal nationality 
verification is a continuous process. Central Gover nment has been vested with power under 
Section 3(2)(e) and 3(2)(c ) of the Foreigners Act,  1946 to restrict movement and deport foreign 

74 
 
nationals staying illegally in the country. Under s ection 5 of The Passport (Entry into India) Act,

who enters India without passport. These powers of the Central Government have also been 
entrusted under Article 258(1) of the constitution of India to all the state Governments since 19 th  
April 1958. Further, under Article 239(1) of the co nstitution of India, the Administrators of all 
the Union Territories have also been directed to di scharge the functions of the Central 
Government relating to the aforesaid powers. Instru ctions regarding  action to be taken against 
illegal migrants is issued by the Central Governmen t to State Government/ UT Administration 
from time to time.

 and targeted action. The Committee, therefore, reco mmends that the 
Ministry should coordinate with State Governments a nd UT Administrations, to track 
detection, detention, and deportation of illegal mi grants. Further, the Committee 
emphasizes that ongoing fencing and infrastructure projects must be completed within 
strict timelines, with periodic progress reviews. T he Committee also recommends that the 
Ministry strengthen coordination with neighboring c ountries to expedite nationality 
verification and repatriation processes, while ensu ring that national security and

3.7.1 The Committee recommends that the Ministry ne eds to expand training programs for 
investigating officers, prosecutors and medical off icers to improve the handling of forensic 
evidence and sexual assault cases. It emphasizes th e need for increased awareness and capacity-
building initiatives to address violence against wo men effectively. The Committee also suggests 
the MHA to consider integrating more technology-dri ven solutions, such as AI powered 
surveillance systems and mobile apps, to enhance women's safety in public spaces.   
(Para 4.16.6  ibid)  
Action Taken 
 
3.7.2 Under the umbrella scheme "Safety of Women”, the Government is undertaking training 
for Investigating Officers, Prosecutors, and Medica l Officers from States/UTs in collection, 
storage and handling of DNA evidence and use of Sex ual Assault Evidence Collection Kits. So 
far 35,306 Investigating Officers, Prosecutors and Medical Officers have been trained by the 
Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPR&D) a nd the LNJN National Institute of 
Criminology and Forensic Sciences (now Delhi campus  of the National Forensic Sciences 
University). The Ministry of Home Affairs has also distributed 18020 Sexual Assault Evidence 
Collection Kits to the States/UTs as part of this t raining. The NFSU is also undertaking training 

75 
 
of forensic scientists in view of the new criminal laws and so far, NFSU has trained 996 
personnel. 
3.7.3  The Committee’s recommendation regarding mor e technology driven solutions has been 
duly noted. 
Further Recommendation 
3.7.4   The Committee appreciates the significant p rogress made by the Ministry under the 
"Safety of Women" scheme, including large-scale tra ining of Investigating Officers, 
Prosecutors, Medical Officers, and forensic scienti sts, as well as the distribution of Sexual 
Assault Evidence Collection Kits. However, the Comm ittee notes that training and 
distribution efforts must be accompanied by periodic evaluation of their effectiveness at the 
ground level to ensure uniformity and quality in ha ndling of sexual assault cases. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that an institutio nalized monitoring and feedback 
mechanism be established to assess the impact of su ch training and ensure capacity-
building translates into better conviction rates and victim support.  
3.8  Demand No. 53 –Chandigarh 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.8.1  The Committee notes that UT administration of Chand igarh has earmarked₹76.60 crores 
for the infrastructure development in technical and  higher education sector and Government 
schools for the Financial Year 2025-26. The Committ ee recommends that efforts must be 
initiated by the concerned agencies to adhere to th e completion of construction/extension of the 
proposed buildings at the earliest.  
(Para 5.3.7 ibid)  
Action Taken  
3.8.2  The Engineering Department (i.e. the executing agen cy) has been directed by the UT 
Administration for strict adherence of time schedule so that the projects are completed on time.  
Further Recommendation 
3.8.3  The Committee notes the assurance that the U T Administration has directed the 
Engineering Department i.e. the executing agency to  strictly adhere to the prescribed 
timelines for infrastructure projects in the educat ion sector. While appreciating this step, 
the Committee emphasizes that timely completion mus t be complemented with close 
monitoring, transparent reporting, and quality chec ks to ensure that the infrastructure 
created is durable and aligned with educational nee ds. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that a structured monitoring mechanism w ith periodic progress reports be 
instituted, and accountability fixed for delays.  
  

76 
 
3.9 Demand No. 57 – Transfers to Delhi 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.9.1  The Committee is of view that a substantial number of private coaching centres and hostels 
for boys and girls are being run in Delhi without a ny strict norms and regulations. These are not 
providing adequate space and basic living condition s to the young population who come from 
far-flung areas for fulfilling their future employm ent aspirations. The Committee would like to 
be apprised about the number of such coaching centr es and hostels that are being run in Delhi 
and what kind of accommodation and other basic faci lities are being provided by them to the 
students and residents of these facilities. The Com mittee may also be informed about the 
provision of licensing of such centres and the last  inspection done to review the conditions of 
these centres and hostels. 
(Para 5.7.10 ibid ) 
Action Taken  
3.9.2  New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) has sanct ioned one building for Hostel for 
boys/girls for YMCA at Jai Singh Road, New Delhi. 
3.9.3  No license is issued by them in respect of p rivate hostels/stay homes for boys and girls 
and no survey has been carried out by NDMC in this regard in its jurisdiction.   
3.9.4 However, NDMC maintains three working women h ostels viz. Akansha, Indira Niketan 
& Swati and three old age home viz. Ashirwad, Sandh ya & Aradhna. No license is issued by 
NDMC in its jurisdiction for Coaching Centres.  
3.9.5 Also, Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) do es not regulate Hostels & Coaching 
Centres. 
Further Recommendation 
3.9.6  The Committee notes with concern that neithe r NDMC nor MCD regulates or 
licenses private hostels and coaching centres in De lhi, despite the fact that a large number 
of students from across the country rely on such fa cilities. The absence of any survey, 
licensing framework, or regulatory oversight raises  serious issues relating to safety, 
adequacy of living conditions, and well being of st udents. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs, in co ordination with the GNCTD and local 
bodies, should initiate the formulation of a compre hensive regulatory framework for 
private hostels and coaching centres in Delhi. This  may include mandatory registration, 
periodic inspections, regulation of rent and minimu m standards for accommodation, 
hygiene, and safety to ensure the welfare of students.

77

Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government have 
not been received  
 
Nil

78 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS — AT A GLANCE 
  
National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)  
Further Recommendation 
 The Committee notes the submission that NDRF batta lions maintain fully 
functional strength at all times and that CAPFs are  being requested periodically to fill 
vacancies. The Committee also takes cognizance of t he approval of Risk and Hardship 
allowance to NDRF personnel. However, the Committee is of the considered view that these 
measures, though positive, may not sufficiently add ress the structural challenge of 
persistent vacancies arising out of the exclusive r eliance on deputation from CAPFs, which 
themselves face acute shortages. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that a comprehensive 
review of deputation policies is imperative. In add ition to allowances, the Ministry may 
consider measures such as flexible deputation tenur es, streamlined nomination procedures, 
career progression incentives, and exploring a limi ted cadre of permanent staff in critical 
operational and technical roles. This would ensure both the long-term stability of 
manpower and enhanced operational readiness of NDRF. 
(Para 3.1.4)  
Cadre Review of CAPFs 
Further Recommendation 
 The Committee notes the Ministry’s acknowledgement  of the importance of Cadre 
Reviews and the positive outcomes already visible i n certain BSF cadres, as well as the 
assurance that the review process for BSF’s Group-‘ B’ & ‘C’ (General Duty) Cadre and 
other cadres is underway. While appreciating these efforts, the Committee is concerned 
that the delay in completing the Cadre Review of BS F’s Group-‘B’ & ‘C’ (General Duty) 
Cadre, pending since 1965, has deprived a large seg ment of personnel of timely 
promotional avenues, retirement benefits and affect ed morale of the force. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates that Cadre Reviews must be co mpleted in a time-bound manner with 
strict monitoring and accountability mechanisms. Th e Ministry may also consider 
institutionalizing an automatic review cycle with c learly defined timelines to ensure 
sustained workforce planning, job satisfaction, and operational effectiveness. 
(Para 3.2.7)

Development of North Eastern Region on the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Fifty 
Third Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Ministry. The Two Hundred 
Fifty Third Report was presented to Rajya Sabha/laid on the Table of Lok Sabha, on 10th March, 
2025. 
 
2. Action Taken Notes as received from the Ministry of DoNER in respect of the 
recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Fifty Third Report have been categorized as 
follows: 
Chapter I: The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos. 2.2.7, 2.4.4, 2.4.5, 2.4.6, 3.1.8, 3.1.9, 3.1.10, 3.1.11, 3.2.3, 3.2.4, 
3.2.5, 3.3.4, 3.8.3, 4.2.6, 4.2.7, 4.2.8, 4.2.9, 4.3.4, 4.3.5., 4.4.3, 4.4.4, 4.5.2, 4.6.7, 4.6.8, 
4.8.11 and 4.9.2 (of Two Hundred Fifty Third Report). 
Total recommendations-26 Accepted. 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted its recommendations as 
mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report. 
 
Chapter II: The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire 
to pursue in view of the Government’s replies: Para Nos. 1.5.3, 2.1.3, 3.6.5, 3.7.4, 3.7.5, 
3.7.6, 3.8.4, 3.9.3, 3.9.4, 4.1.13, 4.7.2, 4.8.7, 4.8.10, 4.10.6, 4.10.7, 4.11.4, 4.11.5, 4.12.2, 
4.13.3, 4.13.5 and 4.13.6 (ibid) 
Total recommendations – 21. Not to be pursued further. 
The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Ministry and, therefore, 
does not want to pursue the recommendations further. 
 
Chapter III: The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee is 
not satisfied with the replies of the Ministry: Para Nos. 3.2.6, 3.6.4, 4.1.12, 4.8.8, 4.8.9, 
4.10.8, 4.12.3, 4.13.4 (ibid) 
Total recommendations – 8. Not convincing replies. 
The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation of its recommendations 
contained in Chapter-III and desires that the Ministry should furnish convincing action taken 
steps in respect of those recommendations. 
 
Chapter IV: The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government have not been received. 
Total Recommendations – NIL

CHAPTER I 
 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
 
1.1 Utilization of Funds 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.1.1 During the deliberations of the Committee, the Secretary, DoNER informed the Committee 
that the utilization as on 27.02.2025 is ₹ 3352 Crore i.e. almost 85% of utilization. The Committee 
hopes that the Ministry may utilize the full budget by the end of March, 2025. 
 
(Para 2.2.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The total expenditure during 2024–25 stood at ₹3,452.99 crore, representing 86.20% of the 
Revised Estimates (RE). This marks a significant increase of 74.68% over the  
₹1,976.76 crore spent in 2023–24. Notably, the 2024–25 expenditure is the highest ever recorded by 
MDoNER, surpassing the previous peak of ₹2,669.72 crore in 2019–20 by 29.34%. MDoNER will 
make all possible efforts to further improve the utilization of allocated funds during 2025-26. 
 
1.2 Outlays for Financial Year 2025-26 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.1 The Committee notes that due to classification in Head of Account MH 4552 under various 
schemes, the major part of the budget outlay has been reflected under the Capital Section. Hence, the 
total Revenue outlay decreased to ₹ 1,882.76 crores in BE 2025-26 from ₹ 2,040.68 crores in BE 
2024-25.The Committee also notes that under the head ‘Schemes of NEC’, there is a shortfall of ₹ 
178.66 crores in BE 2025-26 compared to the projected demand of ₹ 909.30 crores. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry coordinate with NEC to prioritize the expenditure out of the 
present budgetary allocation and seek more funds at the RE 2025-26 stage to meet the shortfalls. The 
Committee also recommends that the requirement of additional funds under the Capital Section may 
also be realistically assessed at the RE stage and additional funds, if required, may be sought.  
(Para 2.4.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.2.2 The Committee’s recommendations have been noted for compliance. 
1.2.3 The requirement of additional funds shall be taken up by MDoNER with the Ministry of 
Finance at the RE stage in FY 2025-26 based on various factors such as progress in expenditure, 
reduction of outstanding UCs, unspent balances, projections and demands made by the concerned 
Divisions etc. and other related considerations. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.2.4 The Committee notes that during 2022-23 and 2023-24, percentage of funds utilization is not 
satisfactory which proves the slow pace of work on the proposed projects. The Committee 

3 
 
appreciates the fact that during 2024-25 almost 85% fund has been utilized till 27.02.2025 and 
hopefully 100% utilization by the end of this Financial Year.  
(Para 2.4.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.2.5 There were multiple reasons for underutilization of funds during 2022-23 and 2023-24. The 
fund flow was hampered due to issues faced in transition to Central Nodal Agency (CNA) system, 
which was adopted from 01.04.2022. Unspent balances with the States/ Implementing agencies were 
also a factor as the CNA system does not allow fresh releases until the previously released amount is 
utilized. Allocations for Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North-East Region (PM-
DevINE), which was announced in Union Budget 2022-23, largely unutilized during 2022-23 and 
2023-24 as the operational guidelines could be notified only in August 2023. Utilization of allocated 
funds was also hampered due to delay in project implementation by State Government/ 
Implementation Agencies because of short working season on account of inclement weather 
conditions; difficulties in transportation of material due to difficult terrain; land acquisition issues; 
local law and order issues etc. and also because of delay in submission of demand/ claims by the 
State Governments. 
1.2.6 The total expenditure during 2024–25 stood at ₹3,452.99 crore, which is 86.20% of the 
Revised Estimates (RE). MDoNER will make all possible efforts to further improve the utilization of 
allocated funds. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.7 The Committee would like to be apprised about the budgetary allocation to the NER from 
2005-2014 and 2014-2024 alongwith a comparative study of the socio-economic as well as 
infrastructural development between the period from 2005-14 and 2014-24. 
(Para 2.4.6 ibid) 
Action Taken

 During 2014-2024, Growth in the North Eastern Region (NER) is as follows:

2.13.12  5. The Govt. of India has taken significant steps to enhance the safety and security of 
women through the creation of a dedicated, non-lapsable corpus known as the Nirbhaya Fund. 
Established in response to growing concerns about crimes against women, this fund has grown 
remarkably over the past decade from supporting a few projects initially to now overseeing 50 
projects with a total outlay exceeding ₹11,300 crore. These initiatives are implemented both 
nationally and regionally, targeting key areas such as behavioural change, legal and institutional 
reform, capacity building and infrastructure development. All the initiatives can broadly be divided 
into three spheres, one being assuring a safe and secure environment in which a woman lives and 
works, the other is to support effective implementation of legislation, and finally, creating a wide 
enabling infrastructure to afford to women speedy justice and support in any crisis. Projects under 
this fund are being executed by various Ministries and Departments including the Ministry of Home 
Affairs, Ministry of Railways, Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, Department of Justice, 
Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Ministry of Tourism, Ministry of Panchayati 
Raj, Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs, Ministry of External Affairs and several State 
Governments across the country. 
2.13.13  6.Under the Nirbhaya framework, an Empowered Committee (EC) of officers constituted 
under the chairpersonship of Secretary, Ministry of Women & Child Development (MWCD), 
appraises and recommends proposals submitted by Ministries/ Departments/ Stale 
Governments/UTs for funding under Nirbhaya Fund. After the projects are appraised and 
recommended by the EC, the responsibility of its execution lies on the concerned Ministries or State 
Governments who utilise funds from their own budget after obtaining approval of their respective 
financial authorities to release the same to the State Governments/ other Implementing Agencies 
(IAs) to implement the approved projects. 
2.13.14  Some of the key initiatives under the fund have been enumerated below: 
i. Launched in February 2019, the Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) provides a 
nationwide, technology-enabled emergency response mechanism accessible a pan-India, single, 
internationally recognised number, i.e., 112. Operational across all 36 States and Union 
Territories, ERSS includes computer-aided dispatch systems and has handled over 43 crore calls 
since inception. ERSS has been integrated with 139 Rail Madad Helpline service (all 36 
States/UTs), 1077 National Disaster Helpline (35 States/UTs), 1098 Child help Line (all 36 
States/UTs) and 181 Women Help Line 181 (35 States/UTs). 
ii.      The system has recorded a national average response time of 18.55 minutes. The 112 India 
mobile app, with over 44 lakh downloads, further enhances accessibility. The ERSS forms the 
backbone of India's emergency safety infrastructure for women-available 24/7 in any location, 
be it home, workplace, or public space. 
iii.    In addition to ERSS, there is fully functional dedicated Women Helpline (WHL) functional 
since April 2015 with the aim to provide emergency and non-emergency response to women 
affected by violence across the country by referral service. Under the scheme, a toll-free 24-

31 
 
hours telecom service through short code 181 is provided to women seeking support and 
information. It is operational in 35 States/ UTs. So far, WHL has handled over 2.1 crore calls 
and assisted over 87.28 lakh women till April 2025 across the country and 69,904 women have 
been assisted specifically in North East states. The Government is in process of automating and 
integrating Women Helpline (181) with Emergency Response Support System (112) to obviate 
the problem of multiplicity of helpline numbers, and also further linking it with OSCs 
iv. The Government launched the scheme of One Stop Centre(OSCs) in April 2015 to provide 
integrated support and assistance to women affected by violence or in distress, both in private 
and public spaces under one roof and facilitate immediate, emergency and non-emergency 
access to a range of services including police, medical, legal aid and counselling, psychological 
support. At present, 820 OSCs are functional across 38 States/UTs, covering entire geographical 
area of the country. These centres have assisted over 11.19 lakh women so far. In North East 
region, a total of 125 OSCs are operational that have assisted 42,763 women till 31st March 
2025.

3.5 Healthcare and Education 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.5.1 The Committee notes that as per the information provided by the Ministry of Development of 
North Eastern Region, the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) (Per Thousand), 2020, is far less in the States 
of Mizoram (3), Nagaland (4), Sikkim (5) and Manipur (6) as compared to the other North Eastern 
States namely, Assam (36) Meghalaya (29), Arunachal Pradesh (21) and Tripura (18). The IMR 
count of the States of Assam and Meghalaya is even greater than national average which is 28. The 
Committee is of the view that death of infants is a key yardstick to determine the larger healthcare 

41 
 
situation and facilities of an area. Multi-departments efforts, provision of health and wellness centres 
with trained professionals and easy accessibilities of healthcare facilities to pregnant women and 
post natal care to new-borns can pave a way for minimising the number of infant deaths in the States 
which have high infant mortality rate. Similarly, best healthcare practices adopted in the States of 
Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Manipur can be adopted in other North Eastern States to improve 
their health infrastructure. The Committee recommends that the MDoNER should take initiative to 
study basic health care facilities available in those States where IMR is quite high and ensure to 
provide sufficient health care facilities to those States to reduce IMR drastically. 
 
(Para 4.10.8 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
3.5.2 The details of basic health care initiatives/programmes taken up by the Governments of 
Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Manipur where IMR is 3,4,5, and 6 respectively, are as under:  
(i) Mizoram -  (a) Capacity Building  through Skilled Birth Attendance and Facility Based 
Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (F-IMNCI) and Integrated 
Management of  Neonatal and Childhood illness (IMNCI); (b) High Immunization Coverage; (c) 
Institutional deliveries; (d) effective  Antenatal and Postnatal Care (ANC/PNC); (e) Extended 
Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyaan (e-PMSMA); (f) SAANS campaign (Social 
Awareness and Action to Neutralize Pneumonia Successfully); (g) Community Health Care 
Workers (HWOs, ANMs and ASHAs); (h) Improved nutrition and Breastfeeding practices; (i) 
Access to Quality Healthcare in remote Areas;  (j) Intersectoral Coordination and Community 
Participation; (k) focus on education; (l) involving NGO and Church for influencing people in 
general; etc. 
(ii) Nagaland: (a) Maternal Nutrition during pregnancy; (b) Feeding practices at Birth and 
Childhood; (c) Facility and community level interventions viz. facility based new born care, 
focus on quality ANC and Identification and Tracking of High Risk Pregnancies, focus on care 
around birth, leveraging presence of Church Organizations (FBO) in improving demand  
generation, streamlining comprehensive VHSND (Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day) 
services. 
(iii) Sikkim: (a) Promotion of Institutional Delivery; (b) Emphasis on facility based new-born 
care at different levels; (c) Appropriate Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF); (d) Universal 
Immunization Programme (UIP); (e) Home based new born care (HBNC); (f) Capacity building; 
(g) Education and awareness; (h) Monitoring and supervision; (i) Improvement in health seeking 
behaviour; (j) Use of Technology (Whatsapp); (k) One year maternity leave to take care of the 
infant: 
(iv) Manipur: (a) Institutional deliveries,; (b) Strengthening of the Village Health Sanitation 
and Nutrition Days; (c) Traditional practice of rooming the mother and the newborn till the 
time of “Yum Senba” i.e. 12th day; (d) Encouragement of initiation of breastfeeding within 
1 hour (Colostrum); (e)”Chak  Umba” a local ritual in which complimentary feeding is 
started along with continuation of breastfeeding; (f) Keeping the baby warm through local 
practice  of wrapping the infants and holding the infants either in the back or on the 
chest; (g) Diet rich in high protein/Iron intake by the community across state; (h) 
Functionality of Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs), Newborn Intensive Care Unit (NICU), 

42 
 
Newborn Stabilization Unit (NBSU) & Newborn Care Corner (NBCC), etc. in Medical Colleges, 
District Hospitals, CHCs & PHCs; (i) Involving of trained staff nurses/ANM in counselling 
vaccination etc.; (j) Capacity building of healthcare workers at various levels; (k) 
Implementation of Home-Based Newborn care (HBNC) and Home-Based Young Child Care 
(HBYC) across 16 districts of the state; (l) Implementation of Anaemia Mukt Bharat(6*6*6 
strategy) 6 beneficiaries-6-59 months children, 5-10 years, 10-19 years, pregnant women, 
lactating mothers and women in reproductive age; (m) Implementation of Mothers’ Absolute 
Affection(MAA)- awareness on breast feeding; (n) Observation of Poshan Maah; (o) Regular observation of intensified Diarrhoea control fortnight/Stop Diarrhoea Campaign and National Deworming Day, Social Awareness and Action to Neutralize Pneumonia successfully(SAANS), Protection and Treatment(PPT)strategy of SAANS; (p) Child Death Reviews(CDR) and Maternal Death Reviews at district and state level; (q) Comprehensive ANC and detection of high-risk pregnancy and tracking (under PMSMA programme – Special Initiatives are taken up, engagement of PMSMA volunteers); (q) Full immunization coverage of infants (91% , HMIS2024-25). 
3.5.3 The above details in r/o Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Manipur have been shared with the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya and Tripura with request to examine and consider adopting such practices/initiatives/programmes, as suitable to them, with the aim to reduce their IMR. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.5.4 The Committee notes that the Ministry has shared the initiatives undertaken by the 
States of Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, and Manipur which have resulted in significantly low 
Infant Mortality Rates (IMR) with other States of North Eastern Region. In addition to this, 
the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region 
(MDoNER), in coordination with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), 
should facilitate a coordinated mechanism for the implementation of best healthcare practices 
of these better-performing States in other North Eastern States where IMR remains high. The 
Committee further recommends that the Health Secretaries of all North Eastern States be 
taken on board to ensure effective inter-State knowledge sharing, capacity building, and 
adoption of proven interventions aimed at reducing IMR across the Region.

generation coupled with improving employability is a priority of the Government. Accordingly, 
Government is implementing various employment generation schemes/ programmes in the country 
including in the North Eastern States. These inter-alia include Prime Minister's Employment 
Generation Programme (PMEGP), Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee

etc. The details of various employment generation schemes/programmes being implemented by the 
Government may be seen at https://dge.gov.in/dge/schemes_programms 
3.7.5 The Aatmanirbhar Bharat Rojgar Yojana (ABRY) was launched with effect from 1st October, 
2020 to incentivize employers for creation of new employment and restoration of loss of employment 
during Covid-19 pandemic. The terminal date for registration of beneficiaries was 31.03.2022. Since 
inception of the scheme, as on 31.03.2024, benefits have been provided to 60.49 lakhs beneficiaries 
in the country including North Eastern States. 
3.7.6 MoLE is running the National Career Service (NCS) Portal which is a one-stop solution for 
providing career related services including jobs from private and government sectors, information 
on online & offline job fairs, job search & matching, career counselling, vocational guidance, 
information on skill development courses, skill/training programmes etc. through a digital platform 
[www.ncs.gov.in]. As on 28.02.2025, more than 4.7 crore vacancies have been mobilised on NCS 
Portal. 
 3.7.7  Further, MoLE had launched eShram portal (eshram.gov.in) on 26th August 2021 for 
creation of a comprehensive National Database of Unorganised Workers (NDUW) seeded with 
Aadhaar. eShram portal is meant to register and support the unorganised workers by providing 
them a Universal Account Number (UAN) on a self-declaration basis. As on 9th March 2025, over 
30.70 crore unorganised workers have registered on eShram portal''. 
3.7.8 MDoNER budgetary allocation has significantly supported Entrepreneurship development 
initiatives in the North Eastern Region (NER), particularly for first-generation entrepreneurs North 
Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi), is an administrative body under 
MDoNER. NEDFi’s Micro Finance Scheme is an effective instrument for financial outreach where 
credit is given to Self Help Groups (SHGs)/ Joint Liability Groups (JLGs) & individuals through 
credible Non-Government Organizations (NGO)/ Microfinance Institutions (MFIs) of the region. 
During the period under review (in last 11 years), the Corporation sanctioned microfinance loan of 
₹764.54 crore in NER. Till date, a total of 69 start-ups has been given investment commitments for 
₹100 crore. 
3.7.9 To support the growth of MSMEs and the Micro Finance sector in the NER, MDoNER has 
been providing budgetary allocations since 2002-03 to facilitate affordable credit access. This 
initiative has supported industrial growth, entrepreneurship, and job creation. Renamed the North 
East Enterprises Development Scheme (NEEDS) in 2021-22, it has been extended until 2025-26. 
Further Recommendation/Observation

Region (MDoNER), in coordination with the concerned Ministries may take a consolidated 
assessment of the socio-economic outcome of the initiatives taken for the development  and 
employment generation in the North-Eastern Region. Assessment may include clear indicators 
such as income enhancement, entrepreneurship development, skill upgradation, and livelihood 
and employment creation. This will help in assessing the real effectiveness of the empowerment 
measures being implemented in the region.

CHAPTER-I 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1  CONSTITUTIONAL AND FUNCTIONAL MANDATE 
 
1.1.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is entrust ed with the responsibility of ensuring 
internal security, border management, administratio n of Union Territories, Centre–State 
relations, disaster management, citizenship matters  and related subjects. The Ministry plays a 
pivotal role in maintaining public order, strengthe ning national integration and ensuring 
coordinated security responses across the country. 
 
1.1.2  Though 'Public Order' and 'Police' are the r esponsibilities of States as per the Seventh 
Schedule to the Constitution of India, Article 355 of the Constitution enjoins the Union to protect 
every State against external aggression and interna l disturbance and to ensure that the 
Government of every State is carried on in accordan ce with the provisions of the Constitution. 
While discharging its duties, the Ministry of Home Affairs continuously monitors the internal 
security situation, issues appropriate advisories, shares intelligence inputs, extends manpower 
and financial support, guidance and expertise to th e State Governments for maintenance of 
security, peace and harmony without encroaching upon the constitutional rights of the States. 
 
1.1.3  The Detailed Demands for Grants (2026-27) re flect the Ministry’s wide-ranging mandate 
covering Secretariat administration, Modernisation of Prisons and Other Administrative Services 
including Civil Defence and Fire Services, Miscella neous General Services and Police 
Infrastructure, among others. 
 
1.2 GOALS AND OBJECTIVES 
 
1.2.1 The MHA administers and implements a wide ran ge of schemes and programmes. In 
brief, the goals and objectives of the Ministry for the year (2026-27) are as follows: 
 
(i) Continuous monitoring of  internal security situati on and issuance of timely 
advisories; 
(ii) Consolidation of gains towards achieving a Naxal-fr ee Bharat through 
coordinated security and development initiatives in  Left Wing Extremism 
affected areas; 
(iii) Implementation of a zero-tolerance policy against t errorism including 
strengthening of counter-terrorism architecture and  intelligence coordination 
mechanisms;  
(iv) Adoption of a Whole-of-Government approach to disma ntle narco-terror 
networks and combat drug trafficking; 
(v) Strengthening border management through integrated border infrastructure, 
coastal security, surveillance technologies and Vibrant Villages Programme; 

2 
 
(vi) Modernisation of the criminal justice system throug h implementation of new 
criminal laws and digitization to ensure a transpar ent, time-bound and victim-
centric criminal justice system; 
(vii) Further development of the Inter-Operable Criminal Justice System (ICJS) for 
seamless data exchange among police, courts, prison s and forensic 
institutions; 
(viii) Strengthening forensic science and investigation in frastructure under the 
National Forensic Infrastructure Enhancement initia tives, including 
modernization of Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs); 
(ix) Further expansion of evidence-based investigation s ystems, and enhancement 
of training and skill-development programmes for police personnel; 
(x) Enhancing cyber security architecture and strengthe ning institutional 
mechanisms to address emerging digital and financial cyber threats; 
(xi) Strengthening disaster preparedness and response ca pacity through capacity 
building, early warning systems and coordinated dis aster management 
frameworks; 
(xii) Modernization, capacity building and welfare measur es for Central Armed 
Police Forces (CAPFs), including provision of secur ity, administrative and 
residential infrastructure; 
(xiii) Ensuring timely reimbursement to States under Secur ity Related Expenditure 
(SRE) and providing Special Infrastructure Support to LWE affected States; 
(xiv) Conduct of Census 2027 and related preparatory acti vities, including 
technological upgradation for census operations; 
(xv) Operationalisation and strengthening of Bhartiya Bh asha Anubhag and 
promotion of Official Languages to support translat ion services and linguistic 
diversity; 
(xvi) Strengthening cooperative federalism through the In ter-State Council and 
Zonal Councils; 
(xvii) Implementing initiatives for women's safety and emp owerment to ensure a 
secure environment for women; 
(xviii) Fostering international cooperation on security iss ues, including counter-
terrorism and transnational crime; 
(xix) Supporting prison reforms and modernization of pris ons, including schemes 
for support to poor prisoners; 
(xx) Streamlining immigration processes through technolo gy-driven systems 
including the Immigration, Visa, Foreigners Registr ation and Tracking 
(IVFRT) and related platforms;  
(xxi) Timely disbursement of funds to freedom fighters an d their eligible 
dependents; 
(xxii) Supporting holistic development of islands and bord er areas in Union 
Territories to enhance local governance and infrastructure; and 
(xxiii) Fostering community engagement programs to promote peace, harmony and 
social cohesion;

THE MHA 
 
2.1 OVERVIEW 
 
2.1.1 There are eleven Demands for Grants which are  administered by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs (MHA). The detailed Demands for Grants of t he Ministry of Home Affairs are divided 
into three volumes: Vol. I, Vol. II-A and Vol. II-B. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volume-I) 
contains three Demands (Nos. 49-51), namely the Min istry of Home Affairs (Demand No. 49); 
the Cabinet (Demand No. 50); and the Police (Demand No. 51). 
 
2.1.2. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volumes-II- A and II-B) relate to the five Union 
Territories (without Legislature), namely Andaman &  Nicobar Islands (Demand No. 52), 
Chandigarh (Demand No. 53), Dadra & Nagar Haveli an d Daman & Diu (Demand No. 54), 
Ladakh (Demand No. 55) and Lakshadweep (Demand No. 56) and  three Union Territories (with 
Legislature), namely Delhi (Demand No. 57- Transfer s to Delhi), Jammu & Kashmir (Demand 
No.58- Transfers to Jammu & Kashmir) and Puducherry  (Demand No. 59- Transfers to 
Puducherry). 
 
2.1.3 The provisions for the Union Territories (wit hout Legislature) form part of the Demands 
of the Ministry of Home Affairs. However, various p rogrammes/schemes are the subject matter 
of different Ministries, which are responsible for scrutinizing, sanctioning and implementing the 
schemes/projects falling under their respective pur view. Provisions for the Union Territories 
(with a Legislature) cover Assistance to the Union Territories of Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir 
and NCT of Delhi, in the form of the Grants and Loa ns. In respect of these three Grants, the 
Ministry of Home Affairs releases the Grants on a q uarterly basis and has a limited role in 
scrutinizing, sanctioning and implementation of the schemes/projects.

3.1 OVERVIEW 
3.1.1 Ministry of Home Affairs contains provisions mainly for various administrative functions 
in respect of MHA Secretariat, Office of Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India, 
various offices functioning under Department of Off icial Language, Zonal Councils, National 
Disaster Response Force, National Disaster Manageme nt Authority (NDMA), Director General 
of Fire Service, Civil Defence & Home Guards, Natio nal Human Rights Commission, National 
Fire Services College and Departmental Accounting Organisation of MHA.  
3.1.2 Apart from the above, provisions have been ma de for schemes like Relief & 
Rehabilitation for repatriates and migrants, Pensio n and other benefits to Freedom Fighters, 
Helicopter subsidies for North-East, Jammu & Kashmi r, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh and 
various schemes of Disaster Management and Establis hment of Bhartiya Bhasha Anubhag 
(BBA).  
3.2 OFFICIAL LANGUAGE 
3.2.1 The allocations under Official Language inclu de provisions for Central Hindi Training 
Institute (CHTI), Central Translation Bureau (CTB),  Technical Cell, Regional Implementation 
Offices (RIOs) and other schemes / programmes being  implemented by the Department of 
Official Language. 
3.2.2  The Committee sought to know about the measu rable outcomes proposed to be achieved 
under the head “Official Languages” during 2026–27 and the specific targets fixed for 
translation, capacity building and inspection activ ities. The Ministry informed that the following 
outputs have been proposed for the year:  
(i)
 Under translation activities, the Indian Languages Section proposes to translate 
approximately 20,000 letters into various regional languages, while the Central 
Translation Bureau has fixed a target of translating 40,000 pages during 2026–27. 
(ii) Under capacity building, the Department aims to exp and the Hindi Shabd Sindhu 
repository from 7 lakh to 7.5 lakh words and prepar e a Medical Shabd Sindhu 
dictionary in 15 Indian languages. It has also prop osed to impart Hindi training to 
25,000 personnel through the Central Hindi Training Institute and provide training to 
1,175 personnel through the Central Translation Bureau. 
(iii) With regard to inspections, the Parliamentary  Committee on Official Language has 
proposed to inspect approximately 7,000 offices. Fu rther, approximately 852 
offices/banks/undertakings are to be inspected by t he Regional Implementation 
Offices. 

21 
 
3.2.3 The Committee further sought to know the addi tional measures and initiatives 
undertaken for promotion of Official Language Hindi  apart from quarterly and annual assessment 
reports. The Ministry informed that the Department of Official Language has undertaken the 
following initiatives: 
(i) Development and upgradation of the Artificial Intel ligence-based translation software 
“Bharati - Bahubhashi Anuvada Sarthi” (earlier Kant hastha), integrated with e-Office 
and expanded to include 15 Indian languages, with p rovision for instant translation 
facility. 
(ii) Establishment of the Indian Languages Section to fa cilitate multilingual 
correspondence between the Central Government and S tate Governments in their 
respective official languages through a universal translation system. 
(iii) Continuous expansion of the fully digital Hindi-to- Hindi dictionary “Hindi Shabd 
Sindhu”, which presently contains over seven lakh words across diverse domains. 
(iv) Inspired by the Hon’ble Prime Minister’s “Panch Pra n,” the Department has organised 
a series of All India Official Language Conferences  and Regional Official Language 
Conferences to strengthen implementation of the Off icial Language Policy and confer 
Rajbhasha awards for exemplary performance. 
(v) Conduct of Technical Conferences for capacity enhan cement of officers of the Central 
Secretariat Official Language Service. 
(vi) Functioning of over 550 Town Official Language Impl ementation Committees 
(TOLICs) across the country, including five oversea s TOLICs, to promote the use of 
Hindi in official work. 
(vii) Periodic review of implementation through the Centr al Hindi Committee, chaired by 
the Hon’ble Prime Minister, and additionally, under  the chairmanship of the Secretary, 
Department of Official Language, a meeting of the C entral Official Language 
Implementation Committee (COLIC) is organized every year.  
(viii) Launch of the e-Saral Hindi Phrasebook containing m ore than 14,000 official-use 
sentences including terms drawn from domains such a s administration, agriculture, 
banking and finance, healthcare, industry, information technology, law, and tourism. 
3.2.4 From the information provided by the MHA, it may be seen that while the allocation in  
RE of 2025-26 was ₹ 97.06 crores, in BE 2026-27 an allocation of ₹ 98.16 crores has been made 
under the head ‘Official language’. 
Observations/Recommendations 
3.2.5  The Committee notes the measurable targets fixed by  the Department of Official 
Language for 2026–27, including translation of 20,0 00 letters and 40,000 pages, imparting 
Hindi training to 25,000 personnel, training of 1,1 75 officials by the Central Translation 

22 
 
Bureau, expansion of the Hindi Shabd Sindhu reposit ory to 7.5 lakh words, preparation of 
a Medical Shabd Sindhu dictionary in 15 Indian lang uages, and inspection of 
approximately 852 offices/banks/undertakings by Reg ional Implementation Offices. The 
Committee appreciates the outcome-oriented approach  reflected in the fixing of 
quantifiable physical targets and expects effective  implementation of the proposed targets. 
Further, the Ministry may explore expansion of domain-specific terminologies, particularly 
in emerging sectors such as digital governance, art ificial intelligence, cyber security and 
health sciences, so as to strengthen the practical usability of Hindi in technical and 
administrative communication. 
3.2.6 The Committee further notes the technological  interventions undertaken by the 
Department, particularly the upgradation of the AI- based translation platform “Bharati – 
Bahubhashi Anuvada Sarthi”, its integration with e- Office, and the establishment of the 
Indian Languages Section to facilitate multilingual correspondence between the Centre and

Ministry may consider instituting a robust performa nce-monitoring framework to assess 
the quality, timeliness and actual utilisation of t ranslated content across Ministries and 
Departments. The Committee also recommends that per iodic impact assessment studies 
may be undertaken to evaluate the effectiveness of Hindi training programmes and the 
functional usage of trained personnel in official work.  
3.3 NATIONAL DISASTER RESPONSE FORCE (NDRF) 
 
3.3.1 The Committee, in its meeting while discussin g the Demands for Grants (2026–27) of the 
Ministry of Home Affairs, appreciated the efforts o f the National Disaster Response Force 
(NDRF) in rescue and rehabilitation during disasters, noting that its personnel have demonstrated 
exceptional courage and professionalism in safeguar ding lives and property across a wide range 
of calamities.  
3.3.2 The Committee was apprised that during the pe riod 2023–2025, NDRF conducted 3,421 
operations deploying 5,256 teams. During these oper ations, 12,528 persons were rescued and 
1,55,387 persons were evacuated. Further, 2,146 dea d bodies were retrieved, 4,322 livestock 
were saved and medical assistance was provided to 3 7,545 persons. In 2025 alone, the Force 
conducted 1,489 operations across 27 States/UTs aff ected by floods, cloudbursts, landslides, 
cyclones and other disasters. The NDRF also underto ok international humanitarian assistance 
under “Operation Bramha” during the Myanmar earthquake. 
3.3.3 The Committee was further informed that NDRF presently has 16 operational battalions. 
No new battalion has been raised during the last th ree years. The authorised strength of the 
NDRF is 18,581 personnel against a posted strength of 14,837 personnel. 
3.3.4 With regard to infrastructure augmentation, t he Ministry informed that ₹140.00 crore has 
been proposed for infrastructure development in FY 2026–27 at nine Regional Response Centres 
(RRCs) located at Agartala, Lucknow, Gorakhpur, Gan gtok, Nurpur, Hyderabad, Ernakulam, 

23 
 
Port Blair and Gandhinagar, along with works at bat talion locations and ₹3.62 crore for 
acquisition of additional land at Dehradun, Chamoli and Uttarkashi. 
3.3.5 The total allocation for NDRF in BE 2026–27 i s ₹2102.11 crores, out of which ₹213.77 
crores (approximately 10.17%) has been earmarked fo r capital expenditure. The capital 
component includes ₹96.35 crore for Buildings & Str uctures, ₹11.00 crores for Motor Vehicles, 
₹90.00 crores for Machinery & Equipment, ₹7.50 cror es for ICT infrastructure, ₹5.00 crore sfor 
Furniture & Fixtures, ₹3.62 crores for Land acquisi tion and ₹0.30 crores for other fixed assets. 
An amount of ₹3.00 crores has been earmarked for training of personnel. 
Observations/Recommendations 
3.3.6 
 The Committee notes the significant increase in ope rational commitments of the 
NDRF, as reflected in the rising number of operatio ns conducted during the last three 
years. The Committee appreciates the role played by  the Force in responding to disasters 
across multiple States/UTs and its participation in  international humanitarian assistance 
operations. However, the Committee observes that de spite increasing operational 
responsibilities, no additional battalion has been raised during the last three years and the 
posted strength (14,837) remains considerably below  the authorised strength (18,581). The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may undertak e a comprehensive assessment of 
manpower gaps and expedite measures to fill vacanci es so as to ensure optimal operational 
readiness. The Terms of deputation may be revised t o incentivize more personnel from 
Central armed police Forces (CAPFs) to join the NDRF.  
3.3.7 The Committee appreciates the critical role o f the NDRF in disaster response and 
emphasizes the need for adequate funding to address  its demands, particularly for 
additional personnel. The shortage of funds for suc h critical schemes can adversely impact 
the functioning of the NDRF. The Committee recommen ds that the MHA may approach 
the Ministry of Finance at the Revised Estimates (R E) stage to secure the additional funds, 
if required, ensuring that operational efficiency a nd preparedness are not compromised 
during emergencies. 
3.3.8 The Committee further observes that only abou t 10% of the total allocation in BE 
2026–27 has been earmarked for capital expenditure.  In view of the increasing frequency 
and intensity of natural disasters, the Committee r ecommends that greater emphasis may 
be placed on strengthening capital assets, advanced  rescue equipment, ICT-enabled 
response systems and regional infrastructure to red uce response time and enhance disaster 
preparedness.

3.9  HOME GUARDS  
3.9.1 The Ministry informed the Committee that the increase between BE 2025–26 and RE 
2025–26, as well as BE 2026–27, is due to additiona l demand by the Directorate General, Fire 
Services, Civil Defence and Home Guards (DGCDFS&HG)  for reimbursement to States/UTs 
and clearing of backlog claims. The Committee was a pprised that Home Guards constitute a 
voluntary force raised by States and Union Territor y Administrations under a broad policy 
framework laid down by the Ministry of Home Affairs . The force supplements State/UT police 
forces in maintaining law and order, traffic manage ment, protection of public property, guarding 
borders and performing election-related duties. The  central provision is meant for assisting 
States/UTs in raising, training and equipping Home Guards. 
3.9.2 In response to the Committee’s query regardin g enhancement of working conditions, 
training, equipment and deployment constraints, the  Ministry informed that the following 
measures have been proposed/initiated by Directorat e General (Fire Services, Civil Defence and 
Home Guards), MHA. As Home Guards fall under the ju risdiction of respective States/UTs, 
implementation would be undertaken by them: 

31 
 
(i) Introduction of Digital Platform - “Seva Path” 
The proposed Model Home Guards Bill, 2025 envisages  a dedicated digital platform for 
transparent and efficient allotment of duties. The platform provides for term-wise 
engagement of Home Guards for a five-year period, e nsuring equitable deployment, 
improved workforce planning and enhanced accountability. 
(ii) Digitalisation of Wage Disbursement 
States/UTs may introduce digital systems for disbur sement of wages/honorarium through 
Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to ensure transparenc y and timely payments. Coordination 
with Government banks is also proposed to extend ac count-linked benefits on lines similar 
to those available to Armed Forces/CAPFs. 
(iii) 
Group Medical Insurance and Health Coverage 
States/UTs may introduce Group Medical Insurance sc hemes or extend coverage under 
existing Central/State health schemes such as Ayush man Bharat to ensure comprehensive 
health protection for Home Guards. 
(iv) 
Modernisation of Training Modules 
A review of training syllabi is under process to al ign with contemporary requirements, with 
emphasis on disaster management, community engageme nt, internal security support and 
awareness of flagship schemes. A conference with St ate/UT authorities has already been 
convened in this regard. 
(v) 
Integration with SDRF as First Responders 
It has been recommended that Home Guards may be tra ined and utilised as first responders 
at the district level, particularly in disaster pre paredness and response, considering their 
wide presence across districts. 
(vi) 
Review of Uniform and Equipment Policy 
A national-level committee has been constituted to standardise uniforms and modernise 
equipment, ensuring climate suitability and functio nal adequacy for duties relating to 
disasters, elections and internal security. 
 
Observations/Recommendations 
3.9.3  The Committee notes that although the alloca tion under the head “Home Guards” 
has improved in BE 2026–27, it remains modest in co mparison to the expanding role of 
Home Guards in elections, disaster response and int ernal security duties. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry, in consultation with States/UTs, may undertake a 
comprehensive assessment of financial and operation al requirements so that central 
assistance is commensurate with the increasing depl oyment responsibilities of the force. 
The Committee further recommends that proposed digi tal initiatives, including the “Seva 
Path” platform and digitalisation of wage disbursem ent, may be implemented in a time-

32 
 
bound manner across States/UTs to ensure transparen cy, equitable deployment and timely 
disbursement of honorarium through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT). 
3.9.4  The Committee further recommends that modern isation of training modules and 
integration of Home Guards as first responders with  State Disaster Response Forces 
(SDRFs) may be institutionalised through structured  joint exercises and periodic refresher 
training. Emphasis may also be placed on provision of climate-suitable uniforms, modern 
protective gear and essential equipment to enable e ffective discharge of duties during 
disasters, elections and internal security operatio ns, thereby enhancing operational 
efficiency and morale of the force.

4.5.6 The Committee appreciates the comprehensive w elfare framework put in place for 
families of CAPF and Assam Rifles personnel killed in action and for rehabilitation of 
retired personnel. The Committee notes the institut ional mechanism established through 
the Welfare and Rehabilitation Board (WARB) and the  deployment of Central, State and

Ministry may evolve a structured outcome-monitoring mechanism to periodically assess the 
effectiveness of financial assistance, pensionary b enefits, scholarship schemes and re-
employment initiatives, so as to ensure timely deli very and long-term socio-economic 
stability of beneficiary families.

Punarvaas” scheme may be strengthened through great er coordination with Public Sector 
Undertakings and private sector entities, and that data regarding placements and self-
employment outcomes may be periodically compiled an d reviewed. Special emphasis may 
be placed on skill development and counselling supp ort for widows and dependents to 
enable sustainable livelihood opportunities. 

41 
 
4.5.8 The Committee observes that the availability of housing units remains significantly 
below the authorised strength, with only 1,35,544 dwelling units presently in place against a 
sanctioned capacity of 2,68,346 units. In addition,  10,430 units are currently under 
construction, which, when completed, will marginally improve the situation. At present, the

The Committee recommends that personnel deployed in  hard-duty, border and 
high-risk operational areas may be accorded priorit y in allotment of residential 
accommodation. Completion of ongoing housing projec ts may be closely monitored and 
that a phased roadmap may be prepared to progressiv ely enhance housing satisfaction 
levels across the Forces. 
4.5.9 Further, the Committee recommends that given the increasing operational stress 
and deployment in difficult terrains, access to qua lity and timely medical care assumes 
critical importance for CAPF personnel and their fa milies. Periodic review of empanelled

comprehensive and timely medical support to serving  and retired personnel and their 
dependents. 
4.5.10 The Committee also take notes of the enhance ment of Central ex-gratia 
compensation and the assurance of a minimum financi al support package from various 
sources. While acknowledging the existing structure , the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may examine the feasibility of evolving a broad and simplified categorisation of

remain sensitive to operational realities while avoiding over-fragmentation of categories.

weapons, equipment, infrastructure and technology t o enhance operational effectiveness, 
mobility and preparedness. Its purpose is to streng then internal security, border management and 
counter-terror operations in line with evolving sec urity challenges. The Committee noted that 
allocation under Modernization Plan-IV for CAPFs ha s declined from ₹610.79 crores in RE 
2025-26 to ₹343.66 crores in BE 2026-27. The Minist ry informed that the Modernization Plan-
IV was approved by the Cabinet Committee on Securit y in February 2022 with a total outlay of 
₹1,523 crores for implementation from 01.02.2022 to  31.03.2026. Due to issuance of Scheme 
Guidelines in May 2022, expenditure during 2021-22 was Nil anda limited expenditureduring 
2022-23. 

44 
 
4.7.2 The Ministry further stated that most of the items under Mod Plan-IV are highly technical 
in nature. They are not available in domestic marke ts off the shelf. Further, procurement 
procedures for the same are rather cumbersome and t ime-consuming. Hence, delivery period of 
these items are longer resulting in long gestation period and delayed procurement process. Also, 
due to incomplete documents/non-fulfilment of tende r requirements, tenders were being 
scrapped. Since, the implementation period of Moder nization Plan IV ends on 31.03.2026,

liabilities which will be booked in 2026-27 owing t o their delivery falling in FY 2026-27, hence, 
amount of ₹343.66 crores are allocated under BE 2026-27.
