highlight the need for more realistic budgeting and improved financial forecasting. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry may take appropriate measures to 
keep tracking the progress of ongoing projects and avoid financial stress during RE 
stage. 
3.1.13  The Committee recommends that the North Eastern Council (NEC) 
should strengthen its project appraisal, monitoring and review mechanisms to ensure 
strict adherence to prescribed timelines and approved cost estimates. It further 
recommends that a robust financial planning framework be evolved to realistically 
assess committed liabilities in advance so as to minimize substantial upward revisions at 
the Revised Estimates (RE) stage. The Committee is also of the view that special 
attention should be accorded to expediting major infrastructure projects such as the 
Agartala-Akhaura Rail Link to prevent further cost overruns and to ensure that the 
intended strategic and connectivity benefits accrue to the region in its scheduled 
timeline. 
3.2 Central Pool of Resources for North East and Sikkim/North East Special 
Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) 
 
3.2.1 The North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) is a centrally-
funded initiative launched in 2017-18 and extended until 2026. It has been restructured into 
two components: NESIDS (Roads), managed by the North Eastern Council, and NESIDS 
(OTRI), overseen by the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region. NESIDS (OTRI) 
includes unfinished projects from previous schemes such as NLCPR, NESIDS, and HADP. 
This restructuring aims to streamline infrastructure development, ensuring efficient resource 
utilization and effective project implementation in the North Eastern region, thereby 
promoting holistic development and economic growth. The Non-Lapsable Central Pool of 
Resources (NLCPR) scheme, initiated in 1998 and managed by the Ministry of Development 
of North Eastern Region (DoNER) since 2001, aims to bridge infrastructure gaps in the North 
Eastern Region (NER) of India. The scheme funds projects prioritized by State Governments, 
with a 90:10 cost-sharing ratio between the Central and State Governments. Over the years, 
NLCPR has sanctioned numerous projects across various sectors to enhance the region's 
development. In 2017, the North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS)

funding.

3.3 North East Enterprise Development Scheme (NEEDS) erstwhile loan to North

3.3.1 In order to provide credit linkage to the Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises (MSME) 
& Micro Finance sectors in the North Eastern Region, the Ministry of Development of North 
Eastern Region (MDoNER), Govt. of India, has been providing annual budgetary allocation 
to North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi) in the form of interest free 
loan since 2002-03. The Scheme has been renamed as North East Enterprises Development 
Scheme (NEEDS) in 15th Finance Commission cycle. The objectives of the scheme are as 
under- 
a) To provide financial resources and to encourage flow of private 
investments in the North Eastern Region. 
 
 b)        To focus primarily on the MSME and Micro Finance Sectors in line with 
the focus areas identified by respective North-eastern state governments. 
 
 c) To target more number of projects especially from first generation 
entrepreneurs to spread the entrepreneurship spirit in the Region. 
 
d) To provide finance to first generation entrepreneurs and socially 
vulnerable& disadvantaged groups at concessional and competitive rates. 
 
e)         To reach out to more number of beneficiaries through microfinance. 
 
3.3.2 During the period 01 January 2025 to 31 December 2025, the Corporation extended 
financial assistance to 7,120 projects with total sanctions of Rs.854.65 crores. Various sectors 
financed were hotels & tourism, healthcare, education & training institute, food processing, 
handlooms & handicrafts, microfinance etc.

3.11 Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE) 
 
3.11.1 The Union Cabinet approved the PM-DevINE Scheme on 12.10.2022, as a Central 
Sector Scheme with 100% Central funding, with a total outlay of Rs.6,600 crore for the 4-year 
period from 2022-23 to 2025-26.  PM-DevINE aims at rapid and holistic development of the 
North-East Region by funding infrastructure and social development projects based on felt 
needs of the States. It strives to fill gaps in various sectors and will not be a substitute for 
existing Central and State Schemes.  
 
3.11.2 The objectives of PM-DevINE are to: 
 
(i) Fund infrastructure convergently in the spirit of PM GatiShakti 
(ii) Support social development projects based on felt needs of the NER 
(iii) Enable livelihood activities for youth and women  
(iv) Fill the development gaps in various sectors 
 
3.11.3 Keeping in view these scheme objectives, 48 projects worth ₹6044.36 crores in 
various sectors including health, education, sports, tourism, power, connectivity, livelihood, 
etc.  have been sanctioned under PM-DevINE as on 31.01.2026. The allocated fund is 
₹2300.00 crores (₹260.45 crores in revenue section and ₹2039.55 crores in capital section) in 

31 
 
BE 2026-27. This allocation will be used to meet the committed liabilities and expenditure of 
projects sanctioned under this scheme. 
3.11.4   Since its inception, 46 projects worth Rs.5910.29 crore have been sanctioned in   
various sectors under PM-DevINE scheme till 31stDecember, 2025; out of which 3 projects 
worth ₹176.11 crores have been completed and the remaining 43 projects worth ₹ 5734.18 
crores are ongoing at different stages of progress. 
 
 
 
Observation/ Recommendation  
 
 3.11.5  The Committee notes that the Prime Minister’s Development Initiative 
for North East Region (PM-DevINE) was approved by the Union Cabinet on 12.10.2022 
as a 100% centrally funded Central Sector Scheme with an outlay of ₹6,600 crores for 
the period 2022-23 to 2025-26. The Scheme aims at rapid and holistic development of 
the North Eastern Region (NER) through infrastructure creation, social development 
initiatives and livelihood generation, in convergence with PM GatiShakti. The 
Committee would like to be informed about the progress made under this initiative with 
regard to creation of infrastructure, support industries,  implementation of social 
development projects and creation of  livelihood activities for youth and women of the 
north east region and thus leading to income and employment generation. The 
Committee may also be informed about how far the projects under this scheme have

3.12 North East Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) 
 
3.12.1 NERAMAC was incorporated in 1982 as a CPSE.NERAMAC has been envisaged and 
is functioning as not just a marketing agency for farmers and entrepreneurs, but also undertakes 
Agri Horti projects, skill curriculum supplies inputs, GI produce promotion activities, Agri- 
events and assists in setting up of horticulture value chain (food processing)etc. to holistically 
approach the aspect of   Agri-horti development. 
 
3.12.2 NERAMAC conducts various initiatives for the development of Agri-Horti sector of 
the region. These are provided as follows:  
(i) Branding of products under NERAMAC umbrella brands ‘ONE’-Organic North East 
and ‘NE Fresh’ enhanced the marketability of the NER Agri-Horti products.  
(ii) Bridging the gap between farmers and markets through establishing backward and 
forward networks in the region.  

32 
 
(iii) G.I. tagging of the authentic produces of the region for global reach.  
(iv) Clustering of farmers by enrolling the Farmers Producers Organizations 
(FPOs)/Farmers groups for procurements.  
(v) Timely supply of planting materials and equipment to the farmers and continuous 
monitoring of the same on behalf of the State Government. 
(vi) Proving a platform to farmers and small entrepreneurs at the national level through 
event participation.  
(vii) Capacity building and skill development encouraged entrepreneurship and agri startups 
amongst the farmers of the region. 
3.12.3 Key achievements and Planned initiatives of Corporations are as under : 
 
(a) Bulk Marketing done: 5500+ MT to support rural farmers of NER (last 5 years). 
 
(b) Successful participation in major expos: 1st North East India Organic Week cum 
Buyer–Seller Meet and the 4th World Organic Youth Summit in Shillong, Viksit 
Odisha,  Pragatishil Maharashtra, World Food India, Ujjwal Rajasthan. 
 
(c) Support to 70+ MSME entrepreneurs and expansion of NERAMAC retail 
presence across major locations (Delhi, Guwahati, Agartala). 
 
 
Observation/ Recommendation  
 
3.12.4  The Committee notes that agriculture and horticulture are one of the 
primary sources of livelihood in the NER and the North Eastern Regional Agricultural 
Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) has been playing a meaningful role in supporting 
farmers and agri-entrepreneurs of the North Eastern Region through bulk marketing, 
promotion of GI and organic products, participation in major national and 
international events. While appreciating these efforts in strengthening market access 
and value-chain development, the Committee is of the view that, considering the vast 
agricultural and horticultural potential of the region, the scale of operations remains 
modest. The Committee, therefore, recommends that North East Regional Agricultural 
Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) substantially scale up its procurement, 
marketing, infrastructure development, branding, and entrepreneurial support 
activities to ensure wider farmer coverage, enhanced value addition, and greater 
national and international market penetration of products from the North Eastern 
Region. 
 
3.13 North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited 
(NEHHDC) 
 
3.13.1 Incorporated in 1977, the North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development 
Corporation Ltd. (NEHHDC) has been playing a pivotal role in the development, promotion, 
and commercialization of the rich and diverse handicrafts and handlooms of the North Eastern 
Region (NER). The Corporation serves as a vital institutional link between artisans and markets 
by facilitating skill development, entrepreneurship promotion, market access, infrastructure 
support, and value-chain strengthening, while simultaneously preserving the region’s unique 
cultural heritage. 

33 
 
 
3.13.2 During 2025–26, NEHHDC focused on strengthening artisan livelihoods and creating 
sustainable economic opportunities through expanded retail presence, e-commerce initiatives, 
participation in national and international exhibitions, capacity-building programmes, 
infrastructure development, and enhanced market linkages 
 
Ongoing Major Projects of (NEHHDC) 
3.13.3 NEHHDC is implementing several major projects under NEC and allied schemes 
aimed at bridging gaps in the handicrafts and handlooms sector and generating sustainable 
livelihoods: 
(a) Ashtalakshmi Haat & Experience Centre, Guwahati 
3.13.4 With a revised project cost of ₹9.07 crores, the Haat will feature 24 permanent stalls 
and an artisan residency facility. It is envisioned as a premier cultural and commercial hub 
showcasing products from all eight Northeastern states and generating recurring revenue for 
NEHHDC. 
 
(b) Eri Silk Spinning Plant, Baksa, Assam 
3.13.5 It was made operational on 2 January 2025 at a revised cost of ₹17.90 crores. Upon 
completion, the facility will have a production capacity of 200 kg per day and will produce 
OEKO-TEX certified “Ahimsa Silk.” 
 
(c) Longpi Black Pottery Project, Manipur 
3.13.6 With a total sanctioned cost of ₹35.74 crores, the project aims to establish an Artist’s 
Village at Longpi to preserve and promote the world-renowned Longpi Black Pottery. The 
project focuses on livelihood generation, export promotion, sustainability, and cultural 
preservation. 
 
(d) Common Facility Centers- Manipur’s Chandel & Imphal East and Mizoram’s 
Thenzawl 
 
3.13.7 NEHHDC is implementing electronic Loom based Common Facility Centers in Manipur’s 
Chandel & Imphal East and Mizoram’s Thenzawl for a Sanctioned amount of ₹4.0 Cr, to provide 
support for skill development, infrastructure and technology upgradation alongwith support for 
clusters, improved labour productivity and to create common facility centres. 
 
Activities for promotion of Handicrafts and Handlooms of NER 
3.13.8 During 2025–26 (up to December 2025), NEHHDC participated in several national 
and international exhibitions, fairs, expos, and buyer–seller meets, including the Surajkund 
International Mela, Ghed Festival (Gujarat), India Textile Fair, India International 
Handwoven Expo (IIHE), Bhutan International Trade Fair, India International Trade Fair 
(IITF), Chiang Mai Design Week and Hornbill Festival. These events generated significant 
sales and market linkages, facilitated bulk buyer connections—particularly for Eri silk—
enhanced export exposure, and improved visibility of NER products.  
 

34 
 
Eri Silk Yarn Production and Sales 
3.13.9 On 2 January 2025, NEHHDC inaugurated the largest Eri Silk Spinning Plant in 
Northeast India at the Integrated Textile Park, Mushalpur, Baksa district, Assam.  
 
3.13.10 From March to December 2025, the Eri Spinning Mill recorded a total yarn 
production of 6,132 kg and yarn sales of 4,910 kg, generating revenue of ₹1.6 crore. The mill 
has significantly strengthened the Eri silk value chain by ensuring consistent production, 
quality assurance, and reliable market supply. During the current financial year, NEHHDC 
expanded its distribution network by opening four new Eri Yarn depots at Itanagar, 
Guwahati, Dibrugarh, and Nongpuh,  
 
Textile Testing Laboratory 
3.13.11 NEHHDC operates the only NABL-accredited Textile Testing Laboratory in the 
North Eastern Region, providing a critical quality assurance backbone for handloom and 
textile products. The laboratory offers a comprehensive range of physical and chemical 
testing services in conformity with national and international standards, supporting artisans, 
weavers, entrepreneurs, and institutions in product validation, certification, and value 
addition.  
 
GI Registration of Handicrafts and Handlooms 
3.13.12 Identification and registration of Geographical Indications (GI) for unique 
handicraft and handloom products of the North Eastern Region is a major focus area of 
NEHHDC. The Corporation has identified 113 distinctive products across the region for GI 
registration, of which 37 products have already been filed. This initiative protects traditional 
knowledge, ensures product authenticity, prevents misuse, and enhances brand value. 
 
3.13.13    Capacity Building and Skill Development:  During the reporting period, 
NEHHDC implemented 11 skill development programmes with a cumulative target of 13,580 
beneficiaries, against which 9,010beneficiaries were trained. These programmes significantly 
enhanced employability, entrepreneurial capabilities, and skill levels among artisans and 
youth.

SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES 
4.1 Agriculture and Allied Sectors 
4.1.1 Agriculture plays a very significant role in the North Eastern Region (NER), the 
region’s economy, livelihood and culture depend heavily on agriculture. A large population in 
the region depends on agriculture for employment. Many agricultural products, vegetable, 
fruits and grains are highly perishable in nature, food processing sectors such as drying, 
freezing, canning and packaging help preserve these products and reduce wastage. The 
Ministry apprised the Committee that as informed by Ministry of Food Processing Industries 
(MoFPI), in order to strengthen and overall development of the food processing sector 
including processing of perishable crops like fruits, vegetables, and spices, Mo FPI has been 
incentivizing setting up/expansion of related infrastructure through its two Central Sector 
Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY) and Production Linked Incentive 
Scheme for Food Processing Industry (PLISFPI) and a Centrally sponsored PM 
Formalization of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PMFME) scheme. These schemes are 
demand driven and implemented across the country including NER. There is also provision 
for earmarking of funds especially for NER, out of total budgetary allocation under PMKSY 
and PMFME schemes. Further, with an aim to encourage wider participation of stakeholders 
from NER, there are special concessions for NER applicants. Following preferential 
provisions have been made in component scheme guidelines of PMKSY- 
i. Net Worth requirement reduced to amount equal to grant sought, in comparison to 1.5 
times for general areas;  
ii. Term Loan requirement reduced to 10% of eligible project cost, in comparison to 20% 
for general areas;  
iii. Equity requirement reduced to 10% of eligible project cost, in comparison to 20% for 
general areas; 
iv. Quantum of grant at enhanced level of 50% of eligible project cost, in comparison to 
35% for general public (Subject to the maximum ceiling under respective sub-
schemes);  
v. Requirement of minimum project cost reduced to Rupees One Crore, in comparison to 
rupees Three Crores in r/o Creation/Expansion of Food Processing and Preservation 
Capacities (CEFPPC) projects [for other schemes, no such criteria is fixed].

related to food processing industries in the NER, worth ₹28.86 crores have been sanctioned,

₹2.87 crores have been completed, as on 31.01.2026.

4.3.3 The Ministry informed that under India’s Act East Policy, India has taken multiple 
measures to strengthen cross-border connectivity between the North Eastern Region (NER) 
and Bangladesh, focusing on trade, transit and people-to-people linkages through road, rail, 
waterways and power connectivity. Key initiatives include development and upgradation of 
Integrated Check Posts and Land Customs Stations (At present, 8 land ports are operational 
along the India–Bangladesh border, 6 land ports are at various stages of development and 
there are plans to develop 22 more land ports), operationalization of inland waterways under 
the Protocol on Inland Waterways Trade and Transit (At present, 6 routes are operational), 
restoration of 6 historical rail links and construction of the Akhaura–Agartala rail line, 
operation of cross-border bus and passenger train services and use of Chittagong and Mongla 
ports for NER cargo. Further, connectivity-oriented development cooperation projects such as 
the Ashuganj River Port–Akhaura Land Port Road and Ramgarh–Baruerhat road are under 
implementation, alongside cross-border power trading through the Tripura–Comilla 
interconnection. Efforts are also underway to operationalize the BBIN Motor Vehicle 
Agreement to enable seamless movement of vehicles. 
 
4.3.4 Further, the Ministry informed that under the Act East Policy, India has undertaken 
several initiatives to enhance cross-border connectivity between the North-East Region 
(NER) and Myanmar across road, trade, power, digital and people-to-people domains, despite 
challenges arising from the prevailing security situation in Myanmar. These include 
development of border infrastructure such as Land Customs Stations at Moreh and 
Zokhawathar (currently not operational after COVID & due to security constraint in 
Myanmar) and the Integrated Check Post at Moreh, with plans for a mirror ICP at Tamu; 
implementation of major road connectivity projects including the Kaladan Multimodal 
Transit Transport Project (KMMTTP). The Government is expediting completion of the 
KMMTTP, which will establish connectivity from Kolkata Port to Sittwe Port in Myanmar 
and further link the North-East Region through Mizoram. The project is expected to 
substantially shorten the distance between West Bengal and Mizoram and provide a major 
boost to trade and industry. The road component of KMMTTP comprises construction of a 
109.2-km greenfield double-lane road from Paletwa in Myanmar to Zorinpui on the India–
Myanmar border in Mizoram, to National Highway specifications, with the current physical 
progress at about 18%. The waterways component of the project, with an approved cost of 
₹982.99 crores, has been completed and was inaugurated on 9 May 2023; and negotiations on 
the IMT Motor Vehicle Agreement to enable seamless vehicular movement. Efforts are also 
underway to operationalise border haats and border crossing points, strengthen cross-border 

46 
 
power supply to Tamu from Manipur, maintain digital connectivity through the Moreh–
Mandalay fibre optic link, and improve air connectivity through direct flights, with continued 
engagement to advance these initiatives as ground conditions permit. 
 
4.3.5 The Ministry also informed that under India’s Act East Policy, the India-Myanmar-
Thailand Trilateral Highway is a cornerstone connectivity project aimed at linking India’s 
northeastern region to Southeast Asia by road, thereby facilitating direct land connectivity 
from Moreh (Manipur) through Myanmar to Thailand, and extending economic ties with 
countries like Vietnam and Laos. The implementation of the project has been done in phases, 
under Phase I (Km 60–112.141, Kalewa section), about 98% physical progress has been 
achieved, with 52 km of bituminous concrete completed and expected completion by July 
2025. The phase III (Km 39–60) has achieved around 52% progress, targeted for completion 
by July 2026. The phase II (Km 0–39, Yagyi section) remains constrained due to 
inaccessibility for over a year, with overall physical progress at about 18% and completion 
now expected by December 2026. 
 
4.3.6 The Ministry informed that Bharatmala Pariyojana, envisaged in line with the Act 
East Policy, aims to strengthen economic corridors and enhance strategic road connectivity. 
At present, around 3,035 km of road projects are under implementation with an investment of 
about ₹69,569 crores. In addition, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) 
continue to provide sustained support for national highway development in the region through 
the NH(O) programme, under which 10% of its Gross Budgetary Support is exclusively 
earmarked for the North-East Region. 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.3.7 The Committee notes that the length of National Highways in North Eastern 
Region was 10,905 Kms in 2014 and it has increase to 16,207 kms in 2025. The 
Committee appreciates the 48% expansion of the National Highway network since 2014 
and the successful delivery of strategic landmarks like the Maitri Bridge (connectivity 
from NE region to Chittagong port in Bangladesh) and Dhola-Sadiya Bridge (direct 
inter-state connectivity between Assam and Arunachal Pradesh), which have 
fundamentally transformed regional connectivity. To build on this momentum, the 
Committee recommends that Ministry of DoNER should intensify its role as a central 
coordinator to expedite the remaining road components of the Kaladan Multimodal 
Transit Transport Project which will establish connectivity from Kolkata Port to Sit we 
Port in Myanmar and further link the NER through Mizoram and the Trilateral 
Highway which is aimed  at linking country’s NER to Southeast Asia, ensuring these 
vital corridors are fully operationalized.  By leveraging dedicated funding, the Ministry 
can effectively transition the Act East Policy from infrastructure milestones into a 
robust, integrated economic gateway for the North East.

4.6 Healthcare and Education 
 
4.6.1 The Committee was apprised that under the National Health Mission (NHM), various 
initiatives are implemented across the country to improve maternal and newborn health 
outcomes, which include the followings: 
 
 Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) is a demand promotion and conditional cash transfer 
scheme for promoting institutional delivery.  
 Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) entitles all pregnant women delivering 
in public health institutions to have free and no-expense delivery, including caesarean 
section. The entitlements include free drugs and consumables, free diet during the 
stay, free diagnostics, free transportation and free blood transfusion, if required. 
Similar entitlements are also in place for sick infants.  
 Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA) provides pregnant 
women a fixed day, free of cost, assured and quality antenatal checkup by a 
Specialist/Medical Officer on the 9th day of every month. Extended PMSMA strategy 
focuses on quality antenatal care (ANC) for pregnant women, especially high-risk 
pregnant (HRP) women and individual HRP tracking with financial incentivization for 
the identified high-risk pregnant women and accompanying Accredited Social Health 
Activists (ASHAs) for extra 3 visits over and above the PMSMA visit.  
 Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN) aims to provide assured, dignified, 
respectful and quality healthcare at no cost and zero tolerance for denial of services 
for every woman and newborn visiting a public health facility, to end all preventable 
maternal and newborn deaths.  
 The Mothers’ Absolute Affection (MAA) Program is implemented to promote 
breastfeeding practices, emphasizing the importance of early initiation of 
breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding for first six months.  
 The Social Awareness and Actions to Neutralize Pneumonia Successfully 
(SAANS) initiative targets pneumonia-related childhood morbidity and mortality 
through enhanced awareness and early intervention.

Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.6.12  The Committee appreciates the comprehensive coverage of maternal and 
child health initiatives under the National Health Mission (NHM) and recommends that 
Ministry of DoNER may serve as a strategic facilitator to ensure these services reach the 
"last mile" in the North Eastern Region. To maximize the impact of schemes like Janani 
Suraksha Yojana (JSY), Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), and Surakshit 
Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN), the Ministry should prioritize strengthening the 
underlying physical and digital infrastructure—such as all-weather road access to 
health centres and reliable tracking systems for high-risk pregnancies—which are often 
the primary barriers to institutional care in hilly terrains. By ensuring that financial 
incentives reach beneficiaries and Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) promptly 
and that rural health facilities are fully equipped, the Ministry can effectively bridge the 
gap between national policy and regional health outcomes, ensuring dignified and 
quality healthcare for every mother and child in the North Eastern Region. 
 
4.6.13  The Committee notes with satisfaction the robust growth in medical 
education across the North Eastern Region, highlighted by a 172.7% increase in medical 
colleges and a 206.1% surge in under Graduate (UG) seats since 2013-14. However, the 
Committee observes a significant intra-regional disparity, with Assam accounting for 
over 50% of the total medical colleges and seats, while states like Sikkim remain without 
a government medical college and others like Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland 
and Tripura are limited to a single institution. To rectify this imbalance, the Committee 
recommends that Ministry of DoNER, in coordination with the Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare, prioritize the establishment of new government medical colleges in 
these underserved States and focus on doubling the Postgraduate (PG) seat capacity, 
which has lagged behind UG growth at only 108.2%. By strengthening the tertiary 
healthcare education pipeline in every North Eastern State, the Ministry can ensure a 
more equitable distribution of specialist doctors and a stronger, self-reliant healthcare 
workforce across the entire region. 
 
4.6.14  The Committee appreciates the multi-layered strategy for improving 
immunization coverage through Mission Indradhanush and the digital integration via 
the U-WIN (Universal Immunization Win platform) portal, but recommends that the 
Ministry of DoNER leverage its regional coordination role to address the logistical "last-
mile" challenges unique to the North Eastern terrain. To ensure the success of National 
Immunization Days (NIDs) and other activities/programmes, the Ministry should 
provide targeted support for strengthening the cold chain infrastructure in remote hilly 

55 
 
districts and incentivize Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) with terrain-
specific mobility allowances to reach unvaccinated children in unserved/underserved 
areas. 
 
4.6.15  The Committee notes that  there are 54574 primary schools in North 
Eastern Region whereas in comparison there are only 5325 higher secondary schools,   
indicating a drop in institutional availability to students as they progress. Therefore, to 
address this imbalance and reduce potential dropout rates, the Committee recommends 
that Ministry of DoNER prioritize the upgradation of existing secondary schools to the 
higher secondary level through targeted infrastructure funding and establishment of 
more higher secondary schools.  By focusing on States with steep institutional gaps and 
ensuring that these upgrades are geographically distributed to ensure "last-mile" access 
in hilly terrains, the Ministry can safeguard that the region’s youth have the necessary 
institutional support to complete their schooling and transition into higher education or 
skill development programs.

4.7.1 The Committee was informed that to promote traditional music, dance forms, and folk 
theatre of the North Eastern Region, the Ministry of Culture promotes traditional music, 
dance and folk theatre of the North Eastern Region (NER) through the Scheme of Financial 
Assistance for Promotion of Art and Culture, which includes Cultural Function & Production 
Grant (CFPG) where financial assistance is provided to NGOs/Societies/Trusts/Universities 
for organizing seminars, conferences, workshops, festivals, exhibitions and production of

and Eastern Zonal Cultural Centre (EZCC), Kolkata have been actively promoting the

4.7.2 The artists from the North Eastern States are regularly provided platforms at major 
national events such as Rashtriya Sanskriti Mahotsav (RSM), OCTAVE and other cultural 
festivals coordinated by the Ministry of Culture. Both Centres also undertake documentation 
of rare, endangered and vanishing art forms and implement the Guru–Shishya Parampara 
Scheme to encourage transmission of traditional knowledge to younger generations, in 
collaboration with State Governments, NGOs and senior artists.  
 
4.7.3 Initiatives have been taken by government for supporting artisans and weavers of 
NER in marketing their handicrafts and handlooms, both domestically and globally. The 
Committee was apprised by Ministry of DoNER that Ministry of Culture has informed that 
the Government, through NEZCC and EZCC, supports artisans and weavers of the North 
Eastern Region by facilitating their participation in national-level festivals, exhibitions, fairs

cultural festivals at Shilpgram Crafts Village, Guwahati, Stone Sculpture Garden, Dimapur 
and other venues, providing artisans with direct market access, publicity and exposure.

traditions, and indigenous knowledge systems unique to the North Eastern Region, the 
Ministry of Culture launched a flagship initiative Gyan Bharatam aimed at unearthing,

comprehensive national platform to survey, conserve, digitize, transliterate and disseminate 
the rich cultural and intellectual wealth embedded in Indic manuscripts across diverse scripts, 
dialects, languages, regions, and traditions. Beyond preservation, Gyan Bharatam also 
highlights the contemporary and scientific relevance of these manuscripts, bridging India’s 
timeless knowledge with modern scholarship.

4.7.10  The Committee appreciates the work done by the Ministry of Culture and

The Committee recommends that Ministry of DoNER may collaborate with the 
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship to address the geographical 
imbalance in training infrastructure—specifically by establishing Jan Sikhshan 
Sansthan (JSS) centers in Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim and expanding the low 
apprenticeship engagement in smaller States like Nagaland and Mizoram. By aligning 
these skill-building initiatives with the region’s emerging logistics and digital sectors, the 
Ministry can ensure that the local workforce is not only certified but also effectively 
integrated into high-value employment opportunities within the growing NE economic 
corridors. 
 
(Para 4.5.9) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the Ministry’s strategic push in securing investment 
interests through the Rising Northeast Investors Summit 2025 and the forward-looking 
integration of Industry 4.0 technologies. To capitalize on this unprecedented private 
sector interest, the Committee recommends that Ministry of DoNER should provide 
technical assistance to North Eastern States for the swift on boarding of knowledge 
partners and the detailing of the 30 identified high-tech project concepts. By 
synchronizing Uttar Poorva Transformative Industrialisation (UNNATI) Scheme’s 
fiscal incentives with the implementation of the Logistics Roadmap, the Ministry can 
ensure that the transition toward AI-powered systems and smart cold chains effectively 
reduces the cost of doing business, thereby converting regional investment leads into a 
sustainable and technologically advanced industrial base. 
 
(Para 4.5.10) 
 
Healthcare and Education 
 
 The Committee appreciates the comprehensive coverage of maternal and child 
health initiatives under the National Health Mission (NHM) and recommends that 
Ministry of DoNER may serve as a strategic facilitator to ensure these services reach the 
"last mile" in the North Eastern Region. To maximize the impact of schemes like Janani 

69 
 
Suraksha Yojana (JSY), Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), and Surakshit 
Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN), the Ministry should prioritize strengthening the 
underlying physical and digital infrastructure—such as all-weather road access to 
health centres and reliable tracking systems for high-risk pregnancies—which are often 
the primary barriers to institutional care in hilly terrains. By ensuring that financial 
incentives reach beneficiaries and Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) promptly 
and that rural health facilities are fully equipped, the Ministry can effectively bridge the 
gap between national policy and regional health outcomes, ensuring dignified and 
quality healthcare for every mother and child in the North Eastern Region. 
 
(Para 4.6.12) 
 
 The Committee notes with satisfaction the robust growth in medical education 
across the North Eastern Region, highlighted by a 172.7% increase in medical colleges 
and a 206.1% surge in under Graduate (UG) seats since 2013-14. However, the 
Committee observes a significant intra-regional disparity, with Assam accounting for 
over 50% of the total medical colleges and seats, while states like Sikkim remain without 
a government medical college and others like Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland 
and Tripura are limited to a single institution. To rectify this imbalance, the Committee 
recommends that Ministry of DoNER, in coordination with the Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare, prioritize the establishment of new government medical colleges in 
these underserved States and focus on doubling the Postgraduate (PG) seat capacity, 
which has lagged behind UG growth at only 108.2%. By strengthening the tertiary 
healthcare education pipeline in every North Eastern State, the Ministry can ensure a 
more equitable distribution of specialist doctors and a stronger, self-reliant healthcare 
workforce across the entire region. 
 
(Para 4.6.13) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the multi-layered strategy for improving 
immunization coverage through Mission Indradhanush and the digital integration via 
the U-WIN (Universal Immunization Win platform) portal, but recommends that the 
Ministry of DoNER leverage its regional coordination role to address the logistical "last-
mile" challenges unique to the North Eastern terrain. To ensure the success of National 
Immunization Days (NIDs) and other activities/programmes, the Ministry should 
provide targeted support for strengthening the cold chain infrastructure in remote hilly 
districts and incentivize Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) with terrain-
specific mobility allowances to reach unvaccinated children in unserved/underserved 
areas. 
 (Para 4.6.14) 
  
 The Committee notes that  there are 54574 primary schools in North Eastern 
Region whereas in comparison there are only 5325 higher secondary schools,   
indicating a drop in institutional availability to students as they progress. Therefore, to 
address this imbalance and reduce potential dropout rates, the Committee recommends 
that Ministry of DoNER prioritize the upgradation of existing secondary schools to the 
higher secondary level through targeted infrastructure funding and establishment of 
more higher secondary schools.  By focusing on States with steep institutional gaps and 
ensuring that these upgrades are geographically distributed to ensure "last-mile" access 
in hilly terrains, the Ministry can safeguard that the region’s youth have the necessary 

70 
 
institutional support to complete their schooling and transition into higher education or 
skill development programs. 
 
 (Para 4.6.15) 
ART AND CULTURE  
 The Committee appreciates the work done by the Ministry of Culture and the 
Zonal Cultural Centres in preserving regional heritage through the Guru–Shishya 
Parampara Scheme and national festivals like OCTAVE and Rashtriya Sanskriti 
Mahotsav (RSM). To further strengthen these efforts, the Committee recommends that 
Ministry of DoNER help local artists turn their traditional crafts and performances into 
sustainable livelihoods by integrating them directly into the region's Model Tourism 
Circuits. By creating permanent village-level performance spaces and providing better 
financial support to NGOs for documenting endangered art forms, the Ministry may 
ensure that the North East’s rich cultural identity is not only preserved for future 
generations but also becomes a key driver of local economic growth. 
 
(Para 4.7.10) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the market linkage provided through "Karu Biponi" 
a craft outlet in Santiniketan, West Bengal for exhibition and sale of handicrafts and 
handlooms products from North Eastern Region. It also appreciates organising of craft 
exhibitions and sale stalls and cultural festivals at Shilpgram Crafts Village, Guwahati, 
Stone Sculpture Garden, Dimapur and other venues, providing artisans with direct 
market access, publicity and exposure. The Committee recommends that Ministry of 
DoNER may scale these efforts by establishing a robust e-commerce platform 
specifically for North Eastern handlooms and handicrafts to reach global buyers. 
Further, the Ministry may focus on creating permanent hubs in major Indian metro 
cities and providing artisans with training in digital marketing and quality 
standardization. The Ministry may push for expanding Geographical Indication (GI) 
tagging among the North Eastern States to improve the marketability of products. 
 
(Para 4.7.11)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One hundredth Report on the Demands for Grants (2003-04) relating to the Department
of Development of North Eastern Region.
2. The Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary of the Department in its sitting held
on 26th March, 2003.
3. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied upon the
following:—
(i) Presentation made by the Secretary of the Department;
(ii) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Department for the year 2003-04;
(iii) Explanatory Notes on the Demands for Grants (2003-04) received from the
Department;
(iv) Annual Report of the Department for the year 2002-03;
(v) Written replies furnished by the Department to the Questionnaire sent to it by the
Secretariat; and
(vi) Written clarifications to the points/issues raised by the Members in the meetings of the
Committee.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on 9th April, 2003.
5. For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

REPORT
The North Eastern Region comprises of 8 States of Arunchal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur,
Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura and Sikkim. Excluding Sikkim, the region covers an area
of 255,000 sq. kms representing around 7.8 per cent of the total area of the country. It is a
distinct geographical entity connected with the rest of the country through a narrow corridor in
North Bengal thereby standing out as a classic example of cultural and geographical isolation from
the other composite States of India. The region shares 98 per cent of its borders with other South
East Asian countries viz. Bhutan and China in the North, Myanmar in the East and Bangladesh in
the South and West.
1.2 The region has a total population of 38.5 million as per 2001 census which is around 3.75
per cent of the country’s population.
1.3 The North Eastern States are categorised as Special Category States which entitles them to
receive 90% of the Central plan assistance as grants. However funds are not allocated State-wise.
Instead, Project specific assistance is released for sanctioned projects under the Central Pool. The
release of funds to the State Governments depends on their capacity to formulate sound project
proposals, utilize the funds released and the pace of implementation of the projects on the ground.
These funding sources and quantum of funds broadly take care of the requirement for development
programmes of the North Eastern States and are intended to continue till the Region reaches a
certain minimum level in terms of infrastructure development.
2. The Department of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) was constituted in
September, 2001. An extract of the amendments to the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961 containing the work allocation to the Department is as follows:
• Matters related to the planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes
and projects of North Eastern region including those in the sectors of power, irrigation,
roads and communications.
• Hill Areas Development Programme and Border Areas Development Programme in
North Eastern region.
• Non-lapsable fund for the North Eastern region.
• North Eastern Council.
• North Eastern Development Finance Institution (NEDFI).
• North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited (NERAMAC).
• Sikkim Mining Corporation Limited (SMC).
• North Eastern Handlooms and Handicrafts Development Corporation (NEHHDC).
• Road works financed in whole or in part by the Central Government in the North
Eastern region.
• Planning of road and inland waterways transport in the North Eastern region.
3. The thrust of the Department in the development of North Eastern region consists of
improving infrastructure, providing greater access to basic social services like education, health,
drinking water and sanitation, etc., expanding economic and social opportunities for all, building

2
capacities aimed at increased efficiency, creating an environment for private participation conducive
to growth, and providing a policy frame to influence in a positive manner, wide ranging economic
activities having employment/income generation potential.
BUDGET OF DEPARTMENT OF DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH EASTERN REGION
4. Grants were made available to the Department for the first time in 2002-03. In respect of
North Eastern Council (NEC) the Budget had been earlier provided by the Ministry of Home
Affairs. The outlay for the Plan Schemes of NEC for 2001-2002 was Rs. 450 crore and the same
was for 2002-03. However, in 2002-03 the total allocation towards plan expenditure for DoNER
in BE 2002-03 was Rs. 469.90 crores and Non-Plan expenditure Rs. 8.61 crore approximately
while in RE 2002-03 plan expenditure was Rs. 1019.90 crore and Non-Plan expenditure
Rs. 7.53 crore. The Ministry of Finance and Company Affairs has approved Rs. 7.8 crore towards
Non-Plan expenditure during 2003-04. The Planning Commission has approved plan assistance of
Rs. 569.90 crore for DoNER and Rs. 500 crore for the Plan schemes of NEC. The detailed

6.1 The Secretary, DoNER in his deposition before the Committee, stated that DoNER was
one of the few Departments which had fully utilised the Plan allocation for the year 2002-03
despite the fact that the first release was made in September, 2002 and second was in the end of
February, 2003. He further stated that this was the first regular budget of the Department.
PLAN SCHEMES OF DoNER
7. The Plan Schemes relating to the Department consist of:-
(i) Other Social Services
* Advocacy and Publicity
* Technical Assistance and Capacity Building
(ii) Industrial Financial Institutions
* Loans to North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd.
(iii) Non-ferrous Mining and Metal Industries
* Equity to Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC)
7.1 Under ‘Other Social Services’, the Department proposes to promote private sector
investment in the region. Accordingly, it organised a Business Summit in Mumbai on
19 and 20 July, 2002. DoNER also proposes to advocate the strengths and potential of the region
through other suitably designed programmes cutting across the Governmental and non-
Governmental sector. It also address the institutional capacity constraints of the region through
Capacity Building and Technical Assistance Programme.
7.2 Under ‘Industrial Financial Institutions’, DoNER extends long term interest free soft loan to
NEDFi. During 2002-03, an amount of Rs.15.40 crore has been disbursed to NEDFi. For
BE 2003-04, a similar amount has been approved.

4
7.3 As part of assistance to non-ferrous mining and metal industry, Sikkim Mining Corporation,
a joint venture of Governments of India and Sikkim with equity share capital ratio of 51:49
respectively, receives funds from the Central Government in proportion to its equity share.
8. When asked about the objectives of DoNER, the Government, in its written reply, has stated
that DoNER attempts to promote development of North Eastern region by creating synergies and
convergence of the various programmes of different Departments of Government of India taking
up activities in the North-East. DoNER, however, has no mechanism or mandate to implement the
projects directly by itself. This apart, for meeting the gaps in the infrastructure sector, DoNER
assists the State Governments and Central agencies. DoNER has also been regularly monitoring the
requirement of 10% expenditure by Central Government Ministries/Departments in the North
Eastern region.
9. Regarding cultural activities the Department has stated that it is taking up cultural and sports
activities in a major way. It has partially funded the Sports Complex in Imphal (Khumlanpak) where
the 1999 National Games were held. In Sikkim, Paljor Stadium has been funded from NLCPR.
Another Sports Hall has been sanctioned this year at Mokokchung in Nagaland. In Bodo
Autonomous Council area in Assam, a mini stadium at Chapaguri and apex stadium at Kokrajhar
have also been sanctioned. In the field of culture, the Shankardev Kalakshetra in Guwahati is also
being assisted by the DoNER. Besides, a large number of schools, colleges and universities have
been assisted under NLCPR. In addition, NEC has also extended support for creation of
infrastructural facility for sports. It has assisted a sports complex each at Aizawal, Silchar and
Agartala. Rs. 34.50 crore has been earmarked for Tenth Plan. The proposed outlay for 2003-04
is Rs. 4 crore. On the cultural side, Fashion Shows, Crafts Exhibition, North Eastern Day and various
other cultural exchange programmes have been sponsored in North Eastern region by the DoNER.
10. On the greater use of Doordarshan for disseminating of information pertaining to the region
the Department has informed that the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has declared the
year 2003 as the “Year of the North East”. On its part, DoNER has also taken up with Prasar
Bharati the need for screening North Eastern news and programmes on the National hookup of
Doordarshan. Besides, strengthening and upgradation of the low power transmitters in the North
Eastern region has been identified as an area to be attended to by the Ministry of Information and
Broadcasting.
11. As regards, ensuring financial discipline in the States of the region, the Department has
stated that in so far as DoNER’s own projects/schemes are concerned, a strict regime of on-
releases based on utilisation, photographs and quarterly progress reports is followed. The States
have been asked to reflect DoNER’s projects in the Annual Budget at the major and minor head
levels so that actual expenditures as per Accountant-General’s accounts can also be verified. For
the general financial discipline among the States, however, DoNER does not have a direct mandate
or authority. DoNER, however, is represented in the Core Group of Officers constituted by
Ministry of Finance which inter alia is looking into these aspects.
12. Regarding funding of more developmental programmes through Central Government
agencies the Department has stated that the budgetary allocation to DoNER is classified as
‘Assistance to State Plan’. Therefore, like State Plan, the DoNER funds are released as 90% Grant
and 10% Loan which is the liability of the respective State Governments. While DoNER does strive
to give as much projects for execution directly by Central Government agencies as it can, this can
only be done if the State Government agrees to it since it is the State Government which would
be repaying the 10% loan. With the consent of the State Governments, the DoNER has engaged
Central Government agencies like Border Roads Organisation (BRO), Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd.
(BHEL), Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL), etc. for execution of some of the
projects.

5
13. In relation to the formulation of a master plan for the region, the Department has stated
that S.P. Shukla Commission Report, 1997, is in the nature of a Master Plan for ‘transforming the
North East’. It has identified the gaps in the infrastructure sector and basic minimum needs in the
North Eastern Region.
14 As for setting up of national institutions like IITs and IIMs in the North Eastern region, the
Department has stated that DoNER is already funding the Central University in Mizoram, North
Eastern Hill University, Shillong, Central University in Nagaland, Central University in Tezpur,
Central University in Silchar, IIT, Guwahati, North Eastern Regional Institute of Science and
Technology (NERIST) in Arunachal, Regional Institute of Medical Sciences at Imphal, etc.
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
15. The North-Eastern Council was set up in 1972, following the enactment of the North
Eastern Council Act, 1971. For a long time, the North Eastern States had been demanding
restructuring of the Council so as to make it more effective. In pursuance of the demand, the
North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Act, 2002 came into force on 23rd December, 2002. In terms
of the amendment, Sikkim has become the eighth member of the Council. The composition of the
Council has been revised and now consists of the Governors and Chief Ministers of Arunachal

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
The Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) became operational in April,
1998. The pool has come into existence out of the shortfalls in the stipulated expenditure
norm of 10% by each Central Ministry/Department for the North-Eastern region. The total
amount accrued to this pool during 1998-2002 was Rs.5806.07 crore. Thus, on an average a
little over Rs.1400 crore accrued to NLCPR. Consequent upon the exercise undertaken by
DoNER to ascertain the actual size of the pool, Rs.2853.97 crore were calculated to be
available in it as on 1 April, 2002, after taking into account the debits. However, only
Rs.1318.66 crore have been released to the States during 1998-2002. The release of
Rs.1318.66 crore during 1998-2002 is less than 50% of the cost of the sanctioned projects
worth Rs.2728 crore. (Para 25)
As on date, a total of 548 projects have been sanctioned out of NLCPR with an
approved cost of Rs.3097.24 crore. In sharp contrast to that only Rs.1868.66 crore have
actually been released leaving a committed liability of Rs.1228.58 crore. Against this
requirement, a provision of only Rs.550 crore has been made in BE 2003-04. (Para 25.1)
The above figures clearly indicate that the amount being released out of this central
pool of resources is far less than the accruals to it. There are two aspects of the mechanism
evolved to ensure adequate flow of funds to the process of socio-economic development in
the North-Eastern region. One, Central Ministries/Departments (except for a few exempted)
are required to earmark 10% of their gross budgetary support exclusively for North-Eastern
region. However, statistics prove that Central Ministries/Departments have only been, able
to spend in the range of 6 to 7% out of the earmarked 10% of their gross budgetary
support. (Para 25.2)
The second aspect flows from the first one. The inability of the Central Ministries/
Departments to spend the whole of the 10%, paved the way for creation of NLCPR which
is, as stated elsewhere, constituted of the shortfalls in the stipulated expenditure norm of
10%. As stated in the preceding paragraphs, the release of funds out of this pool is less
than 50% of its actual size. (Para 25.2.1)
After having had a look at the two aspects of the mechanism evolved to ensure flow
of funds, it becomes amply clear that neither 10% norm nor NLCPR has been able to
maintain a steady flow of funds. Although, on an average Rs.1400 crore accrue to this pool
every year, the annual release out of it has hovered around Rs.300 crore or so. This proves
that there is a clear mismatch between the accruals and the release of funds. As against
a projected requirement of Rs.1050 crore for 2003-04, the Planning Commission has
approved only Rs.550 crore. The amount sanctioned by Planning Commission is on the lower
side keeping in view the fact that Sikkim has also become part of the North-Eastern region.
In this way, the purpose behind setting up of NLCPR is getting defeated as adequate funds
are not flowing out of it. (Para 25.3)
25.4 In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Government should not
only release the backlog amount of Rs.1228.58 crore out of NLCPR to enable the DoNER
13

14
to maintain the momentum of developmental activities in the North-Eastern region but it
should also ensure pro rata release of funds out of total accruals to NLCPR henceforth.
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
During Ninth Five Y ear Plan, an outlay of Rs. 2114 crore was made for NEC. Out of
that Rs.1970.90 crore were allocated to it and Rs.1937.71 crore were actually spent by
it. The annual allocation during the plan period progressively grew from Rs.324 crore in
1997-98 to Rs. 450 crore in the terminal year i.e. 2001-02. Similarly, during the Tenth Plan,
the Planning Commission has made an outlay of Rs.3500 crore for NEC. Out of this
plan outlay, Rs.450 crore were allocated for 2002-03 which has now been enhanced to
Rs.500 crore.
Thus, the pattern of allocations to NEC followed during the Ninth Plan is being
adhered to in the Tenth Plan also. In other words, the flow of funds to NEC continues to
be progressive in nature starting with lower allocation in the first year and then gradually
going up with the progression of the Plan. In contrast to NEC’s projection of Rs. 800 crore
for 2003-04, only Rs. 500 crore have been provided to it and that too when Sikkim has
recently joined as the eighth member of the Council.
Here, the Committee would like to emphasise the point that annual allocations out
of plan outlay should be on the higher side in the initial years of the plan period so that
the projected activities get underway with a head start. The Committee is of the view that
the maximum momentum should be provided in the beginning of the Plan so that its steady
progression is maintained in later years also. Besides, as a Plan progresses, the value of the
allocations in real terms declines with the passage of time. Therefore, by providing a
sizeable chunk of the outlay in the first two years of the Plan, an optimum use of the funds
can be made. In this background, the Committee is of the view that the Government should
enhance NEC’s allocation as per actual requirements projected by it.
In addition, the Government may also consider to place the unutilised funds of the
NLCPR at the disposal of the North-Eastern Council. (Para 26, 26.1, 26.2 and 26.3)
The North-Eastern Council has recently been remodelled as a regional planning body
with its emphasis on projects and schemes involving two or more States. Over the years,
NEC has, primarily, been playing the role of a central funding agency. As a result, it has
not been able to focus its attention on a balanced regional growth. In the absence of a
comprehensive planning for the region aimed at all-round development, the North-Eastern
region continues to lag behind. The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that the
North-Eastern Council should play a proactive role in the development of the North-Eastern
region while focusing its attention on regional planning. (Para 27)
VRS PACKAGE FOR SIKKIM MINING CORPORATION
28. Sikkim Mining Corporation has been incurring losses ever since it came into
existence. Efforts to revive it by way of providing budgetary grants and loans have proved
futile. As a result of that the burden of losses, interests, salaries, etc. continues to mount.
With a view to bring about a turnaround in the ailing PSU, a restructuring plan was
submitted by DoNER to the Planning Commission which has since been rejected by it. After
the rejection of restructuring plan, there is another proposal which seeks to rationalise the
manpower of the corporation by offering ‘Voluntary Retirement Scheme’ package which
entails an expenditure of Rs.2.5 crore. The implementation of this VRS package is expected
to reduce the burden of salaries to the employees to a great extent which, in turn, will help

15
in putting the loss making PSU back on track. Therefore, the Committee recommends that
the VRS package for the employees of Sikkim Mining Corporation should be put through
at the earliest. (Para 28)
IMPROVEMENT IN ROAD INFRASTRUCTURE
Roads are an important engine of growth. For a region as remote as the North-East,
the development of a good network of roads is a sine qua non for an all-round socio-
economic development. There is an urgent need to take necessary steps to bring about
qualitative and visible improvement in the condition of roads. For, poor condition of roads
will prove to be a big hurdle in attracting private investment in various sectors. Therefore,
keeping in view the crucial importance of a good road network, the Committee recommends
that a comprehensive action plan should be formulated by the Government to improve,
expand and maintain a durable and reliable road network in the North-Eastern region.
(Para 29)
TECHNOLOGY MISSIONS
30. North-Eastern region is full of natural resources such as medicinal plants, bamboo,
horticulture, floriculture, agricultural products such as ginger and potato, etc. These natural
products have a potential to catapult the region to the position of being a major base for
agri-business and agri-exports. Another bountiful natural resource is water which can be
harnessed in a big way to generate hydel-electricity. The hydel-electricity potential of the
region is 32000 MW which, if realised optimally, can transform the region as the
powerhouse of the country. Similarly, oil and natural gas is also a major potential area
which could prove to be a big help in import substitution.
30.1. Undoubtedly, the North-Eastern region is a resource-rich area. But the abundant
resources of the region have remained untapped. Consequently, it has lagged behind in the
national process of development. Today, the region is beset with multiple problems such as
unemployment, economic backwardness, low industrial development, poor social and
economic infrastructure etc. In order to overcome these problems, concerted, well-
coordinated, focused and persistent efforts are needed.
30.2 The Committee, therefore, is of the considered opinion that the Government should
launch ‘Technology Missions’ with a view to harness the immense potential of various areas
within a fixed time-frame. (Para 30, 30.1 and 30.2)
PROMOTION OF TOURISM
31. North-Eastern States are not rich just in natural resources but they are also endowed
with pristine natural beauty. This virgin beauty has, however, remained beyond the reach
of people from other parts of the country as well as foreigners due to a variety of reasons
such as poor tourist infrastructure, lack of adequate rail and air services, less exposure to
the outside world, spread of insurgency-related violence in various parts, etc. All these and
many other factors have contributed to the non-realisation of the potential of the tourism
sector.
31.1 As the times are changing and the region is now getting more and more exposed
coupled with a strong urge among the people to attain economic prosperity and self-
sufficiency, the time is opportune to showcase the region as a major tourist destination.
Therefore, the Committee is of the view that a comprehensive plan should be prepared and
implemented to give the much-needed boost to the tourism industry in the North-Eastern
region. The Committee hopes that such a step will prove to be a major turning point in the
economic development of the region. (Para 31 and 31.1)

Delimitation Commission
4. Budget Estimates of Election Commission for the year 2003-2004 includes the budgetary
allocation of Delimitation Commission. The parameters for the working of the Delimitation
Commission are contained in the Delimitation Act, 2002 and have also been detailed in the guidelines
framed by the Commission. Pursuant to the enactment of the Constitution (Eighty-fourth
Amendment) Act, 2001, the Delimitation Act, 2002 was enacted. The Delimitation Commission is
a three member body constituted on 12.7.2002, under the provisions of the Delimitation Act, 2002
# Grants of Supreme Court is charged.
∉  Approximately.

3
with Shri Justice Kuldip Singh, a retired Judge of the Supreme Court, as its Chairperson and
Shri B.B. Tandon, one of the Election Commissioners and the third Member of the Commission is
the Election Commissioner of the concerned State that is being delimited. The main task of the
Commission is to readjust the division of territorial constituencies of the seats in the House of the
People allocated to each State and the readjustment of the division of territorial constituencies of
the total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of each State. The rationalisation of the
constituencies shall be on the basis of the 1991 census figures. The Commission will also refix
the seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes on the basis of that census.
The Commission has started functioning with the secretarial assistance from the Election
Commission of India and is expected to complete its work within two years.
4.1 When asked about the guidelines for the Associate Members of the Commission, the
Government in its written reply stated that under the provisions of the Delimitation Act, 2002, the
Commission is required to delimit the Assembly and Parliamentary Constituencies in respect of all
States (excepting Jammu and Kashmir) and the UT of Pondicherry and NCT of Delhi. As per
guidelines the Commission prepares Paper-1 and Paper-2 in respect of each State relating to
distribution of total assembly seats among various districts and entitlement of the seats to be
reserved for Scheduled Castes to various districts respectively in each State. These papers are yet
to be prepared in respect of Assam, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Manipur, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh and West
Bengal where the data of 1991 census prepared and submitted by the Chief Electoral Officers is
being checked for correctness in the Commission.
4.2 The Working Papers (which includes Paper-l and Paper-2) containing detailed proposals
have already been prepared and discussed with the Associate Members from the States of Goa,
Mizoram, Rajasthan and Sikkim. They have been asked to send their dissenting notes and after
receiving their dissenting notes, if any, draft proposals will be published in the State and Central
Gazettes inviting objections and suggestions from the public.
4.3 In respect of the States of Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh,
Haryana, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh and NCT of Delhi, Papers-l and 2 have been sent to the
Associate members who are requested to attend meetings fixed during the period of 1st April to
17th April, 2003. The Members have been requested to give their proposals in writing at the
respective meetings so as to enable the Commission to prepare Working Papers with full proposals
on the basis of the suggestions made by them.
4.4 Out of the eleven remaining States, fresh nomination of 5 MLAs each as Associate Members
from the States of Himachal Pradesh, Tripura, Nagaland and Meghalaya after the formation of new
Legislative Assemblies in February, 2003 are awaited. As soon as the Associate Members are
nominated by the Hon’ble Speakers of the respective Legislative Assemblies, Paper-l and 2 relating
to these States will be sent to the Associate members calling them for meetings.
4.5 For the remaining seven States of Bihar , Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Pondicherry, Tamil
Nadu and Uttaranchal, Papers-l and 2 are ready, and the dates for first meetings will be fixed in
due course.
4.6 When asked about adoption of 1971 procedure instead of framing new procedure, the
Department in its written reply stated that in substance the procedure followed by the Commission
is by and large the same as followed by the 1971 Commission. The Minister of Law and Justice
sent a letter to the Commission on 17 March, 2003 conveying general feeling at the all political
parties’ meeting held on March 13, 2003 regarding consultation with Associate Members in the
process of formulation of draft delimitation proposals. In deference to the general feeling expressed
at the said meeting, the Commission have decided to adopt the revised Guidelines for the
delimitation of constituencies under the Delimitation Act, 2002.

to the views of the Associate Members while carrying out the delimitation exercise and has
endeavoured to do this. However, since it has been brought to the notice of the Delimitation
Commission that there is some dissatisfaction amongst Associate Members on the methodology that
has been adopted by the Commission while carrying out its functions, the Delimitation Commission
has written back to the Minister for Law and Justice saying that from now onwards the Associate
Members would be called for the first meeting soon after the Part I and Part II of the working
paper is finalised indicating the proposed allocation of assembly seats to various districts in the
State and also showing the proposed distribution of seats for Scheduled Castes among the various
districts.
4.8 During the meeting of the Committee held on 26 March, 2003 the matter came up for
discussion. In the light of the deliberations, the Committee is of the opinion that the views
of Associate Members should be taken into consideration at various stages of carrying out
the delimitation exercise.

6.0 This Department has a two-tier organisational set up i.e. the Main Secretariat at New Delhi
and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bangalore.
6.1 The main functions of the Department of Legal Affairs are:
(i) to extend advice to the various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India
on legal matters;
(ii) to carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government;
(iii) to attend to the litigation work in the Supreme Court, High Courts and some of the
Sub-ordinate Courts;
(iv) to deal with the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of Civil Laws;
(v) to authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on behalf of
the President under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution;
(vi) to appoint law officers such as Attorney General of India, Solicitor General of India
and the Additional Solicitors-General of India and
(vii) to sanction grants-in-aid to certain institutions engaged in research in the field of law,
constitutional studies and Parliamentary institutions.
6.2 The Department of Legal Affairs is further concerned with administering the Advocates
Act, 1961, the Notaries Act, 1952 and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. The Department
is also administratively in-charge of the Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange (ATFE), Income
Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITA T), Indian Legal Service and Law Commission of India.

AFFAIRS
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)
7.0 The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs in his deposition before the Committee stated
that the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal which decides appeals against the orders of the
Departmental authorities in respect of all direct taxes, has a pendency of 1,82,625 cases at the end
of February, 2003. Number of measures have been adopted to reduce pendency of cases such as
clubbing of cases having similar issues, identification of small cases for quick disposal,
identification of cases involving issues already covered by the decisions of the Supreme Court,
raising the limit from Rs.l lakh to Rs.5 lakh for appeals to be heard by a single Member, formation
of mobile Benches etc. As a result of these measures the increase in pendency has been arrested
and it is going down. Most of the Benches of ITAT are housed in private accommodation taken
on rent. There is also a problem of providing suitable residential accommodation to Members of
ITAT. On these aspects a public interest litigation is pending in the Supreme Court and the Supreme
Court has been issuing directions from time to time regarding providing office accommodation as
well as accommodation for residential purposes for the Members of ITAT. The Department has
been trying to meet the directions of the Supreme Court within the available financial resources and
there is a genuine need to construct office accommodation for various Benches of ITAT as also
to provide residential accommodation to Members of ITAT. The Department sought the support of
the this Committee for the construction of infrastructure for the Tribunal so as to ensure smooth
and efficient discharge of its functions.
7.1 The Committee recommends that the Government should explore the possibility of
including the financial proposals for the requirement of accommodation for official as well as
residential purposes for the ITAT under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the Development
of Infrastructural Facilities for the Judiciary through hundred per cent central funding.
National Legal Services Authority
8.0 The Secretary in his deposition before the Committee stated that the National Legal Services
Authority is engaged in providing legal services, legal aid and speedy justice through Lok Adalats.

8
The Authority having its office at New Delhi is headed by the Chief Justice of India who is the
ex-officio  Patron-in-Chief. Similarly, State Legal Services Authorities and District Legal Services
Authorities have been constituted in every State. Supreme Court Legal Services Committee, High
Court Legal Services Committees and Taluk Legal Services Committees have also been constituted
in every State. As per the information available with NALSA, as on 31 December, 2002 about
47.43 lakh persons have benefited through court-oriented legal aid programmes. Till date about
1 lakh 55 thousand Lok Adalats have been organised wherein about 1 crore 46 lakhs cases have
been settled. It was felt that a major drawback in the existing scheme of organisation of Lok
Adalats under Chapter VI of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was that the system of Lok
Adalats was mainly based on conciliation/compromise or settlement between the parties. If the
parties do not arrive at any compromise or settlement, the case is either returned to the court of
law or the parties are advised to seek remedy in a court of law. The Legal Services Authorities
Act, 1987, was, therefore, amended in 1995 and provisions for Pre-Litigation Conciliation and
Settlement have been inserted in the Act. With this amendment, Lok Adalats have been given power
to decide the cases involving public utility services like transport service, posts, telephones,
electricity, sanitation, hospitals, insurance services, etc., involving an amount of not more than
Rs. 10 lakh, on merits, in case the parties fail to arrive at any compromise or settlement. The cases
involving these public utility services need to be settled urgently. So most of the cases which ought
not to go in the regular courts would be settled at pre-litigation stage itself which would result in
reducing the work load of the regular courts to a great extent.
8.1 The Committee appreciates the establishment of permanent Lok Adalats which would
go a long way in bringing down the pendency of cases before the courts.
Law Commission
9.0 The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body constituted by the Government once
in three years. The Commission was originally constituted in 1955. The present 16th Law
Commission was constituted on 1 September, 2000. It consists of a  Chairman, three full-time
Members, one Member-Secretary and three or more Part-Time Members depending upon the nature
of work. At present, besides the Chairman and the Member-Secretary, one Full-Time Member are
in position. The Law Commission has submitted 185 Reports ( Annexure-I).
9.1 Law Commission Reports are considered to be primary source of law for Parliament as well
as judiciary. Law Commission present its Report to the Government, the Government then lay those
Reports on the Tables of both Houses of Parliament. Out of 185 Reports, only one Report is yet
to be presented to Parliament.
9.2 Department of Legal Affairs forwards Law Commission Reports for examination/
implementation to the concerned administrative Ministries/Departments. Final decision on a law
Commission Report is taken by the concerned Ministries/Departments and not by the Department
of Legal Affairs. Out of 185 Reports, 45 Reports were pending for implementation/consideration
with different concerned Ministries/Departments as on 28 February, 2003. As per the
recommendation of this Committee in its 56th Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000) and 61st
Report on the Demands for Grants (2000-01) of this Ministry, the Department has submitted in
written reply that the concerned Ministries/Departments must be pursued and periodical meetings
with them be called once in a month to look into the progress in regard to the implementation of
the pending Reports, they were pursued through correspondence as well as 49 meetings were held
on various dates in this Department and as a result, the process of consideration/implementation
of the pending Reports has been accelerated. Consultations with State Governments/Union Territory
Administration with a view to implement reports on subjects falling under List-III of Seventh
Schedule to the Constitution are carried on by the concerned administrative Ministries/Departments.

9
9.3 The Committee recommends that the concerned Ministries/Departments may be
prescribed a time bound action plan for implementation of recommendation contained in the
Law Commission Reports pending with them.
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT
10.0 Legislative Department is one of the oldest Departments, which was set up in the
pre-independence period in 1883 and at one time it was part of the Department of Home. The main
task of the Legislative Department is to draft Bills for enactment of new laws or amendment of
the existing laws and to advise and assist the Administrative Ministries and Departments on
legislative matters at all stages and also to process the Bills at all stages till President’s assent is
received and the Act is published in the Official Gazette.
10.1 Apart from preparing the Bills in the light of the legislative proposals, the Department also
finalises the Statements of Objects and Reasons, Financial Memoranda and the Notes on Clauses,
in connection with introduction of Bills. It also prepares the Memorandum regarding Delegated
Legislation, where required.
10.2 The Department mainly performs the following functions:
(i) It handles the legislative business of the Government of India;
(ii) Administratively handles election laws;
(iii) Administers more than seventy Acts relating to subjects in Concurrent List such as
the Registration Act, the Contract Act, Transfer of Property Act, marriage and
divorce, civil procedure, arbitrations, etc.;
(iv) It translates into Hindi, all Central Bills, Acts and translates Constitution of India and
all Central laws into other official languages contained in the VIII Schedule to the
Constitution; and
(v) It bring out reports in Hindi of decisions of the Supreme Court of India and various
High Courts. It also awards prizes for various books in law brought out in Hindi.
