15.2 The Committee came to know that one of the important reasons for shortfall in 10 per cent
utilisation of Gross Budgetary Support by some of the Ministries is due to the norms prescribed
in the Central Sector Schemes by the Planning Commission. The Committee was informed that the
Ministry of DoNER have prepared a note for the consideration of the Committee of Secretaries
(CoS) which has directed all the Ministries to examine their scheme in the perspective of the
North-east situation and obtain approval for the relaxation in these norms wherever required. The
Committee, recommends that instead of individual Ministries/Departments approaching the
Planning Commission for relaxation of these norms, the Ministry of DoNER may take this
work upon itself as it is the coordinating Ministry for monitoring the ten per cent
expenditure by all the Ministries. It should itself approach the Planning Commission for
relaxation of these norms to enable the Ministries to spend the compulsory funding for
projects/schemes in North-Eastern Region for its proper development.
16. Taking a look at the activities under the NLCPR, the Committee notices that the Ministry
has been more involved in the funding of projects as compared to their implementation. The works
of the inspection teams have only been an eyewash as they have been merely completing the
routine formalities and the physical and the qualitative aspects of implementation of the projects
have not been properly monitored. It appears that the Ministry is merely interested in meeting the
financial targets rather than physical achievements. Therefore, the Committee desires that the
Ministry should devise ways of involving the concerned agencies and general public in
addition to officials in the process of inspection and evaluation in a more effective manner.

8
The Committee further stresses that with regard to utilization of funds, the Ministry cannot
claim that it has done its job after ‘committing’ the funds for projects. It urges upon the
Ministry, that, after releasing the funds for projects to State Governments, the Ministry
should pursue with the concerned State Governments for proper implementation of the
projects so as to avoid time-overrun and thereby cost overrun.
17. Upon close examination, the Committee notices that the role being played by the
Ministry appears to be inadequate, in that the Ministry has been playing the role of a mere
funding agency for State proposed projects and schemes. The Committee is of the
considered view that the Ministry should also conceptualise and initiate developmental
programme on its own in the region within the overall Perspective Developmental Plan for
the NE Region. Considering that some parts of the NE region are extremely backward while
other regions are relatively better placed a proactive role by Ministry of Development of
North Eastern Region in conceptualising and initiating developmental projects and schemes
will result in equitable, balanced and comprehensive development in the region. In this
context, it may be pointed out that the allocation assigned to the Ministry in the
Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules which states-“matters related to the
planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes and projects of North Eastern
Regions including those in the sectors of powers, irrigation, roads and communication” does not
restrict the Ministry to envisage developmental programmes in the region on its own. The
Committee in this regard suggests that  the Ministry may, to begin with, select/review
projects which have already been approved by the respective State Governments in the
region but could not be sanctioned due to one reason or the other for their implementation
and execution in consultation with them. The Committee feels that this would bring about
an equitable development in the region due to proper and effective implementation of
projects. It is hoped that if Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region initiates
projects of its own not only the absorptive capacity of the Ministry to spend more for the
implementation of the developmental projects will improve but will also enable the Ministry
of Finance/Planning Commission to allocate more funds to it. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the matter may be explored by the Ministry in the light of its
observations/recommendations.
18. The Committee further expresses its deep concern with regard to the impact of the
schemes taken up by the Government in the North East Region, in terms of objectives
vis-a-vis achievements and concrete social and economic indicators. It recommends that the
Ministry should focus its programmes and schemes to those that will have a direct bearing
on the increase in Gross Domestic Product, increase in human development indices on
account of expenditure on education, health and infrastructure, improved literacy in terms
of higher percentage of retention in school, employability and reduction in poverty, etc.
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
19. The North Eastern Council (NEC) is a statutory body created under an Act of Parliament,
under the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region. The Members of the Council include
Governors and Chief Ministers of eight North Eastern States. With the recent amendment of the
NEC Act in 2002, NEC has become a regional planning body. North Eastern Council is mandated
to plan, implement and manage regional projects. It is also mandated to review measures taken by
North Eastern States for maintenance of security and public order and make its recommendations
in this regard. Thus, the role of NEC is to promote regional coordination and planning for
development. The Five-Year and Annual Plans and the Projects and Schemes of NEC under such
plans and the release of funds are approved by the Planning Commission and the Ministry of
Development of North Eastern Region.

9
20. The Committee had, in its One-Hundredth Report on Demands for Grants (2003-04) of the
Ministry expressed the view that the NEC should play a proactive role in the development of the
North Eastern Region while focusing its attention on regional planning.
21. The Committee was informed that there has been curtailment of NEC budget in 2003-04
to Rs.395.29 crore from Rs.500 crore. The same was, however, restored in March, 2004. The
Ministry informed that the curtailment by the Ministry of Finance was on the ground of low
expenditure during the early quarter of that financial year. Later, on the basis of the representations
from the Ministry and the Chief Ministers of the North Eastern States and the Resolution passed
by NEC, the then Prime Minister intervened and the budget was restored.
21.1 In view of the circumstances mentioned above, the Committee suggests that the NEC
should immediately commence work from the beginning of the financial year so as to avoid
the inconvenience of curtailment of budget due to low performance and expenditure in
future. It should make planned strategy for utilization of funds for its various proposed
schemes and projects. It should put in place a mechanism for continuous monitoring of the
progress of all the schemes and projects for their effective implementation.
22. During the oral evidence before the Committee on 10 August, 2004, the Secretary (NEC)
made a submission that a ‘Road Map’ for the Development of North Eastern Region was
considered at the 48th NEC Meeting held at Gangtok on 11 September, 2003. This is based on the
existing resources and identified potential of the Region and has inter-alia the following main
components:
Construction of North East Express Highway
It proposes to link all the State Capitals of the North Eastern States through all weather
4-lane roads in the valley and 2 lane in the hill areas.
Generation of Power
It will strive to facilitate generation of more power by exploiting the rich hydropower
potential of the region. For the purpose, it will monitor implementation of Power projects within
a particular time-frame as formulated by the Power Ministry or other Implementing Agencies.
Introduction of Commercial Horticulture
It will strive to introduce “Commercial Horticulture” in an organized and planned manner to
enhance production, productivity and to facilitate marketing and processing.
Bamboo Mission Project
North Eastern Region has an estimated 64% of the total national bamboo resources. NEC
proposes to take up Bamboo Mission Project as priority industrial project. Centre for Bamboo and
Cane Technology (CBTC) established by the Department of Science and Technology (DST) at
Guwahati would be the Nodal Agency for implementation of the Bamboo Mission Project.
Promotion of Tourism
In order to take advantage of the scenic beauty, diverse rich cultural heritage, exotic
wildlife, etc., NEC will seek to promote Eco-Tourism with the involvement of community. A
separate Task Force drawn from the Tour Operators, experts in the field, and members from the
constituent States has been set up.

10
23. In view of the “Road Map’ for the Development of North Eastern Region, the
Committee is of the opinion that the NEC will have to actively work on regional
coordination and also with the concerned Ministries/Departments and agencies of the
Central as well as the State Governments. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the NEC
to draw up its action plan along with financial implications thereon in this regard for the
current financial year and submit the same to the Committee for its consideration while
submitting its Action Taken Replies indicating the progress achieved in this regard.
23.1 The Committee, considering that the budgetary projection for NEC has not been
enhanced in 2004-05 as compared to BE 2003-04, is doubtful of the feasibility of the ‘Road
Map’ in the absence of parallel budgetary allocations. It, therefore, recommends that the
NEC may, after working out the financial implications for the ‘Road Map’ may submit a
fresh proposal to the Planning Commission for making supplementary budgetary allocation
for the purpose.
23.2 The Committee further takes note of the fact that, in order to implement the ‘Road
Map’, the NEC will have to seriously look into its technical and strategic planning
competency and therefore, consider this aspect while planning for implementation of the
‘Road Map’.
23.3 In addition to construction of North-East Express Highway as proposed in the ‘Road
Map’ of NEC, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should prepare a
comprehensive plan to connect every region by all-weather motorable roads within a given
time-frame.
23.4 The Committee further stresses upon the point that roads are the foremost
indicators of development of a region and, therefore, should be given topmost priority. In
the light of this, the Committee recommends that the NEC may formulate pilot projects to
connect all the villages in the region, particularly those in the border areas. The Committee
also recommends that NEC may come out with schemes for 100 per cent road connectivity
with all district headquarters of the States of North East.

ADVOCACY AND PUBLICITY
26. The Plan Scheme of Advocacy and Publicity of DoNER has been formulated essentially to

11
understanding of its unique and distinctive features. It also seeks to highlight the role of the

27. During the previous financial year, the eight States of NE Region have received 419

28. The Committee notes the progress made by the Ministry as a result of its advocacy

CAPACITY BUILDING
29. Capacity Building and Technical Assistance to the North Eastern States is the key mandate
of the Ministry. The Capacity Building plan scheme was formulated with a view to filling the gap

30. The Committee was informed that although the literacy rate is normally higher than
the national average in most parts of the States but it lags behind in the sphere of
vocational education and acquisition of skills. The Committee, however, recommends that
the Ministry should make special efforts in the sphere of promoting vocational education
and acquisition of skills by the local populace as it would go a long way in enhancing their
capacity to handle various schemes and projects which in turn would help the region in
proper implementation and execution of projects and schemes in an efficacious way.
31. The Committee notes the enhancement of budgetary allocation in 2004-05 for the
purpose, and therefore, hopes that this aspect of development will be better looked after as
compared to the years gone by . It, however, suggests that due representation of women
should be stressed upon while chalking out schemes for Capacity Building. The Committee
also feels that the focus of these schemes should be the youth, who are the future of the
nation.
VRS PACKAGE FOR SIKKIM MINING CORPORATION
32. The Committee was informed that the Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC) was set up in
1960 which has been a loss making organisation since its inception. The Committee was further
infonned that the corporation has begun implementation of a VRS scheme as the Government of
Sikkim, the majority shareholder had decided to close it as it had no prospects for revival. The
Ministry had concurred with the decision, as advised by the Planning Commission and as of
30 June, 2004, 51 out of 115 workers have availed VRS and that whatever work is there in SMC
will be given to some other organisations.
33. The Committee takes note of the VRS package given to the workers in SMC and
urges upon the Ministry to pursue with the Planning Commission to make parallel
budgetary allocations for the same. The Committee desires that the cases of workers who
are still awaiting the VRS package should be cleared within the current financial year.
PROMOTION OF TOURISM
34. The North Eastern Region has been resplendent with natural beauty, diverse culture and a

12
history of its own but it is beyond the reach of people not only of the country but as well as
foreigners. The sad part is that its tourism potential has not been properly exposed in the domestic
as well as the foreign circuit.
35. The Committee, in its One Hundredth Report had recommended that a comprehensive plan
should be prepared and implemented to give the much-needed boost to tourism industry in the region.
36. The Committee, now recommends that the Ministry should tie-up with the Ministry
of Tourism to formulate perspective plan for development of tourism infrastructure. It has
been informed that there has been a slight increase in the member of foreign tourists
visiting the NE states except Arunachal Pradesh. However, the number of domestic tourists
has shown an overall decline. The Committee feels that the uncertain law and order
situation combined with some other factors like lack of adequate rail, road and air services
and that of availability of proper accommodation prevent tourists to come to the region. The
Ministry of DoNER should pursue it with the respective State Governments in the North
Eastern Region as well as with the concerned Central Ministries for developing better
tourism related infrastructure so as to attract more tourists which would give a fillip to the
sagging economy of this region.
AIR CONNECTIVITY IN THE NORTH-EAST
37. The North-Eastern Region is plagued with excessive rainfall which does not favour efficient
upkeep of surface road. This affect the smooth movement of road traffic to and fro from the
North-Eastern Region. The lack of proper transportation system coupled with its tricky terrain
makes air connectivity as the best option for communication and linkage of the region with the rest
of the country.
38. The Committee was informed that M/s Alliance Air had acquired four 50 seater aircrafts in
2002-03 with support of NEC and in 2003-04, an amount of Rs.35.00 crore was released to the
Alliance Air. In the Tenth Plan, Rs.175 crore has been provided for the purpose.
38.1 The Committee was further informed that due to introduction of these aircrafts, all the
States in the North-East, except Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim are connected by air and frequency
of flights has increased to 139 per week from 76. There are also proposals in the pipeline to
construct Airports in Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim.
39. While taking note of the progress made in air connectivity of the NE region, the
Committee is of the view that still lot more needs to be done to improve the infrastructure
for developing better air connectivity. The frequency of flights connecting the state capitals
of the NE regions with at least four metropolitan cities of the country, namely, Delhi,
Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai needs enhancement.  The Committee, therefore, recommends
that all the projects concerning development of civil aviation in this region should be taken
up on priority basis and more funds should be allocated for the early completion of those
projects.
NORTH EASTERN REGIONAL AGRICULTURAL MARKETING CORPORATION LTD.
(NERAMAC)
40. North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Ltd. was created by an executive
order and incorporated under the Companies Act 1956 as a Government of India Enterprise. It has
been incurring losses every year since inception. Recently initiatives have been taken to revive the
corporation so as to support the marketing needs of agricultural and horticultural produce. No
allocation in the 2004-05 budget has been made for NERAMAC.

13
40.1 The Committee was informed that for development of storage, preservation, transportation
and marketing of the agricultural produce of the region, was entrusted to some NGOs. These
NGOs failed to achieve the desired results in the matter of developing these facilities. It has,
therefore, been decided to revive and involve the NERAMAC for the development of these facilities
for the benefit of the farmers.
41. The Committee fails to understand how the Ministry proposes to carry out its
intended revival of NERAMAC for development of storage, transportation and marketing
facilities in the absence of any budgetary allocation. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Ministry may take necessary steps to revive and strengthen NERAMAC and also
make the required funds available to it during the current year itself so that it undertakes
these activities to help the farmers in the marketing of their produce. It further
recommends that both the Ministry and NEC should draw up a plan for developing
infrastructure for storage, transportation, marketing etc. so that farmers could sell their
commodities at a remunerative price.
41.1 While noting the fact that a good number of agricultural and horticultural products
are being produced in the NE States, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should
take major steps for development of agro-based food-processing industries in the region
which will provide them a captive market.

The Committee, recommends that instead of individual Ministries/Departments
approaching the Planning Commission for relaxation of these norms, the Ministry of DoNER
may take this work upon itself as it is the coordinating Ministry for monitoring the ten per-
cent expenditure by all the Ministries. It should itself approach the Planning Commission
for relaxation of these norms to enable the Ministries to spend the compulsory funding for
projects/schemes in North-Eastern Region for its proper development. (Para 15.2)
Taking a look at the activities under the NLCPR, the Committee notices that the
Ministry has been more involved in the funding of projects as compared to their
implementation. The works of the inspection teams have only been an eyewash as they have
been merely completing the routine formalities and the physical and the qualitative aspects
of implementation of the projects have not been properly monitored. It appears that the
Ministry is merely interested in meeting the financial targets rather than physical
achievements. Therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry should devise ways of
involving the concerned agencies and general public in addition to officials in the process
of inspection and evaluation in a more effective manner. The Committee further stresses
that with regard to utilization of funds, the Ministry cannot claim that it has done its job
after ‘committing’ the funds for projects. It urges upon the Ministry, that, after releasing
the funds for projects to State Governments, the Ministry should pursue with the concerned
State Governments for proper implementation of the projects so as to avoid time-over run
and thereby cost overrun. (Para 16)
Upon close examination, the Committee notices that the role being played by the
Ministry appears to be inadequate, in that the Ministry has been playing the role of a mere
funding agency for State proposed projects and schemes. The Committee is of the
considered view that the Ministry should also conceptualise and initiate developmental
programme on its own in the region within the overall Perspective Developmental Plan for
the NE Region. Considering that some parts of the NE region are extremely backward while
14

15
other regions are relatively better placed a proactive role by Ministry of Development of
North Eastern Region in conceptualising and initiating developmental projects and schemes
will result in equitable, balanced and comprehensive development in the region. In this
context, it may be pointed out that the allocation assigned to the Ministry in the
Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules which states-”matters related to the
planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes and projects of North Eastern
Regions including those in the sectors of powers, irrigation, roads and communication” does not
restrict the Ministry to envisage developmental programmes in the region on its own. The
Committee in this regard suggests that the Ministry may, to begin with, select/review
projects which have already been approved by the respective State Governments in the
region but could not be sanctioned due to one reason or the other for their implementation
and execution in consultation with them. The Committee feels that this would bring about
an equitable development in the region due to proper and effective implementation of
projects. It is hoped that if Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region initiates
projects of its own not only the absorptive capacity of the Ministry to spend more for the
implementation of the developmental projects will improve but will also enable the Ministry
of Finance/Planning Commission to allocate more funds to it. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the matter may be explored by the Ministry in the light of its
observations/recommendations. (Para 17)
The Committee further expresses its deep concern with regard to the impact of the
schemes taken up by the Government in the North-East Region, in terms of objectives vis-
a-vis achievements and concrete social and economic indicators. It recommends that the
Ministry should focus its programmes and schemes to those that will have a direct bearing
on the increase in Gross Domestic Product, increase in human development indices on
account of expenditure on education, health and infrastructure, improved literacy in terms
of higher percentage of retention in school, employability and reduction in poverty, etc.
(Para 18)
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
The Committee suggests that the NEG should immediately commence work from the
beginning of the financial year so as to avoid the inconvenience of curtailment of budget
due to low performance and expenditure in future. It should make planned strategy for
utilization of funds for its various proposed schemes and projects. It should put in place a
mechanism for continuous monitoring of the progress of all the schemes and projects for
their effective implementation. (Para 21.1)
In view of the “Road Map’ for the Development of North Eastern Region, the
Committee is of the opinion that the NEC will have to actively work on regional
coordination and also with the concerned Ministries/Departments and agencies of the
Central as well as the State Governments. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the NEC
to draw up its action plan along with financial implications thereon in this regard for the
current financial year and submit the same to the Committee for its consideration while
submitting its Action Taken Replies indicating the progress achieved in this regard.
(Para 23)
The Committee, considering that the budgetary projection for NEC has not been
enhanced in 2004-05 as compared to BE 2003-04, is doubtful of the feasibility of the ‘Road
Map’ in the absence of parallel budgetary allocations. It, therefore, recommends that the
NEC may, after working out the financial implications for the ‘Road Map’ may submit a
fresh proposal to the Planning Commission for making supplementary budgetary allocation
for the purpose. (Para 23.1)

16
The Committee further takes note of the fact that, in order to implement the ‘Road
Map’, the NEC will have to seriously look into its technical and strategic planning
competency and therefore, consider this aspect while planning for implementation of the
‘Road Map’. (Para 23.2)
In addition to construction of North-East Express Highway as proposed in the ‘Road
Map’ of NEC, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should prepare a
comprehensive plan to connect every region by all-weather motorable roads within a given
time-frame. (Para 23.3)
The Committee further stresses upon the point that roads are the foremost
indicators of development of a region and, therefore, should be given topmost priority. In
the light of this, the Committee recommends that the NEC may formulate pilot projects to
connect all the villages in the region, particularly those in the border areas. The Committee
also recommends that NEC may come out with schemes for 100 per cent road connectivity
with all district headquarters of the States of North East. (Para 23.4)
REVITALISATION OF NEC
The Committee is of the view that revitalisation of NEC is an imperative need for
achieving the desired level of growth and development in the region. The Committee is
dismayed to note that no time frame has been fixed to implement the report on the
revitalisation of NEC. It, therefore, recommends that the Government should take
necessary measures immediately and implement the report at the earliest. (Para 25)
ADVOCACY AND PUBLICITY
The Committee notes the progress made by the Ministry as a result of its advocacy
and publicity campaigns. It, however, desires to point out that the beneficiaries of these
campaigns have been mostly those living outside the North-Eastern States and the genuine
artisans and artists in the remote corners of the North East do not have access to display
their wares in these campaigns. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the artists and
artisans of the region may be given technical/financial assistance to enable them to market
their products at remunerative prices. Towards that end the Ministry should also organize
cultural exchange programmes and expo within the North Eastern Region itself.
(Para 28)
CAPACITY BUILDING
The Committee was informed that although the literacy rate is normally higher than
the national average in most parts of the States but it lags behind in the sphere of
vocational education and acquisition of skills. The Committee, however, recommends that
the Ministry should make special efforts in the sphere of promoting vocational education
and acquisition of skills by the local populace as it would go a long way in enhancing
their capacity to handle various schemes and projects which in turn would help the region
in proper implementation and execution of projects and schemes in an efficacious way.
(Para 30)
The Committee notes the enhancement of budgetary allocation in 2004-05 for the
purpose, and therefore, hopes that this aspect of development will be better looked after as
compared to the years gone by . It, however, suggests that due representation of women
should be stressed upon while chalking out schemes for Capacity Building. The Committee
also feels that the focus of these schemes should be the youth, who are the future of the
nation. (Para 31)

17
VRS PACKAGE FOR SIKKIM MINING CORPORATION
The Committee takes note of the VRS package given to the workers in SMC and
urges upon the Ministry to pursue with the Planning Commission to make parallel
budgetary allocations for the same. The Committee desires that the cases of workers who
are still awaiting the VRS package should be cleared within the current financial year.
(Para 33)
PROMOTION OF TOURISM
The Committee, now recommends that the Ministry should tie-up with the Ministry
of Tourism to formulate perspective plan for development of tourism infrastructure. It has
been informed that there has been a slight increase in the number of foreign tourists
visiting the NE states except Arunachal Pradesh. However, the number of domestic tourists
has shown an overall decline. The Committee feels that the uncertain law and order
situation combined with some other factors like lack of adequate rail, road and air services
and that of availability of proper accommodation prevent tourists to come to the region. The
Ministry of DoNER should pursue it with the respective State Governments in the North
Eastern Region as well as with the concerned Central Ministries for developing better
tourism related infrastructure so as to attract more tourists which would give a fillip to the
sagging economy of this region. (Para 36)
AIR CONNECTIVITY IN THE NORTH-EAST
While taking note of the progress made in air connectivity of the NE region, the
Committee is of the view that still lot more needs to be done to improve the infrastructure
for developing better air connectivity. The frequency of flights connecting the state capitals
of the NE regions with at least four metropolitan cities of the country, namely, Delhi,
Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai needs enhancement. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that all the projects concerning development of civil aviation in this region should be taken
up on priority basis and more funds should be allocated for the early completion of those
projects. (Para 39)
NORTHEASTERN REGIONAL AGRICULTURAL  MARKETING CORPORATION LTD.
(NERAMAC)
The Committee fails to understand how the Ministry proposes to carry out its
intended revival of NERAMAC for development of storage, transportation and marketing
facilities in the absence of any budgetary allocation. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Ministry may take necessary steps to revive and strengthen NERAMAC and also
make the required funds available to it during the current year itself so that it undertakes
these activities to help the farmers in the marketing of their produce. It further
recommends that both the Ministry and NEC should draw up a plan for developing
infrastructure for storage, transportation, marketing etc. so that farmers could sell their
commodities at a remunerative price. (Para 41)
While noting the fact that a good number of agricultural and horticultural products
are being produced in the NE States, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should
take major steps for development of agro-based food-processing industries in the region
which will provide them a captive market. (Para 41.1)

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been
authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred and Eleventh
Report of the Committee on the Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill, 2003. * 
2.         In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha referred** the Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill, 2003 (Annexure I), as introduced in Rajya Sabha on 22
August 2003 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.0       The Committee held nine sittings in all spreading over 14 hrs on the Bill. In its meeting held on the 9 September
2004, the Committee heard the presentation of the Home Secretary, Government of India on the Bill and held
preliminary discussion thereon.  The Committee, then, decided that a Press Communique, inviting the views/suggestions

of the individuals, organisations, experts, institutions, etc. interested in the subject matter of the Bill, be issued. 
Accordingly, a Press Communique dated 25 September 2004 was issued.   The Committee also decided to hear the
views of some of the legal luminaries, representatives of statutory bodies and eminent experts on the subject and also to

 REPORT
 
            The Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill, 2003 seeks to amend the Indian Penal Code 1860 (IPC), the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.PC) and the Indian Evidence Act, 1892 to improve upon the existing criminal justice
system in the country, which is besieged by huge pendency of criminal cases and inordinate delay in their disposal on

111threport of home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/111threport.htm[01-07-2016 11:30:07]
the one hand and very low rate of conviction in cases involving serious crimes on the other, by introducing the
following measures :- 
 
(i)                  prevention  of the evil of witnesses turning hostile in criminal cases;
 
(ii)
                introduction of the concept of plea-bargaining; and
 
(iii)
               compounding the offence under Section 498A, IPC (Husband or relative of husband of a woman
subjecting her to cruelty).
 
The Bill also proposes for inclusion of more scientific experts to give evidence in cases relating to fake currency notes,
in addition to officers of the Mint or India Security Press, Nasik.
 
2.0       The IPC is proposed to be amended by way of insertion of a new Section 195A after Section 195 for protection
of witness against threat and inducement by prescribing punishment with imprisonment which may extend to seven
years or with fine or both (Clause2). It is also proposed to amend Sections 161, 162 and 344 and First Schedule and to
insert new Sections 164A and 344A in Cr.PC to prevent the evil of witness turning hostile (clauses 3, 4, 5, 11, 12 and
13). The proposed amendments in Cr.PC and the consequential amendments to Section 154 of Indian Evidence Act,
1872 (Clause 14) inter alia provide for the following measures to achieve the aforesaid objective:-
 
(i)         statement of witness to be recorded by Police in the case where punishment is less than seven years, at
the very inception of investigation  if reduced to writing, is to be signed, acknowledged and quickly
transmitted to the Magistrate;
 
(ii)        recording of evidence of material witness by Magistrate in all offences punishable with death or
imprisonment for seven  years or more during investigation; and
 
(iii)       summary trial for perjury and enhancement of punishment therefor.
 
The measures delineated at sl. Nos. (i) and (ii) are covered by clauses 3, 4 and 5 and the measure mentioned at sl. No.
(iii) is covered by clauses 11 and 12 of the Bill.
 
2.1       A new Chapter (Chapter XXI-A) is proposed to be inserted in Cr.PC for making  the concept of plea bargaining
as an essential component of criminal justice system in order to liquidate mounting arrears of criminal cases in various
Courts and alleviate the plights of undertrials and easing congestions in jails (Clause-7).
 
2.2       Section 320 of Cr.PC is proposed to be amended for making punishment to the husband or the relatives of
husband of a woman compoundable in case of cruelty meted out to her under Section 498A of   IPC (Clause -9).
 
2.3       Section 292 of Cr.PC is proposed to be amended to enlarge the list of Offices whose expert opinion on
counterfeit currency can be considered as evidence.  The Officers of Bank Note Press, Dewas (BNP), National Institute
of Criminology and Forensic Science Laboratories (NICFS), Kolkata and Hyderabad, in addition to India Security
Press, Nasik and Government of India’s Mints would be considered for giving expert opinion under Cr. PC. (Clause 8).
 
2.4       Amendment to First Schedule to Cr.PC as envisaged under clause 13 is consequential to amendment to IPC
under clause 2 of the Bill.
 
3.0       The three Acts which are proposed to be amended are considered to be the bulwark of criminal justice system of
the country. The proposed amendments are based on the recommendations contained in various Reports (142
nd, 154th
and 178th Reports) of Law Commission and Committee on Reforms of Criminal Justice System (March 2003) headed
by Dr. Justice V.S. Malimath, Former Chief Justice of Karnataka and Kerala High Courts. 
 
4.0       As already stated, the Bill focuses upon following key issues of criminal justice system:

(i)         Witnesses turning hostile;
(ii)                 Plea bargaining;
(iii)               Compounding the offence under section 498A IPC (Husband or relative of husband of a woman
subjecting her to cruelty); and
 
(iv)
              Evidence of scientific experts in cases relating to fake currency notes.
 
WITNESS TURNING HOSTILE
 
4.1.0    The criminal justice system is evidence based. False and fabricated evidence in the court leads to poor rate
of conviction in criminal cases resulting in large scale acquittal. The Committee is made to understand that
conviction rate in criminal cases is as low as ten percent due to perjury. Perjury is committed by the witness on
his/her own volition or under     threat/ allurement/inducement of third party.      
 
4.1.1    A witness may give false statement at the initial stage of investigation or may make false statement at
subsequent hearing under threat/inducement.  Punishment exists for the witness who makes false statement,
under    Sections 193 to 196 IPC, but punishment for the person who threatens/induces the witness is not
provided in the IPC. Punishment to the witness making false statement is imprisonment of seven years or more
with/without fine
 
4.1.2    The Bill proposes to introduce imprisonment for a term up to seven years with fine or both for the person who
threats/induces the witness to make false evidence (proposed Section 195A).
 
 
(i)         Summary Trial for Perjury
 
4.2.0    The Ministry of Home Affairs has stated that the existing general provisions under section 344 of Cr.PC
prescribing summary trial for perjury have been found to be grossly inadequate.  Thus, to check the witness turning
hostile either out of his own volition/consideration or inducement/threat, summary procedure for trial of such witness
has been provided and the maximum punishment for imprisonment has been extended from the existing three months to
not less than three months but which may extend to two years with fine, under proposed Section 344A.
 
4.2.1    The Malimath Committee has also recommended the provision.
 
4.3.0    To check the witness turning hostile, host of measures have been proposed through the amendments to the
Cr.PC.
           
(ii)        Forwarding of statement made to Police Officer to the  
          Magistrate
 
4.3.1    Under Section 161 (3) of Cr.PC a police officer can reduce into writing summary of  statement made to him/her
during the course of investigation which has no evidentiary value[1]
 in the court of law and which is also not required to
be signed by the witness. However, under Section 164, a person can make statement before the Magistrate for any
offence which has evidentiary value. Thus, the existing procedure leaves scope for the witness to change his/her
statement made to the police officer in the court of law.
 
4.3.2    As per the amendments proposed to Sections 161, 162 of Cr.PC and insertion of Section 164A  into the Code,
the following provisions would be put in place in the criminal justice system:-
 
(a)        Police Officer has to acknowledge  statement made to him/her by the witness and signed by the latter for
the offence for which punishment is less than seven years and quickly transmit the same  to the
Magistrate; and

111threport of home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/111threport.htm[01-07-2016 11:30:07]
 
(b)        recording of evidence of material witnesses by Magistrate for all offences punishable with death or
imprisonment for seven years or more during investigation.
 
4.3.3    It is pertinent to note that the signed statement made to police officer would not have evidential value in the
court of law which may help check perjury.  Therefore, punishment for perjury is intended to be enhanced under
proposed Section 344A of Cr.PC. Further, for cognizable offence punishable with seven years imprisonment, the
Magistrates are empowered to record statement of the material witnesses instead of police officer.
 
4.3.4    These amendments to the Cr.PC are suggested on the recommendations of the Law Commission as contained in
their               154
th and 178 th Reports. The Law Commission (under the Chairmanship of Justice K. Jayachandra
Reddy) had recommended in its 154 th Report[2] reference of all cases to the Magistrate which was further mellowed
down by the Commission (under the Chairmanship of Justice B.P Jeevan Reddy) in their subsequent Report
(178Report[3]) taking into account the physical and economic difficulties in appointing more Magistrates, by confining
the procedure to cases where punishment was more than ten years.  However, the Bill has proposed a mid course
between two recommendations by confining offences punishable to seven years.
 
PLEA BARGAINING
           
4.4.0    “Plea Bargaining” or “mutually satisfactory disposition” in criminal cases in its general sense refers to pre-trial
negotiations between the defendant (accused) through his/her Counsel and the prosecution (complainant), during which
the accused agrees to plead guilty in exchange for certain concessions by the prosecutor. Thus, plea-bargaining can be
described as an agreement by an accused to plead guilty in return for the promise of some benefit.
 
4.4.1    The concept is in vogue in several western countries for a long period and in the United States of America for a
century, where over ninety five percent [4]
 of criminal cases never go to trial because of the bargaining struck between
the prosecution and the accused’s attorney well before the trial commences.  So much so in American Criminal Justice,
plea-bargaining is the norm rather than an exception. This helps in getting rid of weak prosecution cases and lesser
number of trials, thus making available more time to the courts for other cases.
 
4.4.2    The Law Commission (under the Chairmanship of Justice M.P. Thakkar) in its 142 Report[5]
, considered the
concept of plea-bargaining to overcome the problem of mounting arrears of criminal cases[6]. It adduced following five
reasons as expressed by a large section of public opinion in support of this provision:-
(i)          Most people arrested, are guilty anyway;   why bother with a trial;
           
            (ii)        Why waste public money;
 
(iii)         “Plea bargaining” is a compromise; both sides give a  little and gain a little;
 
(iv)       Trials consume time and cost; and
 
(v)        It is best (for both sides) to avail it since on the one hand there is always a chance that even if the
accused is guilty and the evidence is adequate there is a chance of a slip up. On the other, the accused
saves time and money and earns a concession in the form of a less serious offence or sentence.
 
4.4.3    After considering the previous report, the Law Commission in its 154
th Report[7]  was of the strong view that
plea-bargaining can be made an essential component of administration of Criminal Justice.
 
4.4.4    The previous Committee of Home Affairs had also discussed the issue of plea-bargaining in its Eighty fifth
Report[8]
.
 

111threport of home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/111threport.htm[01-07-2016 11:30:07]
4.4.5    The Committee on Reforms of Criminal Justice System [9]            (March 2003) had also recommended
introduction of plea-bargaining in India
 
4.4.6    It is pertinent to note that the proposed plea-bargaining is not a replica of the system prevalent in USA. Under
the scheme available in USA, the settlement is out of court whereas in India it is proposed to involve the court as
adjudicator between the accused and the prosecutor by providing time and opportunity to them to decide quantum of
concession mutually and fix a date for hearing thereafter. Further, the Court has to judge whether the application for
plea-bargaining has been made voluntarily or not. The distinction between compounding of offence and plea-bargaining
of offence is that conviction is exempted in the former situation and lesser conviction/punishment is awarded in the
latter situation.     
 
4.4.7    It would not be available for habitual offenders, serious socio-economic offences, offences against women and
children and other offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more.
 
 
COMPOUNDING OF OFFENCE IN SECTION 498A OF IPC
 
4.5       Section 498A is intended to protect the women from cruelty of husband or his relative.  It has been widely
reported that this provision has been misused and is also harsh as it is non-bailable and non-compoundable.  It is
desirable to provide a chance to the estranged spouse to come together and therefore it is proposed to make the offence
under Section 498A IPC, a compoundable one by inserting this Section in the Table under sub section (2) of Section 320
of Cr.PC, wherein it can be compounded with permission of the Court. The provision has been recommended by the
Law Commission in its 154
th Report[10] and Malimath Committee Report.[11]       
 
 
 
EVIDENCE OF SCIENTIFIC EXPERTS IN CASES RELATING TO FAKE CURRENCY NOTES.
 
4.6       Presently only officers of the Mint or India Security Press, Nasik can give opinion on fake currency notes. 
Evidence from other scientific experts suffers from legal infirmity as they are not included in Section 292 of Cr. PC. 
The provision in the Bill is based on the recommendations of Ministry of Finance.

check the propensity amongst influential people/criminals/gangsters to influence the witness to change his statement.

Observations/Recommendations of the Committee
 
8.0       Under the existing provisions of the IPC punishment is provided for the person giving false evidence. The
proposed Section 195A is a step in the direction of giving punishment to the person who threatens/induces the witness to
give false statement. The Committee observes that trial could not proceed without making investigation into the aspect
of inducement when it comes to the knowledge of the Court.   Therefore, the Committee is of the unanimous view that
the investigation in such case should be completed within a time frame as to expedite the trial.
 
8.1       The Committee recommends that if an innocent person gets convicted because of false evidence tendered under
threat/inducement by anyone then the same punishment which is awarded to the convicted person should be awarded to
the person who gives false evidence as also to the person who threatens/induces to do it.
 
 8.2      Regarding amendment of Section 162 the Committee is of the view that the evidential value of the recorded
statement before police officer does not change even after getting it signed by the witness.  In some situations, it may
violate the Fundamental Right of a person enshrined under Article 20 (3) as some of the potential witnesses can be
accused also. The Committee apprehends that the provision can be misused by the police thereby increase corruption.
Hence, the Committee entirely opposes the provision as it is not a workable proposition. 
 
8.3       The Committee while keeping in mind the views of the witnesses on plea bargaining feel that as a pragmatic
approach to management of crime and streamlining of the criminal justice administration under a system burdened with
three crore pending cases, some dispensations which are fair, just and reasonable can be considered.  However,  it is of
the strong view that this provision of plea bargaining should be introduced only after putting in place the Directorate of  
Prosecution as envisaged in the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1994  and endorsed by the Committee. 
It feels that there is no rationale for introducing plea bargaining in the absence of the institution of the independent
Directorate of Prosecution and empowering the courts to settle the cases through ‘plea bargaining’ in the present set up.
 
8.4       To the query of the Committee whether the compromise between husband and wife under proposed Section
498A, would make the punishment compoundable for the relatives of husband, the Home Secretary clarified that the

8.5.1    The Bill was introduced with a view to introducing some reforms in criminal justice system. The focus of the
Bill was on the following major issues:-
 
(i)
                  prohibition of arrest of women after sunset and before sunrise;
(ii)                time bound post mortem examination in the case of death;
(iii)               making provisions of bail/anticipatory bail more stringent; and
(iv)              establishment of Directorate of Prosecution. 
 
8.5.2    The Committee in its Twenty Eighth Report presented to Parliament on 28 February1996, had suggested
amendments to seventeen clauses of the Bill. The Bill is still pending for consideration of the House.
 
8.5.3    It has come to the notice of the Committee that the recommendations of the Committee was considered by the
Cabinet. Thereafter, Legislative Department drafted a list of official amendments. It has further come to the knowledge
of the Committee that due to change of Government, fresh approval is being taken to implement the recommendations
of the Committee.  
 
8.5.4    To the query of the Committee whether it would be possible for the Government to bring in a composite Bill by
clubbing provisions of the 1994 Bill with the present Bill, the Home Secretary replied in the affirmative and stated that
such a Bill would be introduced during the Budget Session itself or in the Monsoon Session of Parliament this year.
 
9.0       The Committee then undertook clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in the presence of Home Secretary,
Secretary, Legislative Department and representatives of Department of Legal Affairs.
 
Clause 2
9.1.0    The clause seeks to insert new Section 195A after Section 195 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 to provide
punishment for any person who threatens or induces witnesses to give false evidence in court.
 
9.1.1    The Committee recommends insertion of appropriate provision in the clause in the light of its recommendations
made in para 8.1.
 
9.1.2    The Committee is of the view that Section 195 A (b) falls clearly within the ambit and scope of Section 109 of
the Indian Penal Code and that abetment is a separate and distinct offence.   Therefore, there is no need for Section
195A (b) in the proposed amendment.
 
9.1.3    Mens rea is an essential element for constituting offences under Indian Penal Code, its absence from proposed
Section 195A may lead to some unintentional/bonafide acts being covered under it. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that mens rea should be appropriately incorporated in the said Section.
 
9.1.4    Subject to the above, the clause is adopted.
 
 
Clause 3
 
9.2.0    The clause seeks to insert provisos in sub-section (3) of Section 161 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 which
states that any person who is required to be forwarded to the nearest Magistrate for recording his statement under sub-
section (1) of Section 164 A, his statement shall not be reduced in writing under sub-section (3) of Section 161.

Clause 4
 
9.3.0    The clause seeks to substitute sub-section (1) of Section 162 of Code of Criminal Procedure making the
signature of the person mandatory, if his statement is reduced into writing during the investigation by Police and the
statement as recorded shall be given to the person who made that statement, under acknowledgement.
 
9.3.1    The Committee recommends deletion of this clause in view of its observation narrated at para 8.2 of the Report.
 
Clause 5
 
9.4.0    The clause seeks to insert a new Section 164A after Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 to
make it mandatory for recording evidence of material witnesses by Magistrate in an offence punishable with death or
imprisonment for seven years.
 
9.4.1    The Committee recommends deletion of the clause in view of the view points narrated at para 5.2.0 of the
Report.
Clause 6
 
9.5.0    The clause seeks to amend sub-section (1) of Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to widen the
condition requisite for initiation of proceedings.
 
9.5.1    The clause is adopted without any change.
 
Clause 7
 
9.6.0    The clause seeks to introduce the concept of “Plea Bargaining” by inserting Chapter XXIA having Sections
265A-K, after chapter XXI of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 
 
9.6.1    The Committee while endorsing the introduction of this provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure is of the
view that constitution of the Directorate of Prosecution is a sine qua non  for the introduction of  plea bargaining, which
is envisaged in the Criminal Procedure Code (Amendment) Bill, 1994 which was endorsed by the then Committee.  The
Committee recommends that this concept could only be introduced in the criminal justice system once the Directorate of
Prosecution is put in place. 
 
9.6.2    Subject to the above, the clause is adopted.
 
Clause 8
 
9.7.0    The clause seeks to include more scientific experts to give evidence in cases relating to fake currency notes.
 
9.7.1    The Committee recommends that in sub-clause (a) & (b) the words “forensic documents” should be replaced
with the words “forensic department”.
 
9.7.2    The clause is adopted as amended.
 
Clause 9
 
9.8.0    This clause seeks to provide an opportunity for reconciliation between the husband and the wife by making
Section 498A IPC compoundable.
 
9.8.1    The Committee is of the view that express provisions may be made in Section 320 of Cr.PC to reflect the

Clause 10
9.9.0    This clause seeks to substitute clause (b) of sub-section (3) of Section 340 of Code of Criminal Procedure to
enhance the power of court to authorize an officer on its behalf to sign a complaint.
9.9.1    The clause is adopted without any change.

9.10.0  The clause seeks to bring consequential amendments to              Section 344 Cr. PC.
 
9.10.1  The Committee recommends deletion of the clause in view of its recommendation for omission of clause 12.
 
Clause 12
 
9.11.0  The clause seeks to provide enhanced and quick punishment for perjury.
 
9.11.1 Subject to the recommendations of the Committee made in   clause 5, the Committee recommends omission of
this clause.
 
Clause 13
9.12.0  The clause seeks to insert new Section 195A Indian Penal Code in the First Schedule of the Code of Criminal
Procedure for classification of offences.
 
9.12.1  Subject to its observations made in this regard on clause 2, the clause is adopted.
 
 
Clause 14
 
9.13.0  The clause seeks to provide opportunities to the parties to examine/re-examine/cross-examine the witness who
turns hostile.
 
9.13.1  The clause is adopted without any change.

10.0     Clause 1, enacting Formula and Title are adopted with some changes which are of consequential or drafting
nature, namely, “2003” and ‘Fifty-fourth” to be substituted by “2005” and “Fifty-sixth”, respectively.
 
11.0     The Committee has suggested amendments to the Bill in the light of the deliberations held thereon.  The
Committee urges the Government to give due consideration to the observations made and amendments proposed by it.
The Committee is very keen for revamping of criminal justice system and feels that Government should attempt to bring
forward a comprehensive Bill particularly in the light of reports of the various Commissions, Committees and studies on
criminal justice system.   The Committee is of the view that if that takes long time, then at least the Code of Criminal
Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1994 and the present Bill may be merged and a composite Bill be introduced in the
Parliament rather than introducing piecemeal legislation separately.
 
11.1     Deliberations took place in the Committee on the urgent need for introducing ‘Police Reforms’ in the light of the
widespread allegations of corruption, inaction and politicization of the police force.  The Committee urges the
Government for immediate initiation of measures for reforming the police system in the country.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been
authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this  One-Hundred and Twelfth
Report on the Demands for Grants (2005-2006) relating to the Ministry of 
Home Affairs.
2.         The Committee in its previous Reports on Demands for Grants had dealt with almost all the activities which
come under the purview of the Ministry of Home Affairs. However, this time besides considering the Demands for
Grants for 2005-06, the Committee has decided to give special focus to “Disaster Management” in this Report as this
subject has been transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs from the Ministry of Agriculture in 2002 and also keeping
in view the havoc and devastation caused by Tsunami not only in India but in many of its neighbouring Asian countries
on 26th December, 2004. The Tsunami tragedy was followed by unprecedented snowfall in Jammu & Kashmir in early
2005 causing extreme difficulties to the residents of the State and other people. The Committee has therefore devoted an
exclusive chapter (Chapter-IV) to this subject so as to highlight the significance and importance of Disaster
Management The Committee, besides having the presentation of Home Secretary on the subject also heard experts viz.
Dr. A.S. Arya, National Seismic Advisor; Dr. K. Radhakrishnan, Director, Department of Ocean Development; Shri S.K
Subramanian, Deputy Director General, Indian Meteorological Department and Prof. Santosh Kumar from National
Institute of Disaster Management in its sitting held on 28th March, 2005. The Committee also heard the Home Secretary
on Demands for Grants (2005-06) of Ministry of Home Affairs on 29th March, 2005 on the same day the Committee
held in-house discussion on “Disaster Management” and “Demands for Grants”. The Committee considered and
adopted this report in its sitting held on 15th April, 2005.

CHAPTER-I
OVERVIEW
            Maintenance of internal security in the country is the primary responsibility of the Ministry of Home Affairs. In
addition, the Ministry also shoulders the following broad responsibilities:
            (i)         Issue of Notification in respect of Appointment of President/Vice-President, Prime Minister and
Members of the Union Council of Ministers,
            (ii)        Appointment of Governors and Lt. Governors;
            (iii)       Regulation of Pay and Allowances of the Ministers;
            (iv)       Carrying out Census in India once every ten years,
            (v)        Management of the International Borders;
            (vi)       Management and Deployment of the Central Police Forces;
            (vii)      Centre-States Relations/Inter-State Relations;
            (viii)      Administration of Union Territories;
            (ix)       Implementation of the Provisions of the Official Language Act, 1963;
            (x)        Maintenance of Communal harmony and Promotion of National Integration;
            (xi)       Co-ordination of Policy Relating to Human Rights;
            (xii)      Providing Relief and Rehabilitation to Refugees/Displaced Persons;
            (xiii)      Regulation of Entry of Foreigners into India;
            (xiv)     Grant of Pension and Other Benefits to Freedom Fighters;
            (xv)      Prevention and combat of drug abuse and drug trafficking;
            (xvi)     Formulation and implementation of National Disaster Management Programme; and
            (xvii)     Border Area Development Programme.
2.         To discharge the above responsibilities, the Ministry has been divided into following six constituent
Departments:
            (i)         Department of Internal Security;
            (ii)        Department of States;
            (iii)       Department of Official Language;
            (iv)       Department of Home;
            (v)        Department of Jammu and Kashmir Affairs; and
            (vi)       Department of Border Management.
2.1       The Department of Internal Security deals with Police, Law and Order and Rehabilitation, Department of States
deals with Centre-State relations, inter-State relations, Union Territories and Freedom Fighters’ Pension; Department of
Official Language is concerned with the implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating to Official
Language and provisions of the Official Language Act, 1963; Department of Home deals with notification of
assumption of office by the President and Vice-President, notification of appointment of the Prime Minister and other
Ministers, etc; Department of Jammu and Kashmir Affairs deals with all constitutional provisions with respect to the
State of Jammu and Kashmir and all other matters relating to the State of Jammu and Kashmir excluding those with

which the Ministry of External Affairs is concerned; Department of Border Management deals with management of
international borders including coastal borders.
2.2       The Ministry is under the overall charge of Home Minister assisted by three Ministers of State. The Department
of Official Language has a separate Secretary and functions independently. All Departments of the Ministry except the
Department of Official Language are interlinked and are headed by the Home Secretary who is assisted by Secretary
(Border Management), one Special Secretary, three Additional Secretaries and seventeen Joint Secretaries. The Ministry
is further divided into seventeen divisions for administrative purposes and are concerned with the tasks mentioned
below for each division:----
            (i)         Centre State Division
                        The Division deals with Central-State relations, including working of the Constitutional provisions
governing such relations; appointment of Governors; creation of new States; nominations to Rajya Sabha/Lok Sabha;
Inter-State Boundary disputes; over-seeing the crime situation in States, etc.
            (ii)        Internal Security Division
                        The Division deals with matters relating to internal security, including anti-national and subversive
activities of various groups/extremist organizations.
            (iii)       Police Division
                                    The Division functions as the cadre controlling authority of IPS officers and also deals with all
matters relating to Central Police Forces, including their deployment.
            (iv)       Union Territories Division
                        The Division deals with all legislative and Constitutional matters relating to Union Territories including
Delhi and Pondicherry. It also functions as the cadre controlling authority of Arunachal, Goa, Mizoram Union
Territories (AGMUT) cadre of IPS/IAS as also Delhi Andaman Nicobar Islands Civil Service (DANICS)/ Delhi
Andaman Nicobar Islands Police Service (DAMPS). It is also responsible for overseeing the crime situation in UTs.
            (v)        North-Eastern Division
                        The Division deals with the law and order situation in North-Eastern States, including matters relating to
insurgency and talks with various extremist groups operating in that region.
            (vi)       Jammu & Kashmir Division      
                        The Division deals with the Constitutional matters including Article 370 and general policy matters in
respect of J&K and terrorism/militancy in that State; it is also responsible for implementation of the PM’s Package for
J&K.
            (vii)      Foreigners Division
                        The Division deals with all matters relating to Foreigners Act and Passport (Entry into India) Act,
Registration of Foreigners Act, the Citizenship Act, and the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act. It also controls
Bureau of Immigration.
            (viii)      Freedom Fighters andRehabilitation Division
                        The Division frames and implements the Freedom Fighters Pension Scheme and the schemes for
rehabilitation of migrants from former West Pakistan/East Pakistan and provision of relief to Srilankan and Tibetan
refugees.
            (ix)       Human Rights Division
                        The Division deals with matters relating to the Protection of Human Rights Act and also matters relating
to national integration and Ayodhya Affairs.
            (x)        Disaster Management Division
                        The newly created Division is responsible for coordination of relief measures in the event of natural
calamities and man-made disasters (except drought and epidemics).
            (xi)       Border Management Division
                        This Division deals with all matters relating to management of international borders.
            (xii)      Police Modernization Division
                        The Division handles all items of work relating to modernisation of State Police Forces,
provisioning/procurement of various items for modernisation of Central Police Forces, police reforms, police training
and VlP, Installation Security.
            (xiii)      Policy Planning Division
                        It deals with matters relating to policy formulation in respect of counter-terrorism, international
covenants, bilateral assistance treaties and related items of work.
            (xiv)     Finance Division

CHAPTER-III
SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES OF THE MINISTRY
Rehabilitation of J&K Migrants and Security related Expenditure (SRE)
8.0       The targeted attacks by the militants against civilians in the initial phases of the terrorist violence in J&K forced
a large number of Kashmiri Pandits and a sizeable number of Sikhs and other Hindus and a few Muslims-to migrate
from the Valley in 1990s. There were 56487 migrant families as per official records. The Central Government initiated a
policy to provide relief and rehabilitation to such families/people. The thrust of the policy was to minimise the
difficulties and hardships of the migrants and provide a reasonable amount of sustenance and support. Various State
Governments/UT Administrations were reimbursed by the Central Government for providing relief to such Migrants.
8.1.0    On being asked about the reasons for shortfall in the performance of the scheme of rehabilitation of J&K
Migrants and a saving of Rs. 184 crore, the Ministry clarified that the provision of funds were made under “Security
Related Expenditure” and “Relief and Rehabilitation” for J&K for the financial year 2004-05 taking into consideration
the expenditure incurred during the preceding year, as well as the anticipated expenditure during the year. The Ministry
also informed that a Committee was set up to look into the condition of the migrants who were till now living in one
room tenements. It was further stated that since the families living in relief camps have grown and one room tenement is
highly inadequate for them for proper living there is need for at least two room tenements. The Ministry informed that it
has started making efforts to convert one-room tenements into two rooms by merging two tenements.
8.1.1    The Ministry has furnished the details of the BE & RE, final expenditure, savings for SRE and Relief and
Rehabilitation as follows:—

8.1.2    Following reasons have been attributed by the Ministry for the savings under SRE and Relief and Rehabilitation
for the State of J&K:—
            (i)         Surrender of a provision of Rs. 40 crore which was earmarked for Parliamentary Elections 2004. As the
elections were held ahead of schedule, expenditure was met from the budgetary allotment of 2003-04;
            (ii)        Items like arms, ammunitions, vehicles, security and communication equipments, security works
previously funded under SRE were transferred to Police Modernisation Schemes during the financial year 2004-05.
Accordingly, a provision of Rs. 60 crore under SRE was transferred to Police Modernisation Scheme by re-
appropriation for release to the Government of Jammu and Kashmir;
            (iii)       SRE schemes are operated on a reimbursement basis. Because of heavy snowfall and avalanches in the
State, the State Government has claimed less amount of reimbursement;
            (iv)       The reasons for saving under Relief and Rehabilitation inter-alia include less expenditure on surrender
of militants under the new policy than anticipated, slow pace of the construction of 200 flats at Budgam for
rehabilitation of Kashmiri migrants and difficulties faced in the utilization of funds earmarked for shifting of villages on
LoC; and

            (v)        Above all, the scheme is operated on reimbursement basis. Since the State is always under resource
constraints, it is not in a position to incur the expenditure from its own resources to claim reimbursement on a regular
basis. The recent heavy snowfall and avalanche could have affected the compilation of expenditure from the field units
for preferring the claims promptly, thereby adding further increase in savings.
8.2       Replying to a query about commencement of the scheme for the rehabilitation of J&K Migrants and quantum of
expenditure spent so far, the Ministry has informed that Relief to Kashmiri Migrants is being provided since the
migration started in 1990. Till 2003-04, an expenditure of Rs.653.85 crore has been incurred on tents, cash assistance,
free ration, civic amenities, construction of one-room tenements, improvement of infrastructure and grant for
camps/schools. The expenditure was reimbursed under ‘Security Related Expenditure’. During the current financial
year, an amount of Rs. 35.74 crore has been reimbursed as ‘Assistance to Kashmiri Migrants’. In addition, an amount of
Rs. 6.60 crore was provided under PM’s Special Package in 1996 for construction of one-room tenements for migrants.
The Committee was also informed that a study team of Advisor, Planning Commission and Joint Secretary in Ministry
of Home Affairs had studied the living conditions of migrant camps. The team had found living conditions grossly
inadequate.
8.3       The Committee expresses its deep concern over the living conditions in rehabilitation camps of Kashmiri
migrants in Jammu and Delhi and Government’s dilemma and lack of clear vision on the future of these migrants. The
Committee is of the considered view that the migrants should be sent back to the valley only when adequate security of
their lives and properties is ensured. Keeping in view the living conditions in the camps, the Committee feels that
Government instead of projecting a saving Rs. 174 crore under Relief and Rehabilitation, should have utilised the full
amount allocated under the said head for improving the living condition in these camps. The Committee is also of the
view that instead of conducting studies on migrants some concrete steps to improve their living conditions should be
taken urgently.
Police strengthening on Indo-Nepal Border
9.0       The stretch of 1751 Kms. of Indo-Nepal border covering 5 States and 20 districts is now being guarded by the
Shasastra Seema Bal (SSB). Its charter of duty was amended on the recommendation of the Group of Ministers under
the policy of ‘One border One force’. Earlier the Indo-Nepal border was guarded by BSF and ITBP. Besides that, the
respective State Police also take care of the security aspects in the area for which the Ministry of Home Affairs has a
special scheme of reimbursement of expenditure on Police infrastructure and intelligence network.
9.1       On being asked about the reasons for shortfall in the ‘Police strengthening on Indo-Nepal border’ the Ministry
has stated that pursuant to the acceptance of recommendations of Group of Ministers on Reforming the National
Security System by Government of India, the State Governments having border with Nepal were asked to send proposal
for strengthening of policing infrastructure and intelligence network in their respective areas. A provision of Rs.21 crore
was kept in the BE 2004-2005 for reimbursing the expenditure to be incurred by the respective State Governments on
police strengthening and intelligence network etc.
9.2       The Ministry further stated that while reviewing the scheme it was found that there was a lot of overlapping
between the proposed scheme and the scheme of Modernization of Police Forces (MPF). The MPF scheme also
provides for similar assistance to the State Governments for modernizing their police forces. It was, therefore, felt that it
would be administratively prudent to link this scheme with the existing scheme of Modernization of Police Forces by
providing a special component under the MPF scheme for giving assistance to the States having border with Nepal to
strengthen their policing and intelligence network. Due to this change in policy necessitated by administrative and
financial propriety, the funds kept for this purpose in BE 2004-2005 could not be utilized under the specific scheme.
However, the same were reappropriated at the RE stage and utilized in some other schemes.
9.3.0    The Committee feels that the scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces is taking proper care for strengthening
infrastructure and intelligence network in the States bordering Nepal. However, in light of the recent spurt in Maoist
violence in Nepal and its percolation to bordering States affected by Naxalism, the Ministry should take special
measures to strengthen Policing on the Indo-Nepal Border.
9.3.1    The Committee also recommends for empowering and strengthening of SSB, the border guarding force on the
Indo-Nepal border so as to curb not only the ISI activities through this route but also the Maoist groups in assisting the
MCC. It also feels that the Ministry should explore the possibility of amending the Indo-Nepal Treaty so as to make it
compulsory for everybody crossing the border to have his identity proof.

Multipurpose National Identity Cards (MNICs) based on this register to all citizens of the country, with the main
purpose of providing a credible individual identification system and simultaneous use of MNIC for several multifarious

Modernisation of Police Forces
11.0     “Police” being a State Subject, its modernisation is the primary responsibility of the State Governments.
However, the Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing a Non-plan Scheme for Modernization of State Police
Forces since 1969-70 to supplement the efforts of the State Governments in modernizing their police forces. The
Scheme provided assistance to the State Governments on 50% “Grants-In-Aid” and 50% loan basis. In view of the
changing situation of internal security in the country, the annual Central assistance under the scheme was pegged at
Rs.1000 crore in 2000-01 which was further enhanced to Rs. 1400 crore from 2003-04. While enhancing the annual
Central allocation during 2003-04, it was also decided to give the Central assistance only as “Grants-in-Aid”. The cost-
sharing basis was also changed by grouping the States into three categories A, B1 and B2 depending on the level of
insurgency/terrorism including cross-border terrorism being faced by the State and the funding pattern was decided as
100%, 75% and 60% respectively to these three categories of States. The Ministry is further considering the
recommendation of the Committee to group all the States in two categories (A&B) only.
11.1     On being asked about the effectiveness of the scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces of the States, the
Ministry has stated that the Scheme has made perceptible impact, as proper buildings for police stations/outposts taken
up under the Scheme has provided safe and secure environment, construction of houses for police personnel and
provision of modern weaponry have boosted their morale. From the reports made available by the States and as per the
interim impact assessment report submitted by the Bureau of Police Research & Development (BPR&D), the scheme
has performed well during the last three years and it has made perceptible changes in police mobility, communication,
weapons, housing satisfaction level and Police Station buildings. Besides that, according to BPR&D, the forensic
science laboratories in the States are getting modernized also; for instance, the State Forensic Science Laboratory of
Andhra Pradesh got ISO-9002 Certificate also. Forensic Science Laboratory in Gujarat could add Brain-mapping and
Narco-analysis. State Government of Andhra Pradesh could launch an ambitious computerization project named E-cops.
Gujarat, Haryana and West Bengal have established Wide Area Networks. Training infrastructure in most States
particularly Assam and Haryana have been upgraded. State police are now being provided bullet­ proof vehicles, mine
protected vehicles, bomb detection and disposal equipment. Modern control rooms have been set at major cities. Reports
received from the States also indicate that enhanced mobility and provision of modern communication equipment have
brought down response time of the police force.

11.4     In the light of the fact that the scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces has a significant effect on the morale
and strength of the Police Forces of the States, the Committee endorses the proposal of the Ministry for grant of Rs.
