welcomed Shri Sitaram Yechury, a newly nominated member to the Committee. The Chairperson
then apprised the Committee that it had selected “Administration of Union Territories” as one of
the subjects for examination and report and also visited three Union Territories viz. Andaman and
Nicobar Islands, Pondicherry and Chandigarh to have first hand experience of the working of the
administrations of those UTs and had interacted with a number of public representatives/senior
officers in that connection. She also informed the members about the exemption sought by the
Home Secretary from personal appearance before it in view of his meeting with the Home
Secretary of Bangladesh and requesting that the Special Secretary (Home) may be permitted to
attend the sitting of the Committee on his behalf. She told the members that she had granted the
request of the Home Secretary.
2.1 The Chairperson, thereafter, welcomed the representatives of Ministry of Home Affairs and
other Ministries/Departments to the meeting and briefly mentioned the purpose of the visits of the
earlier and the present Committees to three UTs, viz. Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Pondicherry
and Chandigarh. She also shared the views of the local representatives of the respective UTs as
gathered by the Committee during its visits, with the officers of the Ministry of Home Affairs. She
stated that the Committee’s Secretariat had received the replies to the questionnaire on those issues.
Lastly, she mentioned that the Committee would view/hear the presentations/views of Chief
Secretaries of UTs of Pondicherry, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Chandigarh in that sequence.
2.2 She then referred to the visit of the Committee to Pondicherry and the issues which came
before the Committee like statehood to the UT with special category status and the rehabilitation
after the Tsunami disaster. She invited the Chief Secretary of Pondicherry to express his views
freely on the issue of statehood and governance, problems related to it, etc.

59
3.0 The Chief Secretary, Pondicherry thanked the Chairperson and Members of the Committee
for the visit to Pondicherry. He mentioned that unlike Delhi, law and order and police had been
entrusted to the UT Administration of Pondicherry. He then stated that, at present, the financial
position of the UT Government was very weak as a result of which it had to depend upon the
Centre for assistance upto the level of sixty to seventy per cent of its budget. Grant of Statehood
to Pondicherry without special category status, would halt the progress of developmental projects
of the UT (Airport and port in Karaikal region) due to lack of resources. He stated that the flow
of resources from Centre upto the extent of 60-70% was a must for the all-round development
of Pondicherry. Furthermore, UT of Pondicherry also received support from Union Ministries/
Departments in view of its position as Union Territory. He therefore, laid emphasis on conferment
of special category status as part of the issue of granting statehood to Pondicherry.
3.1 The Special Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs stated that per capita income of UT
of Pondicherry is double that of Tamil Nadu, which was attributable to tremendous inflow of
central funds for the UT. He also apprised that the matter of granting special category status had
been examined a number of times by the Union Government and it was not found to be a viable
proposition for several reasons.
4.0 Some Members also sought clarification on the grant of statehood to Pondicherry. A
Member was of the view that it was not the question of financial position of the UT rather it was
the aspirations of the people which had to be respected. In that context, he referred to the
resolutions passed by the Legislative Assembly of Pondicherry for special category status alongwith
statehood to Pondicherry. He also referred to the graduation of Goa to a State from the position
of UT even though being financially weak. He argued that the difference between special category
state and ordinary state in terms of central assistance is only forty per cent. He requested Chief
Secretary and Special Secretary, Home to examine the recommendations of Twelfth Finance
Commission with regard to flow of resources to States where under States were bound to gain
more compared to Union Territories. He also brought to the notice of the Committee that ninety
per cent of population belonging to SC/ST were not enjoying the benefit of reservation in
employment and education since 1996. Moreover, State Government had very limited role in grass-
root level planning. He also suggested that after the grant of statehood, the UT would be able to
borrow at low interest rates from World Bank, Asian Development Bank and to finance its
development activities/infrastructure like airport, ports, roads, etc. and summed up by saying that
the will of the people must be respected.
4.1 In response to the query of the Chairperson regarding granting special category status to
Pondihcerry, the Special Secretary mentioned that Pondicherry did not fulful the criteria decided
upon by the Planning Commission for the purpose, although Eleventh Finance Commission
recommended for special category status in the event of graduation of the UT of Pondicherry to
a State. He also stated that at the moment, statehood was not a viable proposition, which might
materialize within the next five to ten years. To a query of the Chairperson as to the availability
of administrative power to Chief Minister, the Chief Secretary conceded that all important files
went to the Lt. Governor which was not the case in States where Chief Minister was the final
authority to decide.
4.2 Another Member was of the view that the criteria for statehood like economic status, threat
perception from adjoining country, strategic locations, tribal population etc. as laid down by the
Planning Commission had been fulfilled by Pondicherry. He also referred to a Committee appointed
to look into the viability of granting special category statehood to Pondicherry whose suggestion
in this regard was agreed in principle by the Government headed by Shri P.V . Narsimha Rao.
However, it was shelved thereafter.
4.3 Replying thereto the Joint Secretary in the Planning Commission stated that the decision
with respect to Special Category status was taken by the National Development Council (NDC).

60
The Committee was subsequently informed that the issue of statehood to UT of Pondicherry was
not referred to the National Development Council as it was rejected by the Planning Commission
itself.
4.4 Another Member wanted to know when was the last time special category status granted
to a State; the name of the State; when were those criteria drawn; and whether those had since
been reviewed. It was also queried whether all States which had been accorded special category
status fulfilled the criteria laid down by the Planning Commission and whether the Constitution of
India was ever amended to accord special category status to the State.
4.5 A Member also raised the issue of functioning of four private medical colleges in
Pondicherry, which were not following the reservation policy. The action taken by the Ministry in
that regard was also enquired.
4.6 Yet another Member brought to the notice of the Committee that the capital city of
Pondicherry did not enjoy the status of B-II for HRA purpose although for CCA it enjoyed that
status. Like a small village in A & N Islands, the city of Pondicherry enjoys C-class status for that
purpose. Port Blair and Panaji had been accorded B-I status having a population of 93,000 and 1.25
lakh, respectively. But Pondicherry having a population of 5.5 lakh (2.2 lakh in Pondicherry
municipality) had been denied B-II status. He opined that B-II status to the city of Pondicherry was
long overdue, which drew support from the Chief Secretary as well as the Committee, in view of
the historical importance of that capital city. He also pointed out that the demand for according
Scheduled Tribe status to five communities (Irular, Malaikuravan Kattunayakan, Yerukula, Kuruman)
who are original inhabitations of Pondicherry had been pending for more than fifteen years with
the Government of India. That was due to the confusion primarily created by the office of
Registrar General of India treating them as migrant tribals even though T. Subramanyam Naidu
Committee as well as Pondicherry Legislative Assembly through its resolution had recognized them
as original inhabitants of Pondicherry. Those communities were not recognized as ST as they did
not conform to the five indicators laid down by the Lokur Committee. A member wanted to know
as to whether any Committee reviewed the essential characteristics laid down by the Lokur
Committee for identifying tribals; whether those criteria were defined while States were being
reorganized, etc. Another member sought modification of the indicators prescribed by Lokur
Committee. A member mentioned that STs of other States were entitled to get the benefit of
reservation in Pondicherry thus discriminating and denying social justice to those communities.
Some Members felt that those tribals should be immediately given reservations for the sake of
equity and social justice.
4.7 A Member raised a query regarding rehabilitation in Tsunami affected area and wanted
immediate release of funds for constructing permanent houses. He also raised the questions of not
granting freedom fighter’s pension to about 50-60 freedom fighters allegedly on the ground of lack
of evidence of their imprisonment; power to transfer Government lands to private party and vice
versa; and creation of Pondicherry Civil Service Commission and the Police Service Commission, etc.
4.8 Members were of the view that the elections to the Panchayati Raj Institutions should be
held at the earliest and those should be involved in implementing the Centrally Sponsored Schemes.
A Member enquired from the Chief Secretary about the administration in the Pondicherry prison
where spurious liquor was being smuggled leading to death of prisoners.
4.9 The Special Secretary (Home) and Chief Secretary, Pondicherry replied to some of the
queries of the Members and promised to furnish the detailed replies to the rest later.
(The witnesses then withdrew)
5.0 The Chairperson then welcomed the Chief Secretary, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and his
colleagues and sought the vie ws of the Administration about creation of the Legislative Assembly

61
for the UT; representation in Rajya Sabha; powers available with the UT administration vis-a-vis
the Ministry of Home Affairs, etc.
6.0 The Chief Secretary apprised the Committee that all the developmental activities in the
Islands were being done through the District Rural Development Authority headed by the
Development Commissioner. However, Tribal Councils were involved wherever necessary. He also
stated that although power had been devolved to Panchayati Raj/Zila Parishad but the process was
slow, which needed to be expedited to meet the aspirations of the people which was in favour of
creation of Legislative Assembly for the UT. He then observed that the issue whether there should
be an Assembly or not, may be decided by the Ministry of Home Affairs and the matter may be
left to them. He stated that the main problem of the Administration was with regard to recruitment
of the staff as all the recruitments were routed through the Union Public Service Commission
(UPSC) or the Staff Selection Commission (SSC) and the Administration had no power for direct
recruitment. The ban imposed by the Government of India on recruitment had also created a lot
of problem for the Administration which was grappling with the matter of shortage of staff.
6.1 Speaking on the issue of creation of a Legislative Assembly for the UT, the Special
Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs stated that the matter had been examined time and again
in the Ministry and did not find favour. He stated that in 1997 the Union Cabinet had rejected the
demand for the Assembly for the UT.
6.2 The Chairperson made a query relating to the history of the demand for the Assembly and
the fora at which that demand was placed by the Ministry of Home Affairs and with what results.
The Special Secretary replied that a written note would be furnished to the Committee.
6.3 Members also raised queries such as use of Andaman and Nicobar Islands as an Exclusive
Economic Zone; commercial exploitation of the hydrocarbons; and improvement of aqua-maritime
culture to enhance the income of the Islands and the country. Issues such as intrusion by foreign
poacher, growing influx of people from the mainland in search of employment, bootlegging and the
problems connected with development were also raised. It was opined that those issues led to
increase in crime rates and suffering of the people, and thus justifying the demand for an Assembly.
6.4 Some members also raised queries regarding recruitment; the need for one time relaxation
of ban on recruitment, problem arising out of Tsunami tragedy, future plans for bringing the tribals
to mainstream, etc.
6.5 The Special Secretary, Home and the Chief Secretary, Andaman and Nicobar Islands replied
to some of the queries and promised to furnish written replies to the rest.

3.0 The Home Secretary briefly touched upon the administrative set-up of Chandigarh starting
from the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, under which the Union Territory of Chandigarh was
constituted, to the present dispensation headed by an Administrator. He also touched upon other
mechanisms viz. Home Minister’s Advisory Committee and Advisory council to Advisor in addition

Chandigharh, which was a political issue between two states (Haryana and Punjab), it would be
impractical to have a Legislative Assembly there. However, he was not in favour of creation of a
Pradesh Council and revival of the post of Chief Commissioner of Chandigarh. However, he
advocated the proposal for creation of a Metropolitan Planning Committee consisting of Urban
Chandigarh and eighteen villages.

3. The Committee held interaction with the District level Officers of Nagapattinam in Tamil
Nadu at the District Collectorate on their experience in providing rescue, relief and rehabilitation in
the aftermath of Tsunami.
4. The District Collector, Nagapattinam and his colleagues apprised the Committee in detail of
the devastating effect of Tsunami on the coastal areas of the district and the measures taken by
the Government to rescue the victims and provide relief and rehabilitation to the affected people,
through slide presentations. 187.9 km coastline of the district was affected by Tsunami, which hit
it within five hours from the epicentre at Sumatra. The loss of human life was 6650 in
Nagapattinam out of the total figure of 8018 killed in the State of Tamil Nadu, Tsunami waves rose
30-60 feet high and hit the coastal habitation causing widespread loss of lives, destruction of
houses and vegetation. The number of casualties was more in case of women than men. A number
of tourists were also there. Chief Minister of the State visited the affected places on 26,
27 and 30 December, 2004. All the affected persons were shifted to temporary shelters on
6th January, 2005. 419 NGOs came forward to provide helping hand to the administration in this
gigantic task. It was estimated by the administration that twenty one thousand permanent houses
would have to be constructed for the rehabilitation of the affected people. The State disbursed
75

76
Rs. 113 crore as relief to the victims, opened orphanage for adolescent girls, provided free text
books and notebooks to Tsunami affected school children, exempted fees and gave special focus
to widows and aged persons. The strategy to restore their livelihood, develop port, reclaim
agricultural field, skill upgradation, training, capacity building was in the process of finalization.
5.0 The Chairperson appreciated the work of the administration and sought the opinion/
suggestions of the district authorities on the provisions of the Disaster Management Bill, 2005 in
the light of the experiences gained during the rescue, relief and rehabilitation operations in the
district. The District Collector sought time and assured to furnish written comments on the
provisions of the Bill later on.
5.1 A Member asked about the provisions made regarding supply of drinking water to the
affected people. Another Member enquired about the status of primary aid received by State
Government and relief provided after the first week of the tragedy. It was enquired as to whether
any study had been made about satisfaction level of affected people regarding relief measures
provided by administration, the details of missing persons and reasons of their not been declared
dead; relief provided to non-fishermen as their agriculture land had been adversely affected by
saline water of the sea; coordination with NGOs etc.
5.2. The District Collector replied that on Sunday, 26 December, 2004 when Tsunami hit the
district, all communication systems collapsed. As a result there were some problems in
communication system initially but it was made operational at the shortest possible time. Financial
Powers of District Collector were relaxed as there were problems in providing immediate relief
NGOs relief was distributed through District Collectorate to facilitate distribution of relief in an
equitable manner. Administration had a programme for providing compensation and for treatment
of soil affected by Tsunami which was Rs. 2500/- and Rs. 12500/- per hectare, respectively.
Regarding missing persons, the DC informed that there was a proforma of checklist for checking
missing persons and in most of such cases 50% of the compensation was paid immediately and
50% was to be released after nine months by vetting of the case by Taluka Committees.
5.3 Another Member enquired about the component of loan and subsidy in the relief provided
to the affected people and Action Plan about treatment of the affected land of farmers within three

5.4 The District Collector replied that 60%  subsidy and 40% loan had been provided as relief
to those whose boats were lost. But it also depended on the type and value of the boat. Relief was

boats. 670 boats could be retrieved Some of the boats had been washed away even upto Sri Lanka.
The issue of retrieving them was being taken up with that country through the Ministry of External
Affairs. So far only 8 such boats could be taken back. The Government had posted a Relief
Commissioner on 31st December, 2004 and had posted three Collectors for relief and rehabilitation
purposes. He further informed that many of the affected people wanted their permanent shelter at
places away from their earlier homes. 85 locations for construction of permanent shelters along
with some of the NGOs had been identified. Each home was estimated to cost Rs.1.25 lakhs.
5.5 A Member asked whether orphanages included only children or even old people who are left
with 110 one to take care of and what was the role of local communities in the rehabilitation and
relief efforts.
5.6 The District Collector replied that local people played the most important role in all the
efforts made by administration. He also replied that orphanages were for old people also.

Meeting with the Chief Minister and other Ministers of UT of Pondicherry
12. The Committee held discussion with the Chief Minister and his ministerial colleagues on the
working of the Union Territory administration and the aspects related to relief and rehabilitation
after Tsunami, in the Chamber of the Chief Minister, Pondicherry.
13.0 The Chief Minister, Pondicherry stated that lack of powers to the Council of Ministers in
even day-to-day matters is very dissatisfying and as a result of which the elected Government was
unable to fulfil the democratic aspirations of the people. He stated that the Lieutenant Governor was
the head of the Government but all decisions of the Council of Ministers in Pondicherry were to
be approved by him and advise of the Council of Ministers was not binding on him. Thus, the real
powers were vested with the Lieutenant-Governor and in turn with the Union Home Ministry. The
representatives of the people who constituted the Council of Ministers were not in the reckoning.
The MLAs of the Union Territory of Pondicherry are not even part of the electoral college for
electing the President of India. According to him the Council of Ministers was of the overwhelming
view that the political aspirations of the people of Pondicherry could be fulfilled only when the
Council of Ministers was given real powers, which could be through the grant of full statehood
to Pondicherry. A resolution in that regard had been passed by the Assembly for the sixth time in
a row. While granting the statehood, it was desired that Pondicherry should also be accorded
Special Category Status. Alternatively, it was suggested to look into the Union Territory Act, 1963
affesh, according to which Pondicherry was being ruled till now.

Visit to Brichgunj Intermediate Shelters, Port Blair
21.0 The Committee visited Brichgunj, Port Blair where Intermediate shelters have been
constructed for Tsunami affected people. The Commissioner (Shipping/PWD), made a power point
presentation before the Committee which inter alia covered the effect of severe earthquake
followed by tsunami waves on Port Blair and other Islands in the form of loss of life and property,
the efforts made by the Administration in providing relif, the approach adopted for designing
intermediate shelters. He also mentioned that special attention was given on functional layout with
drainage, water supply and electrification, rain water harvesting, internal electrification, provision
for social infrastructure such as community centre, Balwadi, etc. Intermediate shelters (dwelling
units) measuring 23 sqms have been constructed by using GCI sheets, steel/wooden posts, CFL
lights and fans. LPG cylinders have also been provided to all families in intermediate shelters. About

84
the challenges before the Administration, the Commissioner stated that there was shortage of labour
as labourers were/are leaving the Islands after tsunami. Non availability of building construction

tandem with UT Administration. He mentioned that after tsunami tragedy Hon’ble Supreme Court
waived ban for cutting forests for six months which has since lapsed and the ban is again in force
now. For extension of waiver, the matter should be taken up by the Attorney General with the
Supreme Court. He was also of the view that infrastructure should be rebuilt at a fast speed. He
urged upon the Committee to recommend a Legislative Assembly for the Union Territory of A&N
Islands and representation of the UT in the Rajya Sabha.
23.2 The representatives of tsunami affected people were of the view that interest free housing
loan should be provided to them. Every affected family should be provided with atleast one
Government job. Compensation should be granted to the next of kin of those who had died as was
given to the victims of avalanche disaster in J&K. The Members asked about strength of people
of Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Government service; number of tribals affected by tsunami;
number of them rehabilitated; issue of eviction of tribals from forest lands; whether Government
has taken up the reclamation process; supply of free ration to the affected people especially
farmers; rehabilitation of coconut plantation and package for the affected persons.
23.3 The Chairperson suggested extension of waiver on Supreme Court ban on cutting of forests
in Andaman and Nicobar Islands. She was_also of the view that diversification of fishing to shrimp,
crab and prawn culture and diversification of agriculture to cash crops  such as cashewnut, spice,
coconut should also be encouraged for the benefit of affected. people. Instead of brining the
farming community under BPL, which is a cumbersome process, free ration, may be given to them
as a special case.
23.4 The Chief Secretary informed the Committee that around 4000 posts are vacant in all the
departments of UT,  out of which clearance for filling. 1000 posts have been sanctioned by the

86
Union Government. On the issue of eviction of tribal people from forest land, he mentioned that
post-l978 encroachers of the forest land have been evicted while pre-1978 encroachers have been
given alternate land. Thus around 25,000 people have been given alternate land. He informed that
inhabitants of Chowra Island were rehabilitated in other Islands while other Islanders have been
rehabilitated in the temporary shelters constructed in their respective Islands itself. He mentioned
that 50,000-hectares of paddy fields in entire Andaman and Nicobar Islands have been affected due
to tsunami. The Union Territory Administration has recommended Rs. 30,000 per hectare as
compensation for the loss of paddy field for reclamation and making that useable for cultivation
and Rs.5,000 per coconut tree to Ministry of Home Affairs and the response of the Government
of India is awaited in that regard.
Meeting with Lieutenant Governor
24.0 The Committee called on the Lieutenant Governor, A&N Islands at Raj Niwas and held
discussion with him on various aspects of the UT Administration and the relief and rehabilitation
measures undertaken by the administration in the aftermath of the tsunami tragedy.
24.1 The Chairperson mentioned about the purpose of the visit of the Committee, its meetings
at Intermediate Shelters with the victims and officials during the day to assess the rehabilitation
measures taken after tsunami. She appreciated the efforts made by the administration for providing
relief to the affected people. She also mentioned about the suggestions made by affected people
for making the permanent shelters. She then shared the experiences of Pondicherry and
Nagapattinam (Tamil Nadu) in building the permanent shelters and requested for exploring the
possibility of either giving money or built houses for tsunami affected persons. She also suggested
for diversification of farming and fishing by promoting shrimp/crab culture, jobs for affected
families, financial support to the educated youth in the intermediate shelters and to give tuition to
the school going children etc.
24.2 Lieutenant, Governor mentioned about the problem of livelihood of the affected people and
that the administration’s efforts to ensure that some regular employment was provided to them. He
also mentioned that the administration had been trying to ensure that studies of students remained
unaffected. He requested the Committee to give suggestions/guidance for better rehabilitation, which
would be taken up with the Government of India.
20 June, 2005
Visit to Car Nicobar
25.0 The Committee visited Car Nicobar Island by an IAF aircraft from Port Blair. The Chief
Secretary and IGP accompanied the Committee to Car Nicobar. At Car  Nicobar, the DC made a
powerpoint presentation describing the extent of damage in the district of Nicobar and the rescue
and relief operations undertaken by the administration. He stated that the damages were more
because of proximity of Nicobar district to the epicenter of the earthquake of 8.9 Richter scale
(Sumatra being 163 km from Great Nicobar) followed by surging tsunami waves. He apprised the
Committee that Teressa and Chowra Islands have submerged. The worst affected Island was
Katchal. Entire ring road along the coast in Car Nicobar have been submerged and new roads in
the middle of Car Nicobar are being constructed. Jetties have been badly damaged; floating docks
were created to bring construction material coming from mainland. A total of 3866 intermediate
shelters have been built only in Car Nicobar. Activation of BSNL mobile service in entire Car
Nicobar after tsunami helped a lot to communicate with mainland.
25.1 Thereafter, the Wing Commander, IAF made a powerpoint presentation covering the rescue,
relief operation by Army, Air Force and damage to the IAF station of Car Nicobar. All residential

87
houses of IAF were flattened due to earthquake. As an immediate measure all Air Force officials
were evacuated and new team took over the Air Force Station and started rescue and relief
operations. Runway was partially damaged. Evacuation took faster pace after repairing of runway.
The work was undertaken on war footing. Half of the Air  Force area was submerged under water.
He also mentioned about request to allocate another piece of land to construct residential units for
IAF officials.
25.2 The Committee then visited the Tsunami affected villages (Tamaloo and Chuk chuka) of Car
Nicobar to see the intermediate shelters and interacted with the people and their representatives
called Captains, Vice-Captains. They appreciated efforts made by the administration in providing
relief after tsunami. However, they had reservations about the permanent shelters proposed to be
built of concrete and steel. They wanted construction of permanent shelters with local materials
which could be expanded later on for accommodating more members of their families. Since Iron
is prone to rust due to salinity it was told to be unfit for rehabilitation units by tribals. Though
far from the mainland and from main city of Port Blair, the people of Car Nicobar Island were
very understanding and were able to put their point of views before the Committee in a lucid
manner. The Committee also interacted with the representatives of NGOs i.e. CARE and UNICEF
who are, doing rehabilitation work in that Island.
25.3 The Committee also visited Mus jetty to see damages caused to it by the devastating
earthquake.
25.4 The Committee returned to Port Blair by IAF plane in the afternoon.
21 June, 2005
Port Blair
Meeting with the Chairman, Port Management Board (PMB)
26.0 The Committee visited Haddo wharf and saw the damaged passenger terminal which was
considered to be the biggest in Asia along with the jetty. The Committee inspected central godown
of the wharf where relief goods were lying for transportation to other Islands through ships.
26.1 The Chairman, PMB  made a powerpoint presentation on board the ship Nicobari. He
informed the Committee that his organisation played an important role in supplying relief and
rehabilitation material from Port Blair. There were twenty-three noted ports in A&N Islands.
Reflecting upon the damages to Port infrastructure on 26 December, 2004, he informed that
damage to wharves and jetties included collapse of berthing portion (60 M) of fisheries jetty,
collapse of Junglighat jetty including passenger hall, total damage to passenger terminal at Haddo,
extensive damage to dry dock complex and two local navigational structure. At Hut Bay harbour,
the berthing jetty collapsed, crane over jetty fell in to the sea. Extensive damage to port buildings,
collapse of approach to wharf and damage to PCT building were also mentioned. Similarly, he
mentioned that at Campbell Bay harbour 80 M approach jetty collapsed, sea water ingressed into
port area due to subsidence of land mass resulting in breakwater dislocation and subsidence of
Tetrapods and loss of two local navigational structures. He also displayed with the help of slides
the damage to Katchal, Chowra, Teressa, Campbell Bay Harbours and Nancowry Islands.
26.2 He then showed slides containing relief work undertaken by the PMB and its achievements
in restoration of damaged harbours, jetties and other structures at different Islands. He mentioned
that at Port Blair, Haddo wharf, Chatham wharf and Phoenix bay harbour complex were made
operational from 27.12.2004 onwards; at Hutbay, temporary jetty for vessels of 2.5 M draft
constructed and commissioned on 1.2.2005, damaged portion of breakwater rectified for providing

88
access to temporary jetty; wharf crane was made operational and utilised for cargo operations. A
mobile crane was deployed which was received from Mumbai Port Trust and Hydrographic survey
was also taken up. At Car Nicobar temporary ramp, near sunken portion of approach jetty, was
provided and similarly at Nancowry and Katchal temporary jetty for vessels was constructed. While
presenting the action plan for restoration of damaged port structures, he informed the Committee
about the cost and targeted time for their completion.
26.3 He also touched upon some of the key projects covering the development of Katchal
Harbour for berthing mainland vessels, construction of alternate jetty at Safed Balu, Teressa,
development of additional dry dock for mainland vessels at Port Blair, extension of breakwater and
construction of additional berth opposite to existing berth at Mus, Car Nicobar, construction of
breakwater at Malacca, Car Nicobar and feasibility studies for transshipment port at Campbell Bay,
Great Nicobar.
26.4 A presentation on Relief Inventory Management was made by an Officer of the Indian Navy
to keep tab on use of relief material received trom different quarters. The Committee desired that
the entire inventory system should be put on internet to enable the public at large to know about
the relief material sent and its use.
Visit to Mini LPG Bottling Plant, IOC at Hope Town
26.5 The Committee visited Mini LPG bottling plant of Indian Oil Corporation located at Hope
Town, Bamboo Flat, Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The Officers there informed that the plant
commenced its operations on 20 April, 2003 and the pipelines and plant were not affected by the
earthquake. The plant has the capacity to provide LPG Cylinders to entire Islands. To the query
of Chairperson whether the Indian Oil Corporation is in a position to supply additional cylinders
to all Anganwadis in case administration places a request for the same, the officer of Indian Oil
Corporation replied in affirmative.
Meeting with the NGOs working in the area on Tsunami relief
27. The Committee held interaction with the NGOs (total 13) working in the area of providing
relief to Tsunami victims on their experiences in providing rescue, relief and rehabilitation in the
aftermath of tsunami, in the Conference Hall, Megapode Nest.
27.1 The representatives of NGOs lauded the support of the Administration in providing relief and
mentioned about areas in which they were working such as education, psychosocial issues,
construction of toilet/permanent and temporary shelters, disaster management etc. and their
contribution like fishing boats for victims, mosquito net, gas stoves, besides doing social service
amongst the tsunami victims.
Meeting with the Officials of the UT Administration
28. The Chief Secretary made an audio-visual presentation, which included geography of
Islands, Disaster Management Bill, Administrative Issues, Environmental Issues, Tourism,
Decentralization of District Administration, Personnel Issues, Empowerment of Tribal Council,
Economic Issues and Transport for the Islands.
28.1 Reflecting upon the Disaster Management Bill, 2005, he mentioned that detailed deliberations
on the Bill has not been possible due to paucity of time. However the first impression about
the Bill is that it is a very welcome proposal. He stated that, there is no mention of UTs in the
Bill which should be done. The Administrator may be designated as the Chairperson of UT
Authority for management of any disaster. He further mentioned that guidelines for NGOs should
be drawn up and local Defence forces may have representation at State and District level

89
authorities. The Chief Secretary had agreed to send detailed comments on the Bill in writing in due
course.
28.2 R egarding administrative issues and the need for development of land, the CS stated that
34,000 hectares land were declared as deemed forest, as per Supreme Court orders. The islands
have 85% forest cover against the norm of 33%. The 4000 hectares land sub-merged due to
tsunami and 4000 families (post-1978) require about 300 hectares of land for settlements. He
further stated that drinking water projects, tourism and transportation projects, etc. have suffered
due to the Supreme Court restrictions on forest land use. He also mentioned about the need for
modification of the Supreme Court’s order.
28.3 About the environmental issues, he mentioned that major drinking water projects such as
Dhanikhari Project, Rutland Project, Flatbay Scheme, and Kalpong Downstream Usage were held
up for environment clearance. He further stated that compensatory forestland was not available due
to environmental restrictions and for similar reasons no large-scale storage of rainwater was
possible.
28.4 The Chief Secretary further informed the Committee that though tourism was identified a
thrust area in the islands but only a few areas were opened for tourism. He stated that more islands
were required to be opened for exploring the full potential and for international tourism there is a
need for an international airport in the UT.
28.5 Emphasizing the need for decentralization of District Administration, he stated that creation
of new districts in North and Middle Andaman was needed to improve disaster response and
for checking poaching. It is also needed in view of strategic location of Coco Island which is
under Chinese occupation. He also felt the need for creation of two sub-divisions in Nicobar
District.
28.6 Further reflecting upon the personnel issues, he mentioned that the Islands being far off
from mainland, the best talent was not attracted unless special incentives are provided. He
demanded increase in recruitment age, grant of higher scale of pays to appointees on deputation,
and three free passages to government servant to visit mainland instead of existing one free
passage, every year.
28.7 Pointing out the need for review of instructions, of Central Government the CS placed
before the Committee that UT should be exempted from ten per cent cut in existing vacant posts;
ban on filling up of vacancies; five per cent ceiling on compassionate appointment to dependents
of Government servants who died in tsunami. He also mentioned that power to create new posts
should be vested with Administration. He felt that genuine demands from Tribal Council for
development should be agreed to Permission to give development grant through Deputy
Commissioners were required for which MHA and Ministry of Finance were the competent
authorities.
28.8 T ouching upon the issue of connectivity to Mainland, he stated that faster ships at least
having 20 knots speed were required. Faster clearance to replace old ships and purchase of new
ships were also needed. He mentioned that as Indian Shipyards take very long time, these should
be provided through global tender, which would be cheaper for the Government. Four vehicle
ferries were required to facilitate movement of passengers and cargo.
28.9 Similarly about Air Transport, he stated that the administration had only one helicopter to
cater to 38 islands. The islands were 1200 KMs trom mainland and were spread over 700 KMs.
It makes the administration totally dependent on commercial flights or even army during crisis. He
stated that Pawan Hans Ltd. was unable to lease more helicopters hence it was more economical
to purchase two fixed wing and two helicopters through HAL.

90
28.10 Emphasising the need for improvement in Telecommunications, he stated that the present
bandwidth was 40 mbps for 65,000 connection. In next three years, 400 mbps bandwidth would
be required. According to him, satellite connectivity was neither feasible nor cost effective hence
he suggested that optical fibre cable tram Chennai to Port Blair was necessary and wanted the
Ministry of Communications to expedite the same.
28.11 Lastly he presented before the Committee the post tsunami proposals such as the revised
agricultural package, package for industrial units, package for cooperatives, revised package for
animal husbandry, re-construction assistance to Panchayat Raj Institutions/Port Blair Municipal
Corporation.
28.12 He m entioned that Zila Parishad system has b een introduced in no n-tribal area s of Andaman
and Nicobar Islands in accordance with 73rd Amendment of the Constitution. But Captain System
exists in tribal areas of the islands, who have been elected through their own system.
28.13 A view was expressed by a Member that Village Council has been recognized as panchayat
in North Eastern States in accordance with 73rd amendment of the Constitution, which could be
adopted in Andaman and Nicobar Islands. He was of the view that the Central Sponsored Scheme
(CSS) should be routed through Panchayat Raj Institutions. Another Member wanted to know the
modalities of implementing rural schemes. Yet another Member was of the view that the Captain
system was the most democratic one and functioning smoothly and so he desired to maintain the
traditional organizational set up. Efforts should be made by the administration to bring the
tribes-Jarawas, Sompen and Sentinels to the mainstream of civilization which is lagging on the part
of administration.
28.14 The Chief Secretary, quoting the vibrant system of grassroot democracy (Badagaon System)
of 70s in Arunchal Pradesh, held the view that division in that society has cropped up after the
introduction Panchayati Raj Institutions and the Badagaon system has gone to background. He was
of the opinion that devolution of power should be made to the tribal people without distorting their
cultural set up.
28.15 Thereafter, the Development Commissioner while making a powerpoint presentation on
livelihood issues and plan for post tsunami developments in Andaman and Nicobar Islands inter alia
stated the issues such as general information on the Islands, damage due to tsunami, sector-wise
livelihood plan for agriculture, animal husbandry, fisheries, rural deveiopment, industries and other
departments besides displaying the role of NGOs. General information covered the aspect of main
occupation of the people viz. agriculture, fishery, animal husbandry, services and tourism related
activities. Reflecting upon damage due to tsunami he mentioned that 38 Islands were affected.
10,000 houses and 50,000 people were affected. He also mentioned that 6 islands viz. Chowra,
Little Nicobar, Trinket, Bambooka, Kondol and Pillowmillow were fully evacuated after the tragedy.
28.16 About the damage to the agricultural land due to tsunami, he stated that the total area
damaged was 10837 hectares out  of which paddy and other field crops were on 1730 hectares
whereas plantation crops were on 9107 hectares. The total area under submergence was 4339
hectares comprising paddy and other field crops. The total reclamable area was 6561 hectares
which consisted of 694 hectares of paddy and other field crops and 5867 hectares of plantation
crops. He mentioned that a total no. of 6020 farmers were affected out of which 1743 were
in Andaman district and 4277 in Nicobar district. The total loss in financial terms was to
the tune of Rs. 321 crores. He then showed slides reflecting the package sanctioned by
Government of India for tsunami relief and the strategy prepared by the administration for
implementation of the package. About procurement of agriculture inputs, he stated that process was
in progress for purchase of fertilizer, organic manure, neem cake, gypsum, farm implements, plant
protection equipment, vegetable seeds and planting materials. About reclamation of land, he

91
mentioned that a total of 1417 hectares area was cleared for cropping till date, which will generate
16265 mandays.
28.17 T ouching upon the issue of loss and rehabilitation in animal husbandry sector, the
Commissioner mentioned that out of a total livestock/poultry of 10,85,739 in the islands before
tsunami, 1,57,577 livestock/poultry were lost due to tsunami for which Rs. 11.83 crore as
compensation was sanctioned by Government of India. However, a revised package of Rs 26.72
crore has been proposed for approval of Government of India. He also mentioned about the
components proposed in the package, strategy applied so far for rehabilitation of animal husbandry
and the strategy adopted for the year 2005-06 for the same.
28.18 About the fisheries sector, the Commissioner informed the Committee that the total number
of fishermen in the UT was 4157, the total number of boats prior to tsunami was 2281 and the
total quantity of fish caught a month was 26940 tons. He stated that tsunami affected 2323
fishermen, partially damaged 765 fishing boats, fully damaged 938 fishing boats and the total
loss to the sector accounted for Rs. 35.22 crores for which a compensation package of
Rs.21.05 crores has been sanctioned. His other slides showed the component of package covering
the amount of subsidy and compensation for replacement or repair of different types of boats and
nets. He further mentioned the strategy for implementation of package such as assessment of
losses, payment of advance of Rs. 10,000 to meet initial expenditure, preparing a medium term
perspective to develop the fisheries as a thrust area and a road map for fisheries development in
the islands.. Further mentioning about the strategy for the year 2005-06, he stated that it includes
repair and replacement of boats to restore fishing, purchase and supply of fishing materials and
accessories through the A&N Fisheries Cooperative Federation Ltd., verification and finalisation of
the list of affected pisciculturists, assessment of fishery related projects and crab/lobster fattening
units. In all these would generate 24485 mandays.
28.19 On the rural development front, he stated that 516210 mandays would be generated through
the Panchayati Raj Institutions in the event of sanction of Rs. 54.35 crores as projected by Zilla
Parishad. Reflecting upon Industries Sector, he presented the extent the damage to SSI units after
earthquake and tsunami, the economic losses to the industries and the challenges for livelihood
restoration such as problem of logistics-sheds, transport, electricity, drinking water, etc. and skilled
manpower for construction related skills, IT related repair and servicing, basic engineering related
servicing, training to be conducted. He also showed the strategy for restoration of livelihood
through vocational training programme, revival of Industries Training Centers, etc. He then listed
the areas identified for livelihood vocational training by the Industries Department such as general
engineering, construction, textile, food processing, IT, etc.
28.20 Lastly, he enlisted the contribution of 34 NGOs working in area of livelihood matter, their
sector-wise involvement and the livelihood generation.
28.21 The Chairperson winding up the discussion appreciated the efforts of administration in
providing relief and rehabilitation to the victims of the tsunami. However, she drew attention of the
administration to a few problems encountered by the people of Andaman and Nicobar Islands such
as augmentation of bus service to intermediate shelters for school going children; engaging
educated people in the temporary shelters to provide tuition to the children. She also mentioned that
LPG stove and cylinder should be provided to each of the 547 Anganwadi centers where mid-day
meal is cooked for school children. Recalling the grievances of farmers at Sippighat that their total
agricultural land had been lost causing loss of livelihood to them for which a compensation of
Rs. 7000/- have been provided. She suggested issuance of tsunami relief card as per the order of
Supreme Court and thereby providing free ration under the Antyodaya Anna Yojna. About the
Bambooflat shop owners whose shops were submerged, the Chairperson suggested that
rehabilitation should be provided to them. Mentioning the difficulty in temporary shelters due to tin

92
sheets at Car Nicobar, she suggested that traditional type of houses made of local materials would
be better as it maintains low temperature and easy to expand to adjust their joint families. She also
suggested that instead of material, money should be provided to them so that they can get their
houses made by themselves. Similarly she suggested for giving money and material instead of
making houses to South Andamanese as individual entrepreneurship is always better. She also
shared the experience of Pondicherry Administration with the A&N Administration in making
allotments after identifying the plots but before starting construction. For residents of Campbell
Island, she mentioned that affected people have been settled somewhere else with family members
not getting any relief or compensation and suggested that in such situations the standard rule
should be relaxed. Mentioning about the Campbell Bay, she suggested that settlers at Campbell Bay
should be somehow persuaded to remain there for which separate package maybe formulated.
Lastly she suggested for creation of a Grievance cellforum for dealing with the problems of
affected people.

Study Note
on the visit of the Department-related
Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Home Affairs
to Chandigarh

95

STUDY NOTE
The Department-related Committee on Home Affairs undertook a study visit to Union
Territory of Chandigarh from 13 to 14 September, 2005 as a part of its examination of
“Administration of Union Territories”. At Chandigarh, a number of Organizations/Associations
including some political party delegations called on the Committee and submitted their memoranda
to the Chairperson and Members of the Committee, who joined the said visit (Annexure-I) .
1.1 A list of Associations/Organizations who submitted memorandum to the Committee during
its study visit to Chandigarh is appended at (Annexure-II).
1.2 There was wide spectrum of subjects covered in the Memoranda but following are the
salient points raised in those memoranda:—
(i) Extension of Lal dora limit of villages and regularization of construction made on
and around that area on the lines of Lal dora in Delhi;
(ii) Unsensitive bureaucratic setup of Chandigarh to the needs of people;
(iii) Upgradation of Chandigarh Civil Airport to International Airport as the city is
gateway to the States of Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and
Kashmir;
(iv) Electrification of Chandigarh-Ludhiana railway line;
(v) Four laning of Kalka-Chandigarh-Ambala Highways;
(vi) Flyovers and Mass Rapid Transport System (MRTS) to decongest traffic jams in
the city;
(vii) CNG propelled transport system to ensure green and clean environment;
(viii) Need to constitute Inter-state Development Council consisting of representatives
from Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Union Territory of Chandigarh;
(ix) 3.7% share in power generation from BBMB;
(x) Delimitation of wards of Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC) and direct
election of Mayor and the tern should be extended to five years from the present
tenure of one year;
(xi) General Power of Attorney (GPA) should be recognized as the mode of transfer of
property;
(xii) Conferment of ‘A’ grade status to the city of Chandigarh;
(xiii) Restricting heavy capitation fee in private schools;
(xiv) All women police stations and reform in Chandigarh police;
(xv) All party representation in Advisory Council to the Administrator of Chandigarh;
(xvi) Issuance of license to footpath hawkers and Rehri-Pheri wallas;
(xvii) Official language status to Punjabi and Hindi in addition to English language in Chandigarh;
97

98
(xviii) lmplementation of Value Added Tax (VA T);
(xix) Central Acts for Chandigarh instead of adopting Acts of States of Punjab and
Haryana;
(xx) Speed governors for local buses, trucks and school buses;
(xxi) Check on mushrooming of road side liquor vendors;
(xxii) Large scale power pilferage and huge arrears of power and water bills on
Government offices of States of Punjab and Haryana in the UT of Chandigarh;
(xxiii) Shortage of Staff in Excise and Taxation Department leading to loss in revenue
collection;
(xxiv) Updating websites of Department of Chandigarh Administration, as Chandigarh is
projected as next IT destination in India;
(xxv) Revival of post of Chief Commissioner which was replaced by the present post of
Administrator;
(xxvi) Establishment of Civil Defence Training Organization;
(xxvii) Introduction of paid parking system;
(xxviii) Allotment of forty per cent land earmarked for housing to the cooperative societies
for construction of low-cost houses;
(xxix) No promotional avenues for the teaching community in Education Department.
Proposal regarding promotion of teachers to the post of lecturer in Senior
Secondary School in Chandigarh is pending with the administration. Administration
has fixed 25% as deputation quota and takes lecturer from States on deputation.
Some of those deputationists have got proforma promotion to the post of Principal
in view of their promotion in their parent State(s) and lecturers of UT without
getting the benefit of promotion are working under the supervision of the
deputationists who got promotion in view of the position explained above. Demand
for scrapping of the rule which allows teachers to come on deputation from other
States to the UT of Chandigarh was raised in the memoranda. Besides that,
restoration of six weeks summer break which is at present reduced to four weeks;
change of format of Annual confidential Report (ACR); confirmation in the post of
teacher after completing three years of service; filling up of vacant posts of
teacher; introduction of Sanskrit as subject in all Senior Secondary School
alongwith Hindi and Punjabi; restoration of post of Director, State Institute of
Education to the School cadre;. creation of post of vice-principal in all senior
secondary Schools; stoppage of allotment of houses to the person on deputation
from States of Punjab and Haryana as these States have their own pool of
accommodations; special housing scheme by Chandigarh Housing Board for
teaching community of UT cadres;
(xxx) W ithdrawal of Ministry of Home Affairs Notification No. 14012/2/88 CHD
dt. 13.1.1992 under which State Service Rules of Punjab is made applicable in
Chandigarh, in the place of Central Government Rules, as envisaged in Ministry of
Home Affairs Notification No. 12/1/66 CHO (ii) dated 1.11.1966;
(xxxi) Non-implementation of decisions of CAT and Punjab and Haryana High Court
regarding regularization of services of  daily wages and work charge employees;

99
(xxxii) Stoppage on purchase low floor buses which have been declared defective by
expert Committee of MCC;
(xxxiii) Revocation of ban imposed on payment of bonus to the employees of UT
Administration;
(xxxiv) Restoration of compassionate appointments;
(xxxv) Allotment of E.W.S. Houses in Sectors 37 and 38 to Administration/MCC employees;

(xxxix) R egularisation of need-based alternations effected in the residential buildings (malra

2.0 The Committee. thereafter interacted with the local Member of Parliament, Chandigarh. He
submitted the following points for the consideration of the Committee:—
(i) Legislature for the UT of Chandigarh is not a viable idea at this point of time.
Instead, elected Pradesh Council and Executive Councillors is the need of the hour
in the UT. Estimate Committee of Tenth Lok Sabha has recommended that all files
except such files which relate to reserve subjects be routed through respective
Executive Councillors to the Administrator. The present Local Advisory Council of
the Administrator is no substitute for the elected Pradesh Council on which powers
to exercise financial and budgetary expenditure control need to devolved upon;
(ii) Need of Mass Rapid Transport System (MRTS), Science city with Planetarium, etc.
in the city. The entire surplus revenue deposited in Consolidated Fund of India
should be ploughed back to Chandigarh itself;
(iii) The actual population of Chandigarh has crossed one million and therefore the UT
is entitled to have a Metropolitan Planning Committee. Even District Planning
Committee is yet to be constituted therein. In the absence of those important
bodies, as postulated by the Constitution, there is denial of participation of elected
body in the planning process. In the Action Taken Note to the Report of Estimate
Committee of Tenth Lok Sabha, the Government had accepted that under Article
243 ZD, every UT has to constitute a District level planning Committee to prepare
draft development plan for the district as a whole after consolidating the plans
prepared by the Panchayats and Municipalities in the district;
(iv) Indifference of administration towards the enforcement of building bye-laws has led
to alternations/additions in over 90 per cent houses/flats particularly in the phase II
of the city. Mass scale issuance of notice and occasional demolitions have only

100
added woes to the people. There is need to make one time relaxation of building
bye-laws to regularise the need-based alterations/additions in flats/houses as a
pragmatic approach;
(v) Acceptance of transfer of property through GPA; Issue proprietary rights to the
owners of tenements allotted on lease (Convertible to Hire and Purchase) in 1970’s
without making it contingent on demolition of additional constructions;
(vi) Separate Selection Committee for Chandigarh with members from UPSC, Ministry
of Home Affairs, and UT Administration for timely recruitment as making
appointment through UPSC is time consuming;
(vii) Regularisation of services of daily-wage and work-charged employees, who have
been working for more than ten years. In that context of assurance of Government
to the Estimate Committee of Tenth Lok Sabha for regularisation of  ad-hoc
appointment made against permanent vacancies in Andaman and Nicobar Islands to
the UT of Chandigarh was sought;
(viii) Chandigarh Administration has scrapped the practice of five per cent compassionate
appointment. Instead Rupees five lakh to be distributed amongst all the dependents
(as followed in the State of Haryana) of the person who dies in harness;
(ix) Consideration of transferred employees of administration to MCC on deemed
deputation without deputation allowance;
(x) Payment of bonus particularly to employees of Chandigarh Transport Undertaking
(CTU) as profit was earned by that body;
(xi) Need to permit and regulate road side hawkers;
(xii) Rehabilitation of slum dwellers;
(xiii) Transparent transfer policy;
(xiv) Issuance of SC Certificate to bonafide SC residents of UT of Chandigarh by making
applicable the decision of Delhi government mutatis mutandis to the UT of
Chandigarh
(xv) While acquiring land, adequate compensation be given to the land holder or he be
made partner in the development; and
(xvi) Need for institutionlised grievances, redressal machinery, as the bureaucratic
dominated administration is apathetic to the grievances of the people. Doing away
of all discretionary quota available over the administration.
3.0 The Committee thereafter interacted with Sehior Officers of Administration  (Annexure-III) .
The Advisor to Administrator initiated official presentation of Chandigarh Administration by stating
that technically power remains with Ministry of Home Af fairs. Under the present dispensation, the
Administrator can frame rules under Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952 and
the Central Government can by notification extend any State Legislation to UT Chandigarh through
Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966. Thus the set of rules which governs the UT of Chandigarh have
been either taken from States of Haryana/Punjab or Central Government which creates confusions
in the mind of the people.
3.1 Devolution of powers to Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh has already taken place and
some more powers would be devolved upon the MCC in due course. As to the financial status,
he mentioned that Chandigarh is financially surplus UT having highest per capita income. Municipal

101
services are proposed to be extended to the villages located outside the Sectors of Chandigarh. He
stressed that efforts of administration is to sustain the tempo of growth and ensure that the
benefits of growth reaches to every inhabitants of the UT of Chandigarh. Rupees 300 crore were
deposited last year in Consolidated Fund of India. MCC has also imposed three per cent property
tax on commercial building since last year. The Committee was informed that all children upto class
eight would be provided free education w.e.f. September, 2005 and in health sector, Chandigarh has
specialised hospital known as PGI which also caters to the need of residents of Himachal Pradesh,
Haryana, Punjab and J&K. Co-operative type of organisation is in the pipeline to give the benefit
to the workers working in unorganised sectors. He mentioned that grid system of public transport
is being encouraged to satellite towns of Mohali and Panchakula. He mentioned about proposed
inauguration of IT Park by Prime Minister very shortly and the availability of information relating
to administration in Jan Sampark Centre. He stated that the Chandigarh is geared to fulfil the vision
of Union Government to make India a developed Country by the year 2020. He then left the floor
to Horne Secretary for making presentation on health and education sectors.
4.0 Home Secretary made powerpoint presentation on the said sectors. He began his
presentation on primary level health care (Community Health Centres, polyclinic, A YUSA etc.) and
secondary level health care (general hospital in Sector 16, Government Medical College Hospital,
Sector–32). He submitted that emphasis is more on primary level hospitals so that burden on
specialised hospitals is reduced.
4.1 While comparing demographic data of Chandigarh with national figure, he mentioned that
Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is fourth lowest ( i.e. 19) in the country. The UT of Chandigarh has
achieved the target fixed under National Pupulation Policy for 2010 for National Mortality Ratio and
Total Fertility Rate in 2005 itself. Furthermore, all targets in TB, Leprosy have been achieved by
the Chandigarh Administration. Under the National Rural Health Mission, mobile dispensary have
been put at service to provide basic minimum health services to the villagers not having any
dispensary/sub centre. He brought to the notice of Committee the requirement of additional medical/
para-medical staff to cater to the needs of present population of 9.1 lakhs. He mentioned that the
administration has felt the needs of one more hospital in southern sector, as the density of
population is more in southern sector than northern Sector. He shared proposal/projects regarding
regional trauma centre, centralised ambulance service, artificial limb centre, etc. with the Committee
4.2 On the education sector he shared the statistics with regard to colleges (private and
Government) schools (Government Aided, recognised, Kendriya vidyalayas, Navodaya vidyalaya
etc). He highlighted that every child has access to school within one km. of radius and success
rate in school is highest in India. Chandigarh imparts vocational educational in collaboration with
industry at school level (like skill training in pottery in school at Kumhar Colony). Computer aided
learning process have been introduced. A Memorandum of Understanding has been signed with
Azim Premjee Foundation in that regard. English has been introduced from class I onwards on
public demand.
4.3 He also touched views like tree education upto class VIII, no tuition fees from girls upto
class VII, free text books and uniform to the student of Non-model Schools, (where medium of
instruction is Hindi/Punjabi) upto class VIII w.e.f. academic session 2006, free text books, uniform
and stationery to SC/ST students, tree mid-day meal etc. About 900 posts of teachers have been
filled up. 240 teachers have been recruited under Serva Shiksha Abhiyan. Seven new school
buildings are under construction. Self-auditing and self-appraisal in the ACR of teachers have been
introduced to ensure their accountability.
5.0 Thereafter, the Finance Secretary presented an overview of Budget of Chandigarh for the
year 2004-05 which projects revenue surplus of Rs 288.74 crore. He submitted breakup of revenue
receipts (taxes:–51.7% i.e. Rs 554.2 crore and 43% as non tax revenue i.e. Rs. 418.57 crore) and

102
breakup of non tax revenues {Power (72.48%), Road Transport (16.97%), printing and Stationery
(2.61%) Medical and Health (3.09%) and others (4.85%)}. Most of tax revenue comes trom Sale
Tax i.e. 68.16%. Growth of capital receipts is mainly from the sale of lands, which is not likely
to sustain beyond four to five years as sale of land is expected to State-wise.
5.1 As to recommendations of Second Delhi Finance Commission all recommendations have
been accepted by Chandigarh Administration which includes devolution of 17% tax revenue of the
Administration to Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC), payment of street light bill to MCC,
50% matching grant to MCC for new taxes levied by it.
5.2 He outlined existing as well as proposed major projects which are as under:—
Existing Major Projects
• Augmentation of Water supply to ensure 24 hrs availability.
• Solid Waste Management.
• Sewerage Treatment Plant.
• Recycled Water Supply Network.
• Government Medical College and Hospital, Sector 32.
• Power: Revamping of distribution Infrastructure to ensure uninterrupted quality power.
• Chandigarh Technology Park (CTP).
• E-Governance, E-Sampark and Jan Sampark.
• Modernisation of Public Transport System.
• Development of 3rd Phase Sectors.
• Roads and Bridges.
Proposed Major Projects
• Substitution of physical interface bye-interface with citizens.
• Rehabilitation of Slum Dwellers and Housing for all.
• Desilting of Sukhna Lake.
• Creation of Second lake.
• Decongestion of Traffic by Mass Rapid Transport System.
• Elevated Road from Transport Chowk to Housing Board Chowk, Manimajra.
• Development of infrastructure in 3rd phase and periphery area of Chandigarh.
• Upgradation of Airport.
• Popularization of Solar Power in the city.
• Power: Revamping of distribution Infrastructure to ensure uninterrupted quality power.
5.3 He summed up his presentation by saying that Chandigarh is non-plan surplus UT since
2000-01 and it is in the process of evolving self-sustaining development model.

103
6.0 After that IGP, Chandigarh made presentation on law and order situation in the UT of
Chandigarh. In that presentation he brought to the notice of the Committee the recommendation of
BPR&D on augmentation of man-power/PCRof Chandigarh Police and mentioned about the shortage
of manpower in the force.
6.1 BPR&D had recommended sanctioning of 870 additional posts for the Police Stations, 205
posts of Traffic Police, besides 60 separate posts for the special units i.e. Economic Offence Wing
and Women and Child support unit. BPR&D has also recommended strengthening of Police Control
Room (PCR) with replacement of motorcycles with gypsies. IGP submitted that no additional
manpower has been sanctioned for Police Station since 1988. Even three of the eleven Police
Stations i.e. P.S. Sector 36, Sec-19 and P.S. Industrial Area do not have any sanctioned manpower.
Special Units like Women and Child Support Unit and Economic Offences Wing have no sanctioned
manpower. Recruitment T raining Centre (RTC) has no sanctioned manpower. Proposals are pending
with MHA for sanction of 1081 posts for Police Stations, 450 posts fot Traffic Police. He
mentioned that 10 demonstrations per day on an average are staged in the city of Chandigarh being
capital of two States. Thus the augmentation of staff strength of Chandigarh Police is the need of
the hour. Inspite of manpower shortage, conviction rate is 72%, which is one of the highest in
the country.
6.2 He mentioned that Community Relation Unit (CRU), Community Liasion Groups (CLG) have
been set up in each police station for community policing projects. Round the clock women desk,
all woman police post at PGI are some of the important achievements of Chandigarh Police.
7.0 The Director, Information Technology and Tourism also made power-point presentation on
IT vision for  the year 2010 by which the city would be an automated city/State where total
e-governance would be available to the common man. The application of IT for providing
information and facilitation to the residents of Chandigarh would be through e-sampark,
e-jansampark, e-sampark through its multi-service single window system (presently at seven
locations). The residents of Chandigarh have 80,000 transactions per month with various public
dealing departments. Through e-jansampark project (total 70, one in each sector/village) provides
information to common man through kiosks. Society for Promotion of IT in Chandigarh (SPIC)
is running C-TOSS programme in schools and colleges to develop skilled professional for lTES/
BPO.
7.1 A 370 acres Technology Habitat to support IT/ITES infrastructure earmarked for
Chandigarh Technology Park is ready and would be inaugurated on 24 September, 2005.
8.0 Members sought clarifications/comments of administration on the presentations made and
also offered certain suggestions for consideration of administration which are summarized as
under:—
(i) The Committee noted that funds pertaining to health projects have been surrendered.
It also sought reasons for surrendering of good amount of money on health projects;
(ii) The Committee felt that there is a need for systemic change to increase the role of
elected representatives as they are not involved in the District Planning Committee.
Representation of political parties on the basis of their strength in the Advisory
Council of Administrator;
(iii) Need to have Legislative Assembly for Chandigarh on the lines of Pondicherry having
10 lakh population;
(iv) Reasons for charging high conversion rate for IT and ITES works located in
Industrial Areas;

104
(v) Reasons for not allowing schools on private land;
(vi) Reasons for not having transparent promotion policy for teachers;
(vii) Need for rehabilitation of slum dwellers;
(viii) Reasons for non-issuance of SC certificates to genuine SC candidate after the year
1995 as a result they are deprived of benefits granted to them by the Constitution;
(ix) Need for increasing housing for Non-Gazetted Officers in Chandigarh police;
(x) Backlog in ST reservation;
(xi) There is a delay in transferring subjects to MCC by the administration;
(xii) Maintenance of tourist spots;
(xiii) Not many CGHS dispensary in the city having of large number of Government
servants;
(xiv) Efforts should be stepped up to popularize/advertise Chandigarh Technology Park
(CTP) as it is going to give facelift to the city after Bangalore and Hyderabad;
(xv) Reasons for not extending Lal dora of Kishangarh village;
(xvi) Need-based change in building-bye-laws required to, cater the problems faced by
common man;
(xvii) Reasons for not transferring ownership right to owners of houses constructed by
Chandigarh Housing Board;
(xviii) Revival of post of Chief Commissioner which was considered to be people’s
friendly;
(xix) Insensitive bureaucracy dominated administration to the needs of people; Need for
change in approach of bureaucratic dominated administration.
8.1.0 The Advisor to Administrator responded to the issues raised by the Committee which is as
under:
8.1.1 Creation of some posts in the health sector is pending with Ministry of Home Affairs.
Salary of the projected posts were reflected in the budget in the anticipation of those posts, which
were not actually sanctioned in the financial year leading to surrender of money on health projects.
8.1.2 As to Advisory Council to Administrator, the Advisor mentioned that previous council had
more than fifty members and had many sub-committees but met only once even though it is to
be convened once in three months. District Planning Committee has also not constituted.
8.1.3 As to conversion rate for IT/ITES and BPOs the administration held the view that those
services are not considered as industries, thus conversion rate is very high. Further the rate in IT
park though appears to be lower, investment condition is very stringent which is possible in the
case big players only.
8.1.4 As to running of schools in residential areas, Advisor replied that extensions have been given
to those schools to continue in that area and with reference to play schools in residential areas the
policy for such schools would be framed soon.
8.1.5 Referring to rehabilitation of slum dwellers, it was informed that houses on rent are
available to them. As  to issuance of SC certificate to bonafide SC inhabitants of Chandigarh, the

105
matter has been taken up with MHA. The issue is in advanced stage of consideration of
Government of India.
8.1.6 W ith regard to extension of Lal Dora of Kishangarh village, he replied that the village of
Kishangarh is a part of Mani Majra. 980 houses have been exempted and 104 houses are scattered
and not  in continum and constructed after the issuance of notice, have to be demolished. Those
houses if exempted would make the administration to leave large chunk of land which would be
required for proposed IT park. The original Kishangarh village has not been touched.
8.1.7 As to regularization of the need-based violation of building bye-laws he stated that need-
based violation is treated as greed-based violation by Punjab and Haryana High Court. However, the
sub-committee of Advisory Council of Administrator has recommended change of building bye laws
which is five decade old, but final decision is yet to be taken.
8.1.8 As to revival of post of Chief Commissioner, the Advisor responded by saying that without
elected body, the bureaucratic setup having whatever nomenclature would have the same
characteristics and not be too different.
8.1.9 While responding to traffic problems, he replied that the city of Chandigarh qualifies for the
system for  MRTS and further steps are being taken to introduce the same.
8.2 It was brought to the notice of the Committee that Administration is not responsive to the
needs of the people. It was also brought to the notice that the Administrator is not accessible to
the representatives of  the people and public to hear their grievances. The Commiittee felt that
involvement of  elected representatives in decision making process is very much required in the
absence of any elected body for running the affairs of Administration in an effective manner.
9.0 The Committee thereafter interacted with the Mayor and Councillors of MCC  (Annexure-IV).
Municipal Co mmissioner made powerpoint presentation inter-alia touching upon different initiatives
under taken by MCC i.e. augmentation of  water supply scheme, paid parking, Sehaj Safai Kendras,
garbage processing unit, idle truck parking, multi-level parking, etc.
9.1 The Mayor of MCC welcomed the members of the Committee and mentioned that MCC is
an elected body with a lot of responsibilities but has limited authority and suffers from financial
constraints. She presented written memorandum to the Committee. Thereafter she left the floor to
other Councillers of MCC to put forth the view of MCC. The following points were raised by the
MCC in the meeting:—
(i) The following functions have been transferred either wholly or  partly as indicated
against each to the MCC, viz. (i) Public Health (partly), (ii) Horticulture (partly),
(iii) Fire (wholly), (iv) Enforcement (partly), (v) Sanitation (wholly), (vi) Building and
Roads (partly), (vii) Electrical (partly), (viii) Estate (partly), (ix) Tax (partly). Some
of the obligatory functions viz.  pest control, registration of births and deaths.
Eradication of malaria, regulatory work under Prevention of Food Adulteration
Act, 1954 and Town and Urban Planning have not been transferred to MCC as yet.
In order to make MCC self sustaining body, all functions enlisted under Twelfth
Schedule should be transferred to it by the Administration;
(ii) Budget of MCC comes from the Administration in the form of grant-in-aid which is
determined without any consultation with the MCC. Furthermore, devolution of 17%
budget, as recommended by Second Delhi Finance Commission has not been
communicated to MCC by the Administration. Moreover, 17% of the budget seems to
be inadequate in the face of large scale work to be undertaken by the MCC. Demand
for 23% of tax revenue to the MCC was raised. Even Mayor has not been invited by
the Administrator any time for interaction.

106
(iii) Regularisation of need based violation of building bye-laws as one time measure;
(iv) Issuance of SC Certificate to the genuine Scheduled Caste population of Chandigarh
which has been stopped w.e.f. 1996; and
(v) Increase of tenure of MCC to six years from present five year having two years
term for Mayor on rotation. A resolution has been passed by the MCC to that effect.
10.0. The Comm ittee also called on Administrator to UT of Chandigarh. He appraised the
Committee about new initiatives taken by it for the betterment of the UT.
